REV 7:17.notes: Greek Psalm 22:1–2 (English 23:1–2) describes the Lord shepherding and nourishing the psalmist beside waters of rest. Verse 3 speaks of guidance in righteous paths. Isaiah 49:10 describes guidance by springs. In Revelation the Lamb shepherds the people and leads them to springs of living water. In Greek Isaiah 25:8 God has removed every tear from every face. Revelation promises that God will wipe every tear from their eyes. The promise recurs in 21:4.

REV 6:8.notes: Greek Ezekiel 14:21 lists the four judgments in the accusative: ῥομφαίαν, λιμόν, θηρία πονηρά and θάνατον. Revelation 6:8 moves death before the beasts and uses different constructions in its list. Revelation 18:8 mentions death, grief and famine, then burning. The lists overlap without being identical.

REV 6:10.notes: Imprecatory-‘how-long?’ + avenge-blood lament: (1) DEU 32:43 LXX (‘he-shall-avenge-the-blood-of-his-servants’) — Song-of-Moses justice-promise. (2) PSA 79:10 LXX [PSA 78:10 LXX] (‘avenge-the-shed-blood-of-your-servants’). (3) ZEC 1:12 LXX (the angel asking ‘how long?’ for-Jerusalem-judgment). The martyr-cry-for-justice tradition.

REV 6:12.notes: Greek Joel 3:4 (English 2:31) describes the sun turning dark and the moon to blood. Revelation compares the dark sun with haircloth and the whole moon with blood. Compare also Greek Joel 2:10 and 4:15 (English 3:15) for the darkening of the heavenly lights.

REV 6:13.notes: In Greek Isaiah 34:4 the sky rolls up before the stars fall like leaves from a vine or fig tree. Revelation 6:13 first has stars falling like unripe figs shaken loose by a strong wind. Verse 14 then compares the departing sky to a scroll being rolled up.

REV 6:14.notes: DIRECT CITATION of ISA 34:4 LXX (‘ἑλιγήσεται ὁ οὐρανὸς ὡς βιβλίον’ — ‘the heaven shall be rolled-up as a scroll’). The cosmic-de-creation imagery — heaven-rolled-up-as-scroll. Recurs at HEB 1:12 (citing PSA 102:26 cosmic-rolling-up tradition).

REV 6:16.notes: Greek Hosea 10:8 asks mountains to cover the speakers and hills to fall on them. Luke 23:30 asks mountains to fall and hills to cover. Revelation addresses mountains and rocks together, first asking them to fall and then to hide the speakers from the one on the throne and the wrath of the Lamb.

REV 6:17.notes: ‘Great day of wrath + who can stand?’ cluster: JOEL 2:11 LXX (‘great is the day of the Lord and very-terrible — who shall be able to-bear it?’) + NAH 1:6 LXX (‘who shall stand-against the wrath of his anger?’) + MAL 3:2 LXX (‘who shall endure the day of his coming?’). The OT-Day-of-the-Lord ‘who-can-stand?’ tradition — sets up REV 7's answer (the sealed-144,000 + great-multitude can-stand).

REV 5:1.notes: SBLGNT and NA28 read ὄπισθεν, ‘on the back’. Robinson–Pierpont has ἔξωθεν, ‘outside’. Revelation describes writing inside and on the back. Greek Ezekiel 2:10 puts back before front and names lament, song and woe as the scroll’s contents. The texts share the image of writing on both sides.

REV 5:5.notes: Greek Genesis 49:9 compares Judah to a lion’s cub. Verse 10 says the ruler will remain in Judah until what is reserved for him comes. The wording “Shiloh” in the Hebrew-based reading does not appear as a name in this Greek verse. Revelation names the lion from Judah’s tribe. It also adapts the root of Jesse in Isaiah 11:10 to the root of David. Compare Isaiah 11:1 for the shoot and Revelation 22:16 for David.

REV 5:6.notes: Slain-Lamb-with-seven-horns + seven-eyes draws on (1) ZEC 4:10 LXX (‘seven-eyes-of-the-LORD ranging-throughout-the-earth’) + ZEC 3:9 LXX (‘seven-eyes-on-one-stone’) — divine-omniscience-and-omnipresence. (2) Lamb-of-God Christology corpus-internal-link to JHN 1:29, 36 (Lamb-takes-away-sin-of-the-world). (3) Slain-Lamb echoes ISA 53:7 LXX (‘ὡς ἀρνὸς ἐναντίον τοῦ κείραντος αὐτὸν ἄφωνος’ — like-a-lamb-before-its-shearer dumb). The Lion-Lamb-paradox: announced-as-Lion-of-Judah (v.5), revealed-as-slain-Lamb (v.6) — Revelation's-Christological-key.

REV 5:8.notes: ‘Golden-bowls-of-incense = prayers-of-saints’ echoes PSA 141:2 LXX [PSA 140:2 LXX] (‘κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου’ — ‘let my prayer ascend as incense before You’). The OT-priestly-incense-as-prayer-vehicle is-now-the-prayers-of-saints reaching-the-throne. Cross-reference REV 8:3-4 (golden-altar of-incense-mingled-with-prayers).

REV 5:9.notes: Greek Psalms 32:3, 95:1, 97:1, 143:9 and 149:1 correspond to Psalms 33:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9 and 149:1 in common English numbering. The first three use ᾆσμα for the new song. Greek Psalm 143:9 uses ᾠδή, as does Revelation. The song celebrates the Lamb’s purchase of people from every tribe, language, people and nation.

REV 5:11.notes: Theodotion’s Daniel 7:10 speaks of thousands serving and myriads standing before him. Its verb for service is ἐλειτούργουν with αὐτῷ. Old Greek uses ἐθεράπευον with αὐτόν. Revelation puts the myriads first and uses multiplied genitive expressions. Its description of the angels’ number has no matching service or standing clause.

REV 5:10.notes: This verse coordinates βασιλείαν and ἱερεῖς, kingdom and priests, with καί. Revelation 1:6 uses both nouns without this conjunction between them. Revelation 20:6 calls believers priests and uses a separate verb for their future reign. First Peter 2:9 uses the expression ‘royal priesthood’.

REV 4:8.notes: DIRECT CITATION (with adaptation) of ISA 6:3 LXX (‘ἅγιος ἅγιος ἅγιος κύριος Σαβαώθ’ — Trisagion ‘Holy holy holy Lord of Hosts’). Revelation substitutes ‘ὁ θεός ὁ παντοκράτωρ’ (the standard-LXX rendering of YHWH-Sabaoth) and adds the three-fold-temporal Yahweh-formula (matching 1:4, 8). The Christian-Trisagion liturgical-tradition derives from this verse + ISA 6:3.

REV 4:1.notes: ‘Open door in heaven + Spirit-translation’ echoes EZK 1:1 LXX (‘the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God’) + EZK 8:3 (Spirit-lifts-Ezekiel between-heaven-and-earth) + EZK 11:1 (Spirit-lifts-Ezekiel-to-east-gate). The prophetic-vision-translation idiom. The ‘door-in-heaven’ specific-image is Revelation-distinctive but draws-on-Ezekiel-tradition.

REV 4:2.notes: Heavenly-throne vision-cluster: ISA 6:1 LXX (‘I-saw-the-Lord seated-on-a-throne high-and-lifted-up’) + EZK 1:26 LXX (‘upon-the-throne the-likeness-as-the-appearance-of-a-man’) + DAN 7:9 LXX (Ancient-of-Days throne-vision). The OT-throne-vision tradition converges in Revelation 4.

REV 4:3.notes: In Greek Exodus 28:17–18 sard and emerald appear in the first row of the priestly breastpiece. Jasper appears in the second row. Revelation compares the one on the throne to jasper and sard. The separate comparison to emerald describes the rainbow. Compare the bow-like radiance in Ezekiel 1:28 and the bow in Genesis 9:13–16.

REV 4:6.notes: ‘Sea of glass before the throne’ echoes EZK 1:22 LXX (‘the firmament-like crystal’) + EXO 24:10 LXX (the Sinai-theophany pavement-like-sapphire-stone-clear-as-heaven). Four-living-creatures-with-eyes-around echoes EZK 1:18 + 10:12 LXX (cherubim-wheels-and-bodies-full-of-eyes). The crystalline-pavement = boundary-between-divine-glory-and-creation.

REV 4:7.notes: The allusion adapts Ezekiel 1:10, which gives each living creature four faces, naming human, lion, calf and eagle. Revelation describes four different creatures in succession, with the lion first, the calf second, a human face third, and an eagle in flight fourth. Compare Ezekiel 10:14 for a further description.

REV 3:5.notes: The heavenly register recalls Exodus 32:32–33, Greek Psalm 68:29 (English 69:28), and Daniel 12:1. Matthew 10:32 speaks of acknowledgment before the Father. Luke 12:8 places it before the angels of God. Revelation mentions both the Father and his angels.

REV 3:7.notes: Revelation’s key of David and the acts of opening and shutting correspond closely to Hebrew Isaiah 22:22. The Rahlfs–Hanhart Greek of that verse speaks of the glory of David and authority that no one will oppose. The key and doors in Revelation should therefore be compared with Isaiah by edition.

REV 3:9.notes: Echoes ISA 49:23 + 60:14 LXX (eschatological-bowing-of-the-Gentile-nations + kings-before-Israel-the-elect-people). Per uW: Revelation-INVERTS-the-OT-promise — the Jewish-opponents-who-now-deny-Christ will-eventually-bow-before-the-Christian-church (composed-of-Jews-and-Gentiles together). The ‘they-will-know-I-loved-you’ assurance is Christological-pastoral. Christological-fulfillment-of-the-Isaian-eschatological-vision.

REV 3:19.notes: Greek Proverbs 3:11 speaks of being rebuked. Verse 12 uses ἀγαπάω and παιδεύω of the Lord’s love and discipline. In Revelation the speaker uses φιλέω for love and joins rebuke and discipline in the first person. Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the wording of Proverbs more closely.

REV 2:7.notes: ‘Tree of life in the Paradise of God’ — direct-thematic-allusion to GEN 2:9 LXX (the tree-of-life in-the-garden-of-Eden) + GEN 3:22-24 (humans-driven-from-Eden + cherubim-guarding-the-tree). Per uW: Revelation 2:7 announces the eschatological-restoration of access-to-the-tree-of-life — the eschaton-as-Eden-restored. Recurs at REV 22:2, 14, 19 (corpus-internal protology-eschatology inclusio of-the-Bible). παράδεισος is the LXX-Greek loanword from-Persian-Avestan used to-translate the GEN 2-3 garden.

REV 2:23.notes: Greek Psalm 7:10 (commonly 7:9 in English) has ἐτάζων καρδίας καὶ νεφροὺς, with hearts before kidneys. Greek Jeremiah 17:10 uses a distinct verb for each and relates divine scrutiny to repayment according to conduct. Revelation uses ἐραυνῶν and places kidneys first. The Thai uses ใจและจิตใจ to convey the scrutiny of the inner person.

REV 2:26.notes: ‘Authority over the nations’ direct-thematic-allusion to PSA 2:8 LXX (‘δώσω σοι ἔθνη τὴν κληρονομίαν σου’ — ‘I will give you nations as your inheritance’). The Messianic-Psalm-2 authority-over-nations promise applied to-the-overcomers (sharing-in-Christ's-rule). Sets up v.27 PSA 2:9 direct-citation.

REV 2:27.notes: Greek Psalm 2:9 addresses a ruler in the second person. It names one potter’s vessel and uses an active verb for shattering. Revelation says ‘he will shepherd’ and compares plural earthen vessels being shattered. SBLGNT has present passive συντρίβεται. Robinson–Pierpont has future passive συντριβήσεται. The iron rod and shepherd’s rule recur at 12:5 and 19:15.

REV 1:1.notes: ‘ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει’ (‘what must take place soon’) echoes DAN 2:28-29 LXX (‘what must take place at-the-end-of-days’ ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν — the Nebuchadnezzar-dream-interpretation context). Apocalyptic-framework-marker: Revelation invokes Daniel's-apocalyptic-genre at the very-opening. The shift-from ‘end-of-days’ to ‘soon’ is significant: NT-eschatological-imminence-collapse.

REV 1:4.notes: ‘ὁ ὢν’ (‘the One who is’) — direct-paraphrase of EXO 3:14 LXX divine-self-name (‘ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν’ — ‘I am the One who is’; the Septuagint-rendering of-the-Tetragrammaton-revelation YHWH = HE-IS). Revelation expands this into the three-fold-temporal Yahweh-name (was/is/coming) at-the-formal-blessing position — Trinitarian-greeting-structure’s Father-position. Recurs at vv.4, 8; 4:8.

REV 1:5.notes: Greek Psalm 88:28 (Psalm 89:27 in common English numbering) speaks of making the king the firstborn and exalting him above the kings of the earth. Revelation joins the firstborn from the dead with the ruler of the kings of the earth. Colossians 1:18 independently uses the firstborn-from-the-dead title.

REV 1:10.notes: Trumpet-voice + ‘in the Spirit’ — Sinai-theophany echo (EXO 19:16 LXX trumpet-voice-from-the-mountain + EZK 3:12 LXX Spirit-takes-up-prophet). Apocalyptic-vision-mode established. The κυριακὴ ἡμέρα ‘Lord's Day’ is the earliest-NT-attestation of-Christian-Sunday-as-Lord's-Day (cf. didache 14:1; Ignatius Magn 9:1).

REV 1:12.notes: Seven-golden-lampstands (ἑπτὰ λυχνίας χρυσᾶς) echoes EXO 25:31-40 LXX (the Tabernacle-menorah with its-seven-lamps) + ZEC 4:2 LXX (Zechariah's-vision of-the-lampstand-with-seven-lamps). Ecclesiological-application: the seven-churches as the new-Tabernacle-menorah lighting the world. v.20 explicitly identifies the lampstands = the seven-churches.

REV 1:16.notes: ‘Sword-from-mouth’ (ῥομφαία δίστομος ὀξεῖα) draws on ISA 49:2 LXX (‘he made my mouth like a sharp sword’ — the Servant-of-the-Lord prophetic-witness) + ISA 11:4 LXX (Messianic-judgment by-the-rod-of-his-mouth) + HEB 4:12 (the Word-of-God double-edged-sword corpus-internal-NT-link). Christ's-judgment-by-Word — the Logos-as-eschatological-judge. Recurs at REV 2:12, 16; 19:15, 21.

REV 1:7.notes: Theodotion’s Daniel 7:13 has the figure coming with the clouds (μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν). Old Greek has ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν. Thai พร้อมกับเมฆ follows Revelation’s ‘with’. Greek Zechariah 12:10 has κατωρχήσαντο where the Hebrew speaks of piercing. Revelation and John 19:37 use ἐξεκέντησαν. The mourning in Zechariah 12:10 and the families mourning in 12:12–14 also inform the scene.

REV 1:8.notes: ‘I am the Alpha and Omega’ + ‘who is and was and is-to-come’ + ‘the Almighty’ — divine-self-naming formula echoing ISA 41:4 LXX (‘ἐγὼ θεὸς πρῶτος καὶ εἰς τὰ ἐπερχόμενα ἐγώ εἰμι’) + ISA 44:6 LXX (‘ἐγὼ πρῶτος καὶ ἐγὼ μετὰ ταῦτα’) + ISA 48:12 LXX (‘ἐγώ εἰμι πρῶτος καὶ ἐγώ εἰμι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα’). The Α-Ω formula is the Greek-letter equivalent. Recurs at REV 21:6 + 22:13 (Christological-application of-YHWH-self-name).

REV 1:13.notes: Vision of-Christ-among-lampstands draws on DAN 7:13 (‘like a son of man’) + DAN 10:5 LXX (‘ἀνὴρ εἷς ἐνδεδυμένος βαδδιν’ — man-clothed-in-linen, with-golden-belt) + EZK 9:11 LXX (the man-clothed-in-linen with-the-writing-case-at-loins). The Christological-conflation: Christ-as-Son-of-Man + Daniel's-vision-man + Ezekiel's-priestly-figure. The ποδήρης (long-robe) is LXX-priestly-vestment vocabulary (EXO 28:4, 31; 29:5; 35:9; ZEC 3:5).

REV 1:14.notes: ‘White-hair-like-wool-like-snow’ + ‘eyes-like-flame-of-fire’ — direct-allusion to DAN 7:9 LXX (the Ancient-of-Days: ‘τὸ ἔνδυμα αὐτοῦ ὡς χιὼν λευκόν, καὶ ἡ θρὶξ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ ἔριον καθαρόν’) + DAN 10:6 LXX (the man-of-the-vision: ‘οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ λαμπάδες πυρός’ — eyes-like-flaming-torches). Christological-conflation of-Ancient-of-Days + Daniel-vision-figure attributes — high-Christology divine-attribution.

REV 1:15.notes: Greek Ezekiel 1:24 compares the noise of the creatures’ wings to abundant water. In 43:2 the Greek describes the tumult of a multitude, while the Hebrew and its Thai rendering compare the sound to many waters. Revelation applies the water comparison to the speaker’s voice.

REV 1:17.notes: ‘I am the First and the Last’ — direct-Christological-application of-YHWH-self-name (ISA 41:4 + 44:6 + 48:12 — same cluster as v.8 ‘Alpha and Omega’). The vision-collapse-and-touch echoes DAN 10:9-10 (Daniel-falls-on-face + the-man-touches-him + ‘fear not’). Christ takes-the-role of-the-divine-revealer in-Daniel's-vision.

REV 1:18.notes: ‘Keys-of-Death-and-Hades’ Christological-authority echoes ISA 22:22 LXX (the key-of-the-house-of-David given-to-Eliakim — Messianic-typology) + JOB 38:17 LXX (‘gates-of-death’ + ‘gates-of-Hades’ — divine-knowledge-of-the-realm-of-the-dead). Christ-resurrected = holder-of-the-keys = divine-authority-over-the-realm-of-the-dead. Cross-references: REV 3:7 (key-of-David-explicit); REV 9:1 (key-of-the-abyss); REV 20:1 (key-of-the-abyss + chain-binding-Satan).

JUD 1:23.notes: ‘χιτῶνα ἐσπιλωμένον ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκός’ (‘flesh-stained-tunic’) draws on the Zechariah-3:3-4 ‘filthy-garments’ priestly-defilement vision (Joshua-the-high-priest, the same scene Jude alluded-to-at-v.9 ZEC 3:2 ‘Lord-rebuke-you’) + LEV 13:47-59 priestly-leprous-garment regulations. The ‘snatched-from-fire’ (v.23a) is also-Zechariah (ZEC 3:2 ‘brand-plucked-from-the-fire’). Jude's-Zechariah-3-cluster (v.9 + v.23) frames the false-teachers’ contagion + the believer's-rescue in priestly-defilement vocabulary.

JUD 1:9.notes: ‘Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος’ (‘May the Lord rebuke you’) is a paraphrase-citation of ZEC 3:2 LXX (‘Ἐπιτιμήσαι κύριος ἐν σοί, διάβολε’) — Joshua-the-high-priest scene where Yahweh rebukes Satan. Jude embeds this Zechariah-citation within a reference to the apocryphal ‘Assumption of Moses’ tradition (Michael-disputing-with-Satan-over-Moses-body). The dual-source marks Jude as comfortable citing both canonical-OT (Zechariah) and Jewish-pseudepigraphal-tradition (Assumption of Moses) within the same argument.

JUD 1:11.notes: Three OT-archetypes-of-rebellion: Cain (GEN 4 — fratricidal-jealousy), Balaam (NUM 22-24 — greed-corrupted-prophecy; cf. 2 PET 2:15 corpus-internal-link), Korah (NUM 16 — religious-rebellion against-Moses-and-Aaron). The triad-structure escalates: individual-jealousy → professional-corruption → corporate-religious-rebellion. Each archetype represents a different-flavor of-the-false-teachers’ sin.

JUD 1:14.notes: DIRECT CITATION from 1 Enoch 1:9 (Jewish-pseudepigraphal-text, 3rd-c. BC; not canonical-Scripture in either Jewish or Protestant traditions). The cited-passage matches 1 Enoch 1:9 closely (Greek-recension): ‘ἰδοὺ ἦλθεν σὺν ταῖς μυριάσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ ποιῆσαι κρίσιν...’ Per uW + scholarly-consensus: Jude's citation does NOT entail canonical-status of 1 Enoch (similar-pattern: Pauline-Aratus-citation at ACT 17:28 + Pauline-Epimenides-citation at TIT 1:12). Jude treats 1 Enoch 1:9 as containing a true-prophecy preserved in Jewish-tradition that authentically-attributes-to-Enoch; the prophecy-content is consonant with canonical-eschatological-judgment-tradition. Ethiopic Orthodox Tewahedo Church canonizes 1 Enoch but Protestant tradition does not. Jude's-engagement-with-pseudepigrapha is the strongest NT-instance.

JUD 1:7.notes: Sodom-Gomorrah eternal-fire-judgment paradigm (corpus-internal-link to 2 PET 2:6 + LUK 17:29 + ROM 9:29 — same OT-source). The ‘strange-flesh’ pursuit (σαρκὸς ἑτέρας) interprets-Genesis-19 with-1-Enoch-Watcher-tradition (angelic-human boundary-violation; Jude 6 immediately-precedes establishes the angel-fall context).

JUD 1:6.notes: Jude describes angels who did not keep their position and whom God has kept for judgment. The repetition involves τηρέω. Thai รักษา and ทรงล่ามไว้ convey the two actions with different verbs. Jude has ‘eternal bonds under darkness.’ Second Peter 2:4 also describes darkness and custody for judgment, with a different construction.

JUD 1:5.notes: Exodus-deliverance + wilderness-destruction-of-unbelievers (the EXO 12 + NUM 14 story-cluster). Jude's TEXTUAL VARIANT ‘Ἰησοῦς’ (SBLGNT) vs ‘κύριος’ (Byzantine) points to a distinctive-Christological-pre-existence reading: the One-who-led-Israel-out-of-Egypt = the pre-incarnate-Christ. Cross-reference to 1 COR 10:4 ‘the rock was Christ’ — same Christological-Exodus-reading-tradition (corpus-internal-link). modern critical-text consensus + scholarly-evangelical-position favors Ἰησοῦς.

1JN 3:12.notes: Direct-thematic-allusion to GEN 4:8 LXX (Cain killing Abel — the paradigmatic-fratricide). Per uW figs-explicit: ‘slay’ here uses σφάζω (rare for Genesis-fratricide; the LXX uses ἀνέστη ... ἀπέκτεινεν). The rationale (‘his-deeds-were-evil + brother's-righteous’) glosses GEN 4:5-7 (‘not-well-doing → sin-crouching-at-the-door’). Cain-as-archetype-murderer-from-jealousy of righteous-brother. Echoes JHN 8:44 (devil = murderer-from-the-beginning) + HEB 11:4 (Abel's righteous-blood-still-speaks) — corpus-internal-link.

1JN 2:16.notes: The famous three-fold-worldliness diagnosis (ἐπιθυμία τῆς σαρκὸς + ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν + ἀλαζονεία τοῦ βίου) echoes the GEN 3:6 LXX paradigm: ‘εἶδεν ἡ γυνὴ ὅτι καλὸν τὸ ξύλον εἰς βρῶσιν’ (good-for-food = flesh-desire) + ‘ὅτι ἀρεστὸν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἰδεῖν’ (delight-to-the-eyes = eye-desire) + ‘καὶ ὡραῖόν ἐστιν τοῦ κατανοῆσαι’ (desirable-to-make-wise = pride-of-life). Not a verbatim citation, but the three-fold-temptation pattern is widely identified by patristic + modern commentators (Augustine, Calvin, Brown, Schnackenburg) as a deliberate-Genesis-fall typology applied to ongoing Christian-temptation. The pattern also surfaces in Christ's-three-temptations (LUK 4:1-13 + MAT 4:1-11).

1JN 1:9.notes: Confession-and-cleansing pattern echoes the Davidic-penitential tradition: PSA 32:5 LXX ‘ἐξωμολογησάμην ... καὶ σὺ ἀφῆκας τὴν ἀσέβειαν’ (‘I confessed ... and you forgave the iniquity’) + PSA 51:2 LXX (PSA 50:4 LXX) ‘ἐπὶ πλεῖον πλῦνόν με ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνομίας μου καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας μου καθάρισόν με’ (‘wash me thoroughly from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin’). The lemmas ὁμολογέω + ἀφίημι + καθαρίζω + ἁμαρτία + ἀδικία cluster all map to the same OT-penitential tradition. NOT a verbatim citation; the Davidic-confession-and-cleansing typology is a thematic-tradition-stream that John applies to ongoing-Christian-fellowship-restoration.

2PE 3:5.notes: Echoes the GEN 1:6-9 LXX water-creation cosmology (heavens-and-earth formed from + by waters, by God's word). The deliberate-overlooking-by-the-scoffers is willful-rejection of the foundational-Genesis cosmology that Peter then leverages (creation-by-water + flood-judgment-by-water + future-judgment-by-fire). Petrine-distinctive use of LXX-Genesis-1 cosmology to argue for Day-of-the-Lord credibility.

2PE 3:6.notes: ‘THROUGH THESE the world of that time perished by water’ — direct-thematic-allusion to GEN 7:11-24 (Noah-flood). Cross-reference to 2 PET 2:5 (Petrine-corpus-internal flood-reference) + 1 PET 3:20 (Petrine-corpus flood-typology). The flood-as-precedent for the coming fire-judgment (vv.7, 10-12).

2PE 3:8.notes: Cited proverb-form of PSA 90:4 LXX (PSA 89:4 LXX: ‘χίλια ἔτη ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς σου ὡς ἡμέρα ἡ ἐχθὲς ἥτις διῆλθεν’ — ‘a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday-day that has-passed’). Peter inverts the formula bidirectionally (one-day-as-thousand-years AND thousand-years-as-one-day) for cosmological-time-relativity in answer to the scoffers' ‘where-is-the-promise’ challenge. The Petrine inversion is interpretive — God's eternity-perspective relativizes both human-time-shortness and apparent-divine-delay. This is the foundational-NT proof-text for divine-eternity-relativity. Some rabbinic-traditions (e.g. Pirke Avot, b.Sanh) develop similar millennial-day cosmologies, suggesting Peter draws from a shared Jewish-eschatological tradition.

2PE 3:13.notes: ‘NEW HEAVENS AND NEW EARTH’ (καινοὺς ... οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν καινήν) is direct-lexical-allusion to ISA 65:17 LXX (ἔσται γὰρ ὁ οὐρανὸς καινὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ καινή — ‘for there shall be the new-heaven and the new-earth’) + ISA 66:22 LXX (the new-heavens-and-new-earth promised-in-the-eschaton). The eschatological-renewal hope is the OT-prophetic background for both 2 PET 3:13 and REV 21:1 (‘εἶδον οὐρανὸν καινὸν καὶ γῆν καινήν’ — corpus-internal-link to the Apocalyptic-vision).

2PE 3:10.notes: ‘THE DAY OF THE LORD WILL COME LIKE A THIEF’ (ἥξει δὲ ἡμέρα κυρίου ὡς κλέπτης) is the Synoptic-NT pattern shared with MAT 24:43 (‘ποίᾳ ὥρᾳ ὁ κλέπτης ἔρχεται’ — ‘what-hour the-thief comes’ — Christ's parable), 1 TH 5:2 (‘ἡμέρα κυρίου ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ’ — Pauline-eschatological), REV 3:3 + 16:15 (Christ-warning-Sardis + the-blessing-of-watching). The thief-typology is a NT-cluster eschatological-image with no direct OT-source; it is the apostolic-Christological-development of the OT Day-of-the-Lord formula (AMO 5:18-20 + JOEL 2:1-2 + ZEPH 1:7-18). Peter applies it to support the believer's-vigilance ethic against the scoffers' uniformitarian-skepticism.

2PE 3:12.notes: ‘THE ELEMENTS WILL MELT’ (στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα τήκεται) echoes ISA 34:4 LXX (‘τακήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν’ — ‘all the powers of the heavens shall melt’). The HAPAX τήκομαι matches the LXX-Isaiah verb. Peter's heavens-burned + elements-melted imagery draws on this OT-eschatological source. Cross-reference to MIC 1:4 LXX (mountains-melting under YHWH's coming) + the broader prophetic-cosmic-melting tradition.

2PE 2:22.notes: DIRECT CITATION-PAIR of two proverbs. (1) ‘κύων ἐπιστρέψας ἐπὶ τὸ ἴδιον ἐξέραμα’ (‘a dog returns to its own vomit’) is a paraphrase of PROV 26:11 LXX (ὥσπερ κύων ὅταν ἐπέλθῃ ἐπὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἔμετον — ‘like a dog when it comes upon its own vomit’). The LXX uses ἔμετος; Peter uses ἐξέραμα (HAPAX). The shift may be Petrine-stylistic or follow a wisdom-tradition variant. (2) ‘Ὗς λουσαμένη εἰς κυλισμὸν βορβόρου’ (‘a sow that has been washed returns to wallowing-in-the-mud’) is NOT in the OT. Most-likely-source: Aramaic Ahiqar 8:18 (‘the sow goes back to wallowing-in-the-mud’) — a Jewish-Mesopotamian wisdom-tradition document. Some scholars also see analogues in Heraclitus fragments. Peter cites both as ‘the true proverb’ — identifying them as proverbial-truth without specifying source. The two unclean-animals (dog + pig — both ritually-unclean per Mosaic-law) are paired to depict apostates returning-to-uncleanness. The citation pattern is one-canonical-OT + one-Jewish-wisdom-tradition; mainstream-evangelical-translation practice puts both in quotes as proverbial-citations.

2PE 1:19.notes: ‘THE MORNING STAR RISES’ (φωσφόρος ἀνατείλῃ) draws on the OT-Messianic morning-star tradition: NUM 24:17 LXX (Balaam's prophecy: ‘ἀνατελεῖ ἄστρον ἐξ Ιακωβ’ — ‘a star shall rise out of Jacob,’ canonical-Messianic-prophecy). The φωσφόρος Christological title is sealed at REV 22:16 (Christ-self-identification: ‘ἐγὼ ... ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς ὁ πρωϊνός’ — the bright morning-star). The verb ἀνατέλλω matches both NUM 24:17 LXX and the dawn-imagery. Peter's ‘rises in your hearts’ moves the messianic-fulfillment from cosmic-event to interior-illumination, anticipating the eschatological-day-of-the-Lord (cf. 2 PET 3:10) while applying the partial-fulfillment now to believers' hearts. Some scholars see additional MAL 4:2 LXX echo (‘ἀνατελεῖ ὑμῖν τοῖς φοβουμένοις τὸ ὄνομά μου ἥλιος δικαιοσύνης’ — sun-of-righteousness rising).

1PE 3:6.notes: Sarah-calling-Abraham-‘lord’ alludes to GEN 18:12 LXX (Sarah’s internal monologue at the Mamre-visitation: ὁ δὲ κύριός μου πρεσβύτερος — ‘my lord is older’). Peter cites this as exemplar of OT-holy-women’s submissive-trust. The κύριος here is the human-marital sense (‘master/husband’), not divine. Render preserves the contextual-distinction by using ‘นาย’ rather than the divine-‘องค์พระผู้เป็นเจ้า.’

1PE 3:10.notes: Direct citation of Psalm 33:13–17 in Rahlfs (Hebrew 34:13–17; common English numbering 34:12–16). The citation runs vv.10-12 of 1 PET 3 — covering ‘who-loves-life-and-sees-good-days’ + ‘keep-tongue-from-evil’ + ‘turn-from-evil-do-good’ + ‘seek-peace’ + ‘eyes-of-Lord-on-righteous’ + ‘face-of-Lord-against-evildoers.’ Peter cites Davidic-righteousness-blessing-formula as the rationale-for-non-retaliation in the Christian community.

1PE 3:11.notes: Continued Rahlfs Psalm 33:13–17 citation that began at v.10. v.11 specifically cites (in common English numbering) PSA 34:14 (turn-from-evil-do-good + seek-peace-pursue-it). DB entry combined with v.10.

1PE 3:12.notes: Closes the Rahlfs Psalm 33:13–17 citation that began at v.10. v.12 specifically cites (in common English numbering) PSA 34:15-16 (eyes-of-Lord-on-righteous + face-of-Lord-against-evildoers). DB entry combined with v.10.

1PE 3:22.notes: ἐν δεξιᾷ θεοῦ (‘at the right hand of God’) alludes to PSA 110:1 LXX (κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου — ‘sit at my right hand’). The most-cited OT-verse in NT (cf. MAT 22:44; MAR 12:36; LUK 20:42; ACT 2:34-35; HEB 1:13). The cosmic-powers-subjected language at the verse’s end echoes PSA 8:6 thematically (cf. EPH 1:20-22 + 1 COR 15:25-27 same combination).

1PE 3:14.notes: Citation of ISA 8:12-13 LXX (τὸν δὲ φόβον αὐτοῦ οὐ μὴ φοβηθῆτε οὐδὲ μὴ ταραχθῆτε — ‘do-not-fear-what-they-fear, do-not-be-shaken’). Same OT-context as ISA 8:14 cited at 1 PET 2:8 — Petrine fondness for Isaiah 8 cluster. v.15’s κύριον τὸν Χριστὸν ἁγιάσατε also continues from ISA 8:13 (‘κύριον αὐτὸν ἁγιάσατε’) — Petrine Christological-rereading of Isaiah 8 Yahweh-text applied to Christ.

1PE 3:20.notes: Allusion to the Genesis flood-narrative (GEN 6-8). Specific elements: (1) ‘days of Noah’ when ark was being built; (2) ‘eight souls’ matches GEN 7:13 family-of-Noah (Noah + wife + 3 sons + 3 daughters-in-law); (3) ‘saved through water’ sets up the v.21 baptism-typology. Same Noah-flood referenced thematically at 2 PET 2:5 + MAT 24:37-38 + LUK 17:26-27 + HEB 11:7.

1PE 2:12.notes: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπισκοπῆς (‘day of visitation’) echoes the OT-Hebrew יום פקודה idiom for divine-judgment-day. ISA 10:3 LXX has ‘τί ποιήσετε ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς?’ (‘what will you do in the day of visitation?’) — closest LXX-parallel to Peter’s phrase. Same idiom in JER 6:15, 10:15, 50:27 LXX + LUK 19:44 (Jesus’s lament over Jerusalem). Thematic dependence on the OT-prophetic visitation-day register; not direct citation.

1PE 2:21.notes: Anticipates the v.22-25 ISA 53 Servant-Song citation cluster. ‘Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example’ frames Christ-as-Suffering-Servant pattern that Peter then unpacks via direct ISA 53:9 citation (v.22), composite ISA 53:4-5+11-12 allusion (v.24), and ISA 53:6 allusion (v.25). The vocational-call-to-suffer-like-Christ language presupposes the entire Servant-Song theology.

1PE 2:23.notes: λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει + πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει echoes ISA 53:7 LXX (‘like a sheep led to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so He opens not His mouth’) — the silent-suffering-servant pattern. Same OT-text directly cited at ACT 8:32-33. Thematic dependence on the silent-non-retaliation Servant-pattern; not direct quotation but conceptual-anchor for the v.21-25 Christ-as-paradigm passage.

1PE 2:22.notes: Direct citation of ISA 53:9 LXX (ἀνομίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ — Peter substitutes ἁμαρτίαν for ἀνομίαν but otherwise verbatim). Christ-as-Suffering-Servant fulfillment. Anchors the v.21-25 Christ-as-paradigm-of-unjust-suffering passage in Isaiah’s Servant-Song.

1PE 2:24.notes: Greek Isaiah 53:5 has τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν (‘by his wound we were healed’). Peter has οὗ τῷ μώλωπι ἰάθητε. The second-person ending in ἰάθητε addresses the readers directly. No independent ὑμεῖς is present. The earlier language of bearing sins also recalls Isaiah 53:4, 11–12. The use of ξύλον for the cross can be compared with Deuteronomy 21:23.

1PE 2:25.notes: Allusion to ISA 53:6 LXX (πάντες ὡς πρόβατα ἐπλανήθημεν — ‘all-of-us-like-sheep-have-strayed’). Closes the Servant-Song echoes (ISA 53:5, 53:9, 53:11-12 already cited at 1 PET 2:22, 24) with the sheep-straying motif. The shepherd-and-overseer Christological-titles applied to Christ as the gathering-point for the once-straying sheep — possibly echoing EZK 34:11-16 + ISA 40:11 shepherd-imagery.

1PE 1:13.notes: ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν alludes to the OT-Passover-readiness imagery at EXO 12:11 LXX (αἱ ὀσφύες ὑμῶν περιεζωσμέναι ‘your loins shall be girded’) — Israel was to eat the Passover with loins-girded, ready-for-departure-from-Egypt. Peter applies the imagery metaphorically to the believer’s mind: prepared-for-action / sober-and-alert. Same Hebraic-idiom of girding-loins-for-action also at LUK 12:35 (Jesus’s parable of girded-servants) + EPH 6:14 (girded-with-truth). Thematic dependence.

1PE 1:16.notes: Both clauses match the wording in Rahlfs Leviticus 19:2 (ἅγιοι ἔσεσθε ὅτι ἐγὼ ἅγιος). Leviticus 11:44, 11:45 and 20:7 offer related formulations. Anchors the be-holy ethic in the Sinai-covenant holiness-code. Same theme cited thematically in MAT 5:48 (be-perfect-as-Father-is-perfect) + 2 COR 7:1 + HEB 12:14.

1PE 1:19.notes: Peter has ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου, a lamb without blemish or spot. Greek Exodus 12:5 has πρόβατον τέλειον, while Leviticus 22:20–21 describes the condition of an acceptable offering. Isaiah 53:7 compares the servant to a sheep going to slaughter and a lamb before its shearer. These are related sacrificial images.

1PE 1:24.notes: Peter quotes Rahlfs Isaiah 40:6–7 with two differences in the first line: he adds ὡς before χόρτος and uses αὐτῆς for ἀνθρώπου. The wording quoted from 40:7 matches. James 1:10–11 echoes the flower imagery. The citation continues at v.25 with Isa 40:8 (‘word-of-Lord endures forever’).

1PE 1:25.notes: Direct citation of ISA 40:8 LXX (τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα — Peter substitutes κυρίου for τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν). Continues the v.24 ISA 40:6-7 citation — together vv.24-25 form a contiguous-citation of ISA 40:6-8. The Petrine application: the OT-eternal-word IS the gospel-proclaimed-to-you (v.25b interpretation). Same word-of-the-Lord-endures-forever theme echoed thematically at MAT 24:35 / MAR 13:31 / LUK 21:33.

JAS 5:1.notes: James tells the rich to weep (κλαύσατε), wailing (ὀλολύζοντες) over coming misery. The prophetic allusion has several points of comparison. Greek Isaiah 13:6 and Zechariah 11:2 call for wailing. Greek Joel 1:5 calls for weeping and lamenting but does not use the wailing verb found in James.

JAS 5:6.notes: οὐκ ἀντιτάσσεται ὑμῖν (the righteous-one does-not-resist) echoes ISA 53:7 LXX (καὶ αὐτὸς διὰ τὸ κεκακῶσθαι οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα ‘he-was-afflicted-but-opened-not-his-mouth’) — Suffering-Servant tradition. The non-resistance + condemnation + killing + righteous combination has Christological-overtones (cf. ACT 8:32-33 directly cites this Isaiah passage of Christ’s passion). James may also be alluding to general persecution-of-righteous tradition (cf. WIS 2:10-20 LXX similar pattern). Thematic dependence; not direct quotation.

JAS 5:4.notes: The allusion to Greek Isaiah 5:9 shares the phrase εἰς τὰ ὦτα κυρίου σαβαωθ. James applies it to the harvesters’ cries. Deuteronomy 24:14–15 connects failure to pay wages with a worker crying to the Lord. Leviticus 19:13 and Malachi 3:5 also address withheld wages. James uses จอมโยธา for the title, while Romans 9:29 uses จอมทัพ. SBLGNT reads ἀφυστερημένος for the withheld pay, NA28 and RP ἀπεστερημένος.

JAS 5:5.notes: Jeremiah 12:3 speaks of a day of slaughter. The other allusion is to Jeremiah 25:34 in Hebrew numbering, 32:34 in Rahlfs–Hanhart Greek: the days for slaughter have come and the shepherds will fall like choice rams. James addresses people who have fed their own hearts in a day of slaughter. บำรุงเลี้ยงใจ paired with วันแห่งการประหาร conveys the irony of indulgence in the face of judgment. RP adds ὡς (“as”) before the day phrase.

JAS 5:11.notes: The allusion to Job highlights endurance and what the Lord brought about. ผลที่องค์พระผู้เป็นเจ้าทรงให้ reads τέλος as outcome. Another possible sense is purpose. Greek Exodus 34:6 and Psalm 102:8 (Hebrew and English 103:8) pair οἰκτίρμων and ἐλεήμων. James shares οἰκτίρμων but pairs it with πολύσπλαγχνος.

JAS 5:17.notes: The allusion draws on Elijah’s drought prediction in 1 Kings 17:1 and the return of rain in 18:41–45. First Kings 18:1 locates the word to Elijah in the third year. James and Luke 4:25 explicitly give three years and six months. James emphasizes Elijah’s prayer. In 1 Kings 18:43 seven refers to the servant being sent back to look toward the sea. Kings supplies no count of Elijah’s prayers.

JAS 5:18.notes: The allusion draws on Elijah’s drought prediction in 1 Kings 17:1 and the return of rain in 18:41–45. First Kings 18:1 locates the word to Elijah in the third year. James and Luke 4:25 explicitly give three years and six months. James emphasizes Elijah’s prayer. In 1 Kings 18:43 seven refers to the servant being sent back to look toward the sea. Kings supplies no count of Elijah’s prayers.

JAS 5:20.notes: The allusion evokes Hebrew Proverbs 10:12, where love covers offenses. Greek Proverbs has friendship covering people who do not quarrel. First Peter 4:8 uses love as the subject of covering a multitude of sins. James uses the same object, πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, with the future καλύψει and no explicit mention of love. In this context of returning a sinner, covering can be understood in relation to forgiveness.

JAS 4:6.notes: Direct citation of PROV 3:34 LXX (κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσιν χάριν), with κύριος replaced by ὁ θεός. Same verse cited at 1 PET 5:5 (also with the same κύριος → θεός substitution — possible early-Christian-tradition shared between James + Peter, or independent-citation of the LXX-text from the Christian-version that already had the substitution). The proverb anchors James 4:7-10 imperative-cluster: humility-receives-grace, pride-is-opposed.

JAS 3:9.notes: καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν θεοῦ γεγονότας echoes the imago-Dei language of GEN 1:26-27 LXX (κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν). The Greek ὁμοίωσις (only here NT) is the same word LXX-Genesis uses for the divine-likeness component. James’s argument: cursing-fellow-humans = cursing-the-divine-image-they-bear, making the bless-and-curse-with-same-tongue paradox theologically devastating. Same imago-Dei thread at GEN 5:1, 9:6, 1 COR 11:7, COL 3:10.

JAS 1:27.notes: James uses ἐπισκέπτεσθαι for attending to orphans and widows in distress, rendered ดูแล, and joins it with keeping oneself unstained. The allusion reflects a wider scriptural concern. Exodus 22:21 in Hebrew and Greek numbering (English 22:22) forbids mistreating widows and orphans. Deuteronomy 10:18 describes God doing justice for them, 24:17–21 provides legal and gleaning protections, and Isaiah 1:17 urges people to seek justice on their behalf.

ACT 10:12.notes: CLEAN/UNCLEAN CREATURE CATEGORIES (τετράποδα + ἑρπετὰ + πετεινὰ) in Peter's vision mirror the LXX Leviticus 11 threefold-classification: quadrupeds vv.2-8 (split-hoof + cud-chewing = clean), swarming-creatures vv.29-31, 41-45 (reptiles mostly unclean), birds vv.13-19 (specific not-to-eat list). Peter's refusal at v.14 ('never eaten anything common/unclean') invokes this Mosaic-distinction explicitly. The divine voice's 'what God has cleansed' (v.15) overrides the Levitical classification — establishing God's sovereign-authority to redefine clean/unclean in the new-covenant era (anticipated by Mark 7:19 'cleansing all foods'). DEU 14:3-21 parallel.

ACT 10:34.notes: Job 3:1 uses opening the mouth to introduce speech. Genesis 22:11 describes the angel calling to Abraham without that expression. In Deuteronomy 10:17–19 God shows no partiality, upholds the vulnerable and loves the resident foreigner. Peter applies that scriptural principle to people of every nation.

ACT 10:36.notes: PREACH PEACE formula εὐαγγελιζόμενος εἰρήνην — the specific combination of εὐαγγελίζω + εἰρήνη is Isaianic-Nahum-lexical. ISA 52:7 LXX 'ὡς πόδες εὐαγγελιζομένου ἀκοὴν εἰρήνης' (feet-of-the-one-announcing-peace); NAH 1:15 LXX (MT 2:1) 'ἰδοὺ ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη πόδες εὐαγγελιζομένου καὶ ἀπαγγέλλοντος εἰρήνην.' Both texts envision a herald announcing salvation-after-exile. Peter applies the Isaianic-feet-of-the-messenger image to the apostolic-gospel-proclamation — and implicitly to himself as such a feet-of-messenger reaching Caesarea. Paul also cites ISA 52:7 at ROM 10:15. PSA 147:14 LXX 'ὁ τιθεὶς τὰ ὅρια σου εἰρήνην' secondary-resonance.

ACT 10:38.notes: SPIRIT-ANOINTING formula ἔχρισεν αὐτὸν ὁ θεὸς πνεύματι ἁγίῳ — direct lexical echo of ISA 61:1 LXX 'Πνεῦμα κυρίου ἐπ’ ἐμέ, οὗ εἵνεκεν ἔχρισέν με εὐαγγελίσασθαι πτωχοῖς.' The χρίω + πνεῦμα combination is Isaianic-Servant-anointing vocabulary. Jesus himself read this passage in the Nazareth synagogue and claimed fulfillment (LUK 4:18-21). Peter's kerygma makes Jesus's entire ministry (εὐεργετῶν καὶ ἰώμενος 'doing-good and healing') the fulfillment of the Isaianic-anointed-servant mission. The καὶ δυνάμει addition ('and power') echoes LUK 1:35 Gabriel-to-Mary 'δύναμις ὑψίστου ἐπισκιάσει σοι' and LUK 4:14 'ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ πνεύματος'.

ACT 10:39.notes: HANGING ON A TREE (κρεμάσαντες ἐπὶ ξύλου) — formulaic echo of DEU 21:22-23 LXX 'κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ θεοῦ πᾶς κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου' (cursed-by-God is everyone hanging on a tree). The apostolic preaching deliberately uses Deuteronomy-language to frame Jesus's death within the cursed-tree category — a paradox that Galatians 3:13 will unpack ('Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us, as it is written, Cursed is everyone hanging on a tree'). Peter's sermonic formula 'killed by hanging on a tree' recurs at ACT 5:30, 10:39, 13:29 — consistent primitive-apostolic framing that Paul inherits and theologizes. 1 PET 2:24 'ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον' continues the pattern.

ACT 10:4.notes: Leviticus uses μνημόσυνον for the memorial portion of a grain offering, including Greek Leviticus 6:8 (English 6:15). Acts 10:4 compares the prayers and gifts to the poor with a memorial before God. In 10:31 Cornelius is told that God heard his prayer and remembered his gifts. The account does not establish whether he could offer a sacrifice or equate his giving with a particular sacrifice.

ACT 10:42.notes: In verse 39 μάρτυρες is the noun “witnesses.” Verse 42 has the infinitive διαμαρτύρασθαι for bearing solemn witness. Greek Psalm 95:13 (English 96:13) speaks of judging the world. Daniel 7:13–14 describes receiving dominion after the courtroom scene in 7:9–10. Neither parallel supplies the exact title “judge of the living and the dead.”

ACT 10:43.notes: Peter speaks collectively of the prophets bearing witness that believers receive forgiveness through Jesus’ name. He does not list passages here. Jeremiah 31:34 promises that God will no longer remember sin. Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9 provide other thematic comparisons rather than a list given by Peter.

ACT 10:45.notes: The pouring out of the Spirit recalls Joel 3:1–2 in Greek and Hebrew numbering (English Joel 2:28–29), quoted in Acts 2:17–18. Acts 10:45 uses a form of the same verb in a new sentence to describe the gift given to the Gentiles.

ACT 11:15.notes: PETER RE-NARRATING SPIRIT-OUTPOURING: ἐπέπεσεν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς ὥσπερ καὶ ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς ἐν ἀρχῇ — Peter's retrospective-interpretation of the Cornelius-Spirit-event EXPLICITLY pairs it with 'the-beginning' = Pentecost (ACT 2:1-4) where Peter had cited JOEL 2:28-29 as the interpretive-frame. The Joel-prophecy's πᾶσαν σάρκα (all-flesh) scope is the theological-bridge Peter here appeals to — the same Joel-outpouring now extends to Gentile-flesh. Parallels ACT 2:17 direct-citation + ACT 10:45 ἐκκέχυται echo.

ACT 11:16.notes: Peter recalls Jesus’ promise in Acts 1:5. The gift of the Spirit also recalls Joel 2:28 through Peter’s Pentecost speech. The words about baptism here come from Jesus’ saying.

ACT 11:6.notes: PETER RE-NARRATING VISION: the four-category list (τετράποδα + θηρία + ἑρπετὰ + πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) expands ACT 10:12's threefold list with θηρία 'wild beasts' added as a distinct group — Peter's first-person retelling more-vividly invokes the LXX Leviticus 11 clean/unclean creature categories (quadrupeds vv.2-8, swarming-creatures vv.29-31, 41-45, birds vv.13-19). Same Mosaic-distinction that Peter will cite as his refusal-ground at v.8. Parallel DEU 14:3-21. See ACT 10:12 DB entry for primary treatment.

ACT 12:11.notes: PETER'S ANGELIC-DELIVERANCE ACKNOWLEDGMENT: 'Νῦν οἶδα ἀληθῶς ὅτι ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ κύριος τὸν ἄγγελον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐξείλατό με' shares close vocabulary and narrative-structure with (a) PSA 34:7 LXX (παρεμβαλεῖ ἄγγελος κυρίου κύκλῳ τῶν φοβουμένων αὐτὸν καὶ ῥύσεται αὐτούς — 'the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them'); and (b) DAN 6:22 LXX/Th (ὁ θεός μου ἀπέστειλεν τὸν ἄγγελον αὐτοῦ — 'my God sent his angel' — Daniel rescued from lions' den by royal decree-execution, structural parallel to Peter rescued from Herod's execution). Peter's phrasing patterns the psalmist's and Daniel's angelic-rescue-from-royal-execution typology onto his own deliverance. Lukan-Acts motif: God's angel as deliverer-agent (ACT 5:19 previous Peter-rescue; ACT 27:23 Paul on ship).

ACT 12:23.notes: DIVINE-JUDGMENT ON ROYAL SELF-DEIFICATION: 'ἀνθ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔδωκεν τὴν δόξαν τῷ θεῷ' inverts ISA 42:8 LXX (Ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεός, τοῦτό μού ἐστιν τὸ ὄνομα, τὴν δόξαν μου ἑτέρῳ οὐ δώσω — 'I am YHWH my God, this is my name; my glory I will not give to another'). Herod received/accepted-without-returning the glory-that-belongs-only-to-God. Also structural-narrative parallel DAN 4:30-37 (Nebuchadnezzar's royal-boast 'Is not this great Babylon that I have built...' → immediate heavenly-voice-judgment → humiliation-until-he-acknowledges-God-rules). Same pattern in ACT 12: royal public-acclamation (v.21-22) → immediate divine-strike (v.23) → death as judgment-for-glory-stealing. ἐξέψυξεν (v.23) clusters lexically with ACT 5:5 Ananias + ACT 5:10 Sapphira — Luke's signature judgment-death verb for lying-against-or-stealing-glory-from-God. The σκωληκόβρωτος 'worm-eaten' motif has apocryphal parallel 2 Macc 9:9 (Antiochus IV Epiphanes); Luke's Greco-Jewish readership would recognize the tyrant-eaten-by-worms topos as judgment-on-self-deifying-rulers.

ACT 12:24.notes: GOSPEL-WORD AS CREATION-BLESSING-FULFILLMENT: 'ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν καὶ ἐπληθύνετο' uses the LXX creation-blessing verb-pair αὐξάνω + πληθύνω, which appears in Gen 1:22, 1:28, 8:17, 9:1, 9:7, 17:20, 35:11, 48:4 (αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε). The blessing originally applied to animal/human procreation is here applied to the λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ as the creational-force Luke sees operating in the post-Pentecost age. Luke-transitional-summary formula (same verb-pair pattern: ACT 6:7 'ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν', ACT 19:20 'οὕτως κατὰ κράτος τοῦ κυρίου ὁ λόγος ηὔξανεν'; thematic 9:31, 16:5). Theological-narrative juxtaposition with v.23: Herod's-claim-to-glory dies; God's-word-true-glory grows. Creation-blessing-continuity implicit: the divine intent of Gen 1:28 ('be fruitful and multiply') is fulfilled through gospel-word reaching all-flesh (echoing Peter-on-Joel at ACT 2:17 and ACT 11:15-18).

ACT 13:10.notes: Greek Hosea 14:10 (English 14:9) describes the Lord’s ways as straight. Greek Proverbs 10:9 has διαστρέφων τὰς ὁδοὺς αὐτοῦ, a person twisting his own ways. Both passages offer parallels for Paul’s rebuke. John 8:44 also uses the image of the devil as father. The verse does not identify the listeners there as Pharisees.

ACT 13:17.notes: Composite allusion: μετὰ βραχίονος ὑψηλοῦ ἐξήγαγεν αὐτοὺς 'with an uplifted arm he led them out' echoes LXX EXO 6:6 (ἐν βραχίονι ὑψηλῷ) + DEU 5:15 + PSA 136:12 (LXX 135:12) — the formulaic uplifted-arm-from-Egypt divine-power language. Also τὸν λαὸν ὕψωσεν 'made the people great' alludes to EXO 1:7, 12, 20 (Israel-multiplied-in-Egypt). Paul begins his Pisidian-Antioch sermon with the standard synagogue-homily pattern of Israel-historical-review.

ACT 13:18.notes: SBLGNT prints ἐτροποφόρησεν, which the Thai renders as putting up with their conduct. The variant ἐτροφοφόρησεν describes caring for them. In the Rahlfs 1935 Greek text of Deuteronomy 1:31, ἐτροφοφόρησέν σε depicts God carrying the people as a parent carries a son.

ACT 13:19.notes: καθελὼν ἔθνη ἑπτά ἐν γῇ Χανάαν alludes to LXX DEU 7:1 (seven nations Israel was to dispossess — Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites). κατεκληρονόμησεν τὴν γῆν αὐτῶν alludes to LXX JOS 14 (land-inheritance distribution). The hapax κατακληρονομέω ('give as inheritance') is a deliberately Septuagintal verb.

ACT 13:21.notes: ᾐτήσαντο βασιλέα 'asked for a king' alludes to 1SA 8:5, 19 — the people's-request-for-a-king episode. ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς τὸν Σαοὺλ υἱὸν Κίς alludes to 1SA 9:1-2 (Saul son of Kish from Benjamin). The 40-year regnal-figure for Saul is not explicit in MT but matches Josephus Ant. 6.378. Paul's attention to Benjamin-tribe origin is possibly self-referential (Phil 3:5).

ACT 13:22.notes: Greek Psalm 88:21 (English 89:20) begins εὗρον Δαυιδ, “I found David.” Greek 1 Samuel 13:14 uses ζητήσει, “the Lord will seek,” and describes a man after his heart. Acts combines these expressions. The final words about carrying out all God’s purposes also recall Greek Isaiah 44:28, where the verb follows πάντα τὰ θελήματά μου and the passage concerns Cyrus.

ACT 13:23.notes: τούτου ὁ θεὸς ἀπὸ τοῦ σπέρματος κατ’ἐπαγγελίαν ἤγαγεν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ σωτῆρα Ἰησοῦν alludes to 2SA 7:12-16 (the Davidic covenant — 'I will raise up your seed after you... and establish his throne forever') + PSA 132:11 (LXX 131:11 — 'the Lord swore to David... I will set upon your throne of your seed'). σπέρμα + ἐπαγγελία language is Pauline-theological-signature (Rom 4, Gal 3-4).

ACT 13:29.notes: Acts describes removal ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου, “from the wood.” Greek Deuteronomy 21:23 has κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ θεοῦ πᾶς κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου. Galatians 3:13 gives ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου. Acts may recall the Deuteronomy passage through its reference to wood. The burial is summarized with plural verbs here. Luke 23:50–53 names Joseph and describes his part.

ACT 13:33.notes: Paul quotes Psalm 2:7 to explain the fulfillment of God’s promise. Verse 33 speaks of raising up Jesus. It can be read in light of the resurrection or of God bringing Jesus forward as the promised Savior. Verse 34 expressly adds “from the dead.”

ACT 13:34.notes: Direct quotation of LXX ISA 55:3: δώσω ὑμῖν τὰ ὅσια Δαυίδ τὰ πιστά 'I will give you the holy and sure [things/promises] of David.' Greek matches LXX; MT reads differently ('I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast-love for David which is sure'). LXX's τὰ ὅσια Δαυίδ τὰ πιστά renders Hebrew חַסְדֵי דָּוִד הַנֶּאֱמָנִים 'faithful-hesed-of-David.' Paul's argument: these permanent-covenant-promises-to-David's-line require an eternal-Messianic-seed (setting up the PSA 16:10 citation at v.35).

ACT 13:35.notes: Greek Psalm 15:10 (English 16:10) and Acts 2:27 introduce the second clause with οὐδέ. Acts 13:35 quotes that clause on its own with οὐ. The psalm addresses God in the second person. Acts 2:31 applies the passage to Christ’s resurrection in the third person. Here Paul contrasts David’s decay in verse 36 with the experience of the one God raised in verse 37.

ACT 13:37.notes: ὃν δὲ ὁ θεὸς ἤγειρεν οὐκ εἶδεν διαφθοράν ('but he whom God raised did not see decay') applies LXX PSA 16:10 (quoted at v.35) to Jesus. The direct citation is at v.35; v.37 is the applicative-conclusion bringing the quotation home to Christ. Same LXX-matching pattern as v.35.

ACT 13:41.notes: Direct quotation of LXX HAB 1:5: ἴδετε, οἱ καταφρονηταί, καὶ θαυμάσατε καὶ ἀφανίσθητε, ὅτι ἔργον ἐργάζομαι ἐγὼ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ὑμῶν, ἔργον ὃ οὐ μὴ πιστεύσητε ἐάν τις ἐκδιηγῆται ὑμῖν. Greek closely matches LXX. LXX reading καταφρονηταί ('scoffers') differs from MT בַגּוֹיִם ('among the nations' — possibly reflecting Aramaic בגדים 'treacherous'). LXX's 'scoffers' reading aligns with 1QpHab interpretation-method. Paul uses HAB 1:5's original-context (Babylonian-invasion-judgment Judah-scoffers-won't-believe) as typological-warning: a new divine-work (Messianic salvation + concomitant-judgment for rejection) will be incredible — don't repeat Habakkuk's-scoffers' fate.

ACT 13:47.notes: Direct quotation of LXX ISA 49:6 (second half): τέθεικά σε εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν τοῦ εἶναί σε εἰς σωτηρίαν ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth.' Greek matches LXX closely. The verse is Messianic in origin (the Servant); Paul applies to apostolic-mission by-extension (as Messiah's-agents participating in the Servant's-commission). Same verse referenced at LUK 2:32 (Simeon's Nunc Dimittis) and ACT 26:23. The 'ends-of-the-earth' echoes ACT 1:8 Great Commission.

ACT 14:10.notes: The verb ἅλλομαι ('jumped up/leaped') in Luke's description of the healed lame man at Lystra verbatim matches LXX Isa 35:6 (τότε ἁλεῖται ὡς ἔλαφος ὁ χωλός 'then will the lame leap like a deer'), the locus classicus of Messianic-age healing prophecy. Luke's lexical choice (rare ἅλλομαι, only 3x NT: John 4:14, Acts 3:8, here) signals deliberate Isaianic-fulfillment framing for Paul's Gentile-healing: the Messianic age has arrived, and signs once promised for Israel's redemption now reach the nations. Also structurally parallels Acts 3:8 (Peter's lame-healing ἐξαλλόμενος) — Peter-Paul typology in Spirit-empowered ministry.

ACT 14:15.notes: Paul's creation-merism (τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς) echoes the Decalogue Sabbath-rationale LXX Exo 20:11 (ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησεν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς) and the near-identical LXX Psa 145:6 (EN 146:6 ὁ ποιήσας τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς). The 4-fold heaven+earth+sea+all-in-them merism is a stock LXX creation-formula also at Gen 1 (implicit), Neh 9:6, Psa 145:6, Isa 42:5, and programmatically at Acts 4:24 (believers' prayer post-arrest) and Rev 10:6 (angel's oath). This formal LXX-formula framing establishes Paul's Gentile kerugma within OT Creator-theology — God's creator-identity is the first premise of Gentile-mission preaching.

ACT 14:17.notes: Paul's general-providence catalogue (οὐρανόθεν ὑμῖν ὑετοὺς διδοὺς καὶ καιροὺς καρποφόρους, ἐμπιπλῶν τροφῆς ... τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν) echoes LXX Psa 146:8-9 (EN 147:8-9 τῷ ἑτοιμάζοντι τῇ γῇ ὑετὸν ... τῷ διδόντι τοῖς κτήνεσι τροφὴν αὐτῶν) and LXX Deu 11:14 (δώσω τὸν ὑετὸν τῇ γῇ σου καθ' ὥραν πρώιμον καὶ ὄψιμον ... καὶ ἐμπλησθήσῃ — rain-in-its-season + grain-abundance covenant-promise to Israel). Paul applies these Israel-specific divine-providence motifs to Gentile humanity generally — the God who sends rain + food is witnessed-by-providence to all nations (cf. Matt 5:45). This is the OT exegetical grounding for Paul's 'general revelation' theology later formalized at Rom 1:19-20 and Athens-Areopagus (Acts 17:24-29).

ACT 15:14.notes: James's phrase λαὸν τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ ('a people for his name') alludes to the OT motif of Israel as YHWH's chosen covenant-people. DEU 14:2 (λαὸς περιούσιος; LXX) 'the LORD has chosen you out of all the peoples' + similar 7:6, 26:18 covenant-election-formulas. 2CH 7:14 'my people who are called by my name' also echoes here. James's rhetorical move is to expand this people-for-God's-name category to include ἔθνη (Gentiles), preparing for the Amos 9:11-12 proof-text in vv.16-18. Not a direct quotation — thematic-allusion using covenant-language.

ACT 15:15.notes: Introduction-formula καθὼς γέγραπται ('as it is written') transitioning into the Amos 9:11-12 LXX citation that follows in vv.16-18. The plural οἱ λόγοι τῶν προφητῶν ('the words of the prophets') anticipates a composite-prophetic-argument grounded in the Amos text. See ACT 15:16, 15:17, 15:18 for the full citation content. James's rhetorical-practice is to preface Scripture-citation with a formula that signals his scriptural-proof is about to follow — standard early-Christian argumentation-pattern.

ACT 15:16.notes: Amos 9:11 in Hebrew and Greek speaks of raising David’s fallen shelter. In the Rahlfs Greek it opens “on that day.” Acts 15:16 opens with a promise to return after these things and rebuild. Verse 17 continues the quotation from Amos.

ACT 15:17.notes: In Hebrew Amos 9:12 the verb means “possess” and the object includes the remnant of Edom and the nations called by God’s name. In Rahlfs Greek Amos, the remnant of humanity and the nations are the subject of “seek,” with no expressed object. Acts follows that Greek construction and supplies τὸν κύριον as the object. These differences alone do not establish how the Greek reading arose.

ACT 15:18.notes: In SBLGNT γνωστὰ ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος follows ταῦτα without a sentence break. The Thai reads the things the Lord does as known from long ago, leaving the knower unspecified. The Robinson–Pierpont edition adds “all” in verse 17 and explicitly says in verse 18 that all his works are known to God. Greek Amos 9:12 closes with God doing these things. Greek Isaiah 45:21 offers a thematic parallel about announcing events long ago.

ACT 15:20.notes: The four-regulation Apostolic Decree alludes to Leviticus 17-18 — the 'Holiness Code' section applied to גֵּר ('resident-alien / sojourner') living within Israel. LEV 17:8-9 (sacrifices-only-at-tabernacle; prohibits-idol-sacrifice), LEV 17:10-14 (prohibits-eating-blood; includes the sojourner), LEV 17:13-14 (proper-slaughter draining-blood; prohibits-strangled-meat), LEV 18:6-30 (sexual-prohibitions explicitly bound on-sojourners at v.26). GEN 9:4 (Noah-covenant blood-prohibition as universal-human-law). Early-Christian-interpretation read these Levitical-sojourner-rules as the natural-framework for Gentile-believers integrating into Messianic-covenant without-full-Torah-conversion. Cited at v.29 with variant wording. Not a direct-quotation — thematic-allusion grounding the four-restrictions in the OT-stranger-code.

ACT 16:17.notes: The girl calls the travelers servants of the Most High God. The title recalls biblical usage, including Genesis 14:18. Her motives and her listeners’ interpretations are unreported. SBLGNT has a present participle for following and ὑμῖν, “to you.” Robinson–Pierpont has the aorist participle κατακολουθήσασα and ἡμῖν, “to us.”

ACT 16:26.notes: The earthquake-prison-deliverance scene (foundations shaken, doors opened, chains loosed) thematically echoes Psalm 107:14-16 LXX (Ps 106 LXX numbering): 'kai exegagen autous ek skotous kai skias thanatou kai tous desmous auton dierrexen ... hoti synetripsen pylas chalkas kai mochlous siderous syneklasen' (he brought them out of darkness and shadow of death, and burst their chains asunder ... for he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars). The Psalm-tradition of YHWH-as-prison-deliverer informs Luke's framing of the divine-action. Paul and Silas singing hymns in v.25 may well have been singing exactly this kind of deliverance-Psalm. Thematic-allusion not verbatim-quotation.

ACT 17:16.notes: Luke's word-choice paroxyneto to pneuma autou ('his spirit was being-provoked') deliberately echoes the LXX divine-anger-against-idolatry vocabulary cluster: PSA 106:29 LXX (Ps 105:29: parexynan auton en tois epitedeumasin auton 'they provoked him with their practices' — re Israel's idolatry); DEU 9:7-8, 9:18 (parexynate kurion 'you provoked the LORD' re golden-calf episode); DEU 32:16, 32:21 LXX (Song of Moses: parexynan me en allotriois 'they provoked me with strange-gods', en eidolois 'with idols'); HOS 8:5; ZEC 8:14. Paul's emotional reaction to Athenian saturation-with-idols is theologically-charged — his anger mirrors divine wrath at idolatry as recorded in OT prophets and Mosaic Law. The verb-cluster preserves a Lukan editorial statement that Paul's pastoral indignation conforms to divine moral-disposition.

ACT 17:24.notes: Paul's opening claim 'God who made the world and everything in it ... Lord of heaven and earth' fuses the Genesis 1:1 LXX vocabulary (epoiesen ho theos ton ouranon kai ten gen) with the merism heaven-and-earth (PSA 115:15 = LXX 113:23 ho ouranos kai he ge; cf. GEN 14:19, 22). The 'does not dwell in temples made-with-hands' (ouk en cheiropoietois naois katoikei) directly echoes 1 KGS 8:27 LXX (Solomon's temple-dedication: 'Will God indeed dwell on earth? Behold heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, much less this house...') and ISA 66:1-2 LXX (heaven my throne, earth my footstool — what house would you build for me?). cheiropoietos is the LXX-technical-term for IDOLS in the prophetic anti-idol-polemic (LEV 26:1, 26:30; ISA 31:7, 46:6; HAB 2:18) — Paul polemically extends the idol-vocabulary to Athenian temple-architecture itself.

ACT 17:25.notes: Paul's 'He himself gives all life and breath' (didous pasi zoen kai pnoen) echoes GEN 2:7 LXX (enephusesen eis to prosopon autou pnoen zoes 'he breathed into his face the breath of life') and ISA 42:5 LXX ('the God who made the heaven ... who gives breath [pnoen] to the people on it'). The premise that God needs nothing from human hands (ouk ... therapeuetai prosdeomenos tinos) echoes PSA 50:10-13 LXX (Ps 49 LXX) where God says 'if I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine and all its fullness ... do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?' Together these texts form the OT-prophetic critique of cultic-feeding-of-the-deity.

ACT 17:26.notes: Paul's anthropological claim 'from one man he made every nation of humans to dwell on the whole face of the earth, having determined appointed times and the boundaries of their dwelling' weaves together: GEN 1:27 LXX (creation of one Adam from whom all descend); GEN 1:28 LXX cultural-mandate (be-fruitful-fill-the-earth); DEU 32:8 LXX (Song of Moses) which contains the Vorlage that Paul presupposes — '[the Most High] set the bounds (horia) of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God' (LXX agrees with DSS 4QDeut-j 'sons of God' against MT 'sons of Israel'); and PSA 74:17 LXX (Ps 73 LXX: 'you set all the borders [horia] of the earth'). horothesia (boundary-setting, hapax NT) is the verbal-cognate of horia in DEU 32:8 LXX — Paul deliberately invokes the Mosaic-eschatological-passage that defines national boundaries as divine-allotment. This is anti-autochthony argument: Athenians cannot claim primacy by virtue of being earth-born.

ACT 17:27.notes: Paul's seek-and-find appeal echoes DEU 4:29 LXX (zetesete ekei kurion ton theon ... kai heuresete) and ISA 55:6 LXX (zetesate ton kurion). The grope-blindly metaphor (psephesian) echoes DEU 28:29 LXX where blind-groping is judicial-curse — Paul's irony: idolaters with eyes nonetheless grope as if blind. The God-not-far claim (ou makran ... hyparchonta) directly parallels JER 23:23 LXX ('Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far off?'), PSA 145:18 LXX (Ps 144: 'the Lord is near to all who call upon him'), and DEU 4:7 LXX ('what nation has gods so near to it as the LORD our God?'). Paul's monotheism is presence-based not deistic-distance — counter to Epicurean view of distant non-interfering gods.

ACT 17:30.notes: Paul's claim that God 'overlooked' (hyperidon) the times of ignorance until now extends his earlier Lystra-speech (ACT 14:16: God 'allowed [eiasen] all the nations to go their own ways' in past generations) and parallels ROM 3:25 (paresin 'passing-over' of former sins in divine forbearance) and ROM 2:4 (the kindness of God leading to repentance). The OT-resonance is implicit rather than direct-citation: divine-forbearance-leading-to-eschatological-judgment is the Pauline theological frame, drawing on the prophetic texts that announce eschatological judgment after a period of divine patience (e.g., HAB 1-3, JOEL 2).

ACT 17:31.notes: Paul's eschatological-judgment claim 'he has set a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness' (krinein ten oikoumenen en dikaiosune) reproduces the formulaic LXX-Psalter judgment-vocabulary: PSA 9:8 LXX (9:9 LXX numbering: krinei ten oikoumenen en dikaiosune); PSA 96:13 LXX (Ps 95 LXX: krinei ten oikoumenen en dikaiosune); PSA 98:9 LXX (Ps 97 LXX: same formula). All three psalter-occurrences use the identical LXX-phrase oikoumenen en dikaiosune. ECC 12:14 closes the wisdom-tradition with universal-judgment-of-all-deeds. Paul deploys the canonical OT-judgment-formula but locates the appointed-judge specifically in the resurrected Jesus — the Pauline eschatological-pivot.

ACT 18:10.notes: Two OT-allusion-clusters in this verse: (1) 'egō eimi meta sou' (I-am-with-you) covenant-presence formula — GEN 26:24 LXX to Isaac; GEN 28:15 to Jacob ('egō eimi meta sou'); EXO 3:12 LXX to Moses; JOS 1:5 LXX to Joshua; JER 1:8 + 1:19 to Jeremiah. Same Greek verbal construction (egō eimi + meta + sou) repeated. (2) Extended 'laos moi polys en tē polei tautē' — 'I have-people many in this city'. The noun laos is LXX-technical for God's-covenant-people (Israel); here Jesus-to-Paul extends the term prospectively to include yet-to-be-converted Gentile Corinthians. Parallel theological-extension at ACT 15:14 (James: 'God chose from among the Gentiles a laos for-his-name'); cf. ISA 43:4 'laos mou' + ROM 9:25-26 (Paul's citation of HOS 2:23 LXX for Gentile-inclusion). The pre-election-of-many theology motivates Paul's 18-month stay (v.11).

ACT 18:18.notes: Acts connects cutting hair at Cenchreae with a vow. Numbers 6:2–5, 18 describes hair and the Nazirite vow, including a completion rite. Acts gives neither the name of this vow nor the full rite. Acts 21:23–26 provides another narrative involving vows.

ACT 18:6.notes: Paul's declaration 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean' draws on the OT watchman/blood-guilt formula. EZE 33:4-6 LXX establishes the watchman-principle — if the watchman warns, the blood-guilt transfers to those-who-ignored-the-warning; if he fails to warn, blood-guilt stays with him. 2SA 1:16 LXX (David's sentence on Amalekite: to haima sou epi ten kephalen sou) and 1KI 2:33 LXX (Solomon on Joab) provide the self-responsibility idiom. Paul applies the Ezekielian watchman-principle: having fulfilled his warning-duty at the Corinthian synagogue, he is ceremonially 'clean' (katharos) of their blood-guilt. The symbolic gesture ektinaxamenos ta himatia (shook-out-garments) parallels the Deut 25:9 ritual and the dominical instruction MAT 10:14 / LUK 9:5 (shake-dust-from-feet).

ACT 18:9.notes: The divine 'me phobou' (do-not-fear) + 'lalei kai me siopeses' (speak + do-not-be-silent) doublet draws on the OT prophet-commissioning formula. GEN 15:1 (Abram: me phobou); GEN 26:24 LXX (Isaac: me phobou, meta sou gar egō eimi); GEN 46:3 (Jacob: me phobou katabenai eis Aigypton); ISA 41:10 LXX (me phobou, meta sou gar egō eimi); ISA 43:1, 5 (me phobou); JER 1:8 LXX (me phobou apo prosopou auton, dioti meta sou egō eimi). Paul is commissioned in the prophetic-patriarch pattern — the Corinthian vision places him in continuity with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Jeremiah as recipients of the same divine-reassurance formula.

ACT 19:17.notes: Acts uses ἐμεγαλύνετο of the name of the Lord Jesus. Greek 2 Samuel 7:26 uses the same verb of God’s name, and Greek Psalm 33:4 (English 34:3) calls people to magnify the Lord and exalt his name. In Rahlfs Greek Malachi 1:11, δεδόξασται speaks of the name being glorified, and μέγα describes it as great. Malachi is a thematic comparison with different wording.

ACT 19:26.notes: Paul's summarized anti-idol polemic 'ouk eisin theoi hoi dia cheiron ginomenoi' ('those made by hands are not gods') preserves the LXX-technical-vocabulary cluster against idolatry. ISA 44:9-20 LXX (idol-maker mock-polemic: wood-half-for-fire-half-for-god); ISA 46:6-7 (gold-silver idol unable to save); JER 10:3-5 LXX (scarecrow-idol cannot walk or speak); PSA 115:4-7 + PSA 135:15-18 LXX (idols have-mouths-but-not-speak — ta eidola ton ethnon ergon cheiron anthropon); DEU 4:28 LXX (man-made-gods that cannot see/hear). cheiropoietos (made-with-hands) is LXX-technical-term for idols (LEV 26:1, 26:30; ISA 31:7, 46:6; HAB 2:18). Parallel to Paul's Athens-speech application at ACT 17:24-25 (cheiropoietoi temples) and Stephen's at ACT 7:48. Demetrius accurately summarizes Paul's teaching here — the summary itself is witness-to-Paul's consistent anti-idol proclamation across the Asia Minor mission.

ACT 1:20.notes: Acts joins two adapted Psalm quotations with καί and applies them to Judas. In Greek Psalm 68:26 (Rahlfs), the dwelling belongs to “them” (αὐτῶν), and the final clause mentions their tents. Acts 1:20 speaks about “his” dwelling (αὐτοῦ) and says “in it.” Compare Thai Psalm 69:26 and English Psalm 69:25. The second quotation takes up the petition about the office in Psalm 109:8b (Greek 108:8b). Rahlfs has the optative λάβοι, and Acts has the imperative λαβέτω.

ACT 1:3.notes: FORTY-DAY MOTIF. δι' ἡμερῶν τεσσεράκοντα ('throughout forty days') is Luke's distinctive post-resurrection datum (not found in Matthew/Mark/John resurrection sequences). The forty-day span is a deliberate typological echo of OT forty-day revelatory periods: Moses with YHWH on Sinai (EXO 24:18; 34:28); Elijah's journey to Horeb (1KI 19:8); Jesus' own wilderness-temptation forty days (LUK 4:2). In each case, forty days marks a revelatory/formational period between-times. Luke frames Jesus' post-resurrection teaching as analogous revelatory preparation — the apostles receiving decisive kingdom-instruction before the new-covenant Pentecost. Typological pattern, not lexical quotation.

ACT 1:8.notes: ENDS-OF-THE-EARTH commissioning phrase ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς is a direct lexical match to Isa 49:6 LXX (ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς, Servant-as-light-to-the-nations). Luke deliberately echoes Isaiah's Servant-mission at the programmatic outset of Acts, framing the disciples' witness-task as continuing the Isaianic Servant's mission to the nations. Paul makes the citation explicit at ACT 13:47 (when he and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles). This single allusion controls the geographical outline of the book: Jerusalem → Judea/Samaria → ends-of-the-earth.

ACT 1:9.notes: CLOUD-ASCENT IMAGERY: νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτόν — a cloud receives Jesus as he ascends. Deliberate echo of DAN 7:13 (LXX/Θ) cloud-borne Son-of-Man ascending to the Ancient-of-Days. Luke's gospel-ending already invoked this (LUK 24:51 entry); here in Acts the cloud is lexically explicit (νεφέλη). The enthronement-coronation reading of Dan 7:13-14 (Son-of-Man given dominion and kingdom) fits the Ascension-as-Exaltation Christology. Companion verse to LUK 24:51 allusion; also resonates forward to the angels' second-coming promise at v. 11 (returning in the same way — cloud-accompanied).

ACT 20:10.notes: The proposed allusion concerns bodily contact and the child’s life. In Rahlfs Greek 1 Kings 17:21 Elijah breathes on the child three times and asks that his life return. In verse 22 the child cries out. The Hebrew of verse 21 describes Elijah stretching himself over the child. In 2 Kings 4:34 Elisha lies on the child. Acts describes Paul going down, falling upon Eutychus and embracing him.

ACT 20:26.notes: WATCHMAN BLOOD-GUILT FORMULA — Paul's 'καθαρός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος πάντων' invokes the Ezekielian watchman-paradigm. EZK 33:6 LXX 'ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς τοῦ σκοποῦ ἐκζητήσω τὸ αἷμα αὐτοῦ' (from the watchman's hand I will require his blood); EZK 33:8-9 the inverse: faithful-warning discharges the watchman's blood-responsibility. Paul positions himself as Ezekielian-watchman over the Ephesian church — innocent-of-blood because faithfully-warned (cf. v.27 πᾶσαν τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ θεοῦ). Spiritual-not-physical death-language (per uW figs-explicit). Recurrent-Pauline-self-exemption from-blood-guilt (cf. ACT 18:6 same-formula 'τὸ αἷμα ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑμῶν').

ACT 20:28.notes: The acquisition of a people recalls Greek Isaiah 43:21 and Psalm 73:2 (English 74:2). The church is called “of God” in SBLGNT, “of the Lord” in Tregelles, and “of the Lord and God” in Robinson–Pierpont. With the selected τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ ἰδίου the Thai reads “his own blood.” Another interpretation is “the blood of his own one,” understood as his Son. The word “Son” is inferred in that interpretation. Robinson–Pierpont places “own” before “blood.”

ACT 20:29.notes: WOLVES-AGAINST-FLOCK FORMULA — λύκοι βαρεῖς preserves the LXX-prophetic-vocabulary for predatory-leaders threatening God's-people. JER 5:6 LXX 'λύκος ἕως τῶν οἰκιῶν ὠλέθρευσεν αὐτούς' (a-wolf even-to-their-houses destroyed-them); EZK 22:27 LXX 'οἱ ἄρχοντες αὐτῆς ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῆς ὡς λύκοι' (her-rulers in-her-midst as-wolves); ZEP 3:3 LXX 'οἱ κριταὶ αὐτῆς ὡς λύκοι' (her-judges as-wolves). The OT-wolves are corrupt-Israelite-leaders abusing-the-flock; Paul reapplies the trope to false-teachers-from-within-the-church. Echoes Jesus's similar wolves-in-sheep's-clothing warning at MAT 7:15 + the good-shepherd-versus-hireling discourse JOH 10:12. Pauline-prophecy-fulfilled in 1-2 TIM Asian-apostasy + REV 2:1-7 letter-to-Ephesus.

ACT 20:32.notes: SANCTIFIED-INHERITANCE FORMULA — τὴν κληρονομίαν ἐν τοῖς ἡγιασμένοις πᾶσιν preserves LXX-Mosaic-blessing language. DEU 33:3-4 LXX 'πάντες οἱ ἡγιασμένοι ὑπὸ τὰς χεῖράς σου ... νόμον ὃν ἐνετείλατο ἡμῖν Μωυσῆς κληρονομίαν' (all-the-sanctified under-your-hands ... the-law which-Moses-commanded-us as-an-inheritance). WIS 5:5 'ἐν ἁγίοις ὁ κλῆρος αὐτοῦ' (his-lot among-the-saints). Pauline-application: the Christian-inheritance is in-the-sanctified, transferring the Mosaic-Israel-as-sanctified-inheritors trope to-the-church. Echoed in EPH 1:11,14,18; COL 1:12; HEB 9:15; 1 PE 1:4.

ACT 20:33.notes: DECALOGUE-COVETING FORMULA + SAMUEL'S-FAREWELL pattern. ἐπεθύμησα 'I coveted' echoes the 10th-commandment LXX οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις (EXO 20:17, DEU 5:21 LXX) — Paul self-asserts compliance with the foundational-Mosaic-prohibition. The silver-gold-clothing triad also echoes Samuel's-farewell self-defense: 1 SA 12:3 LXX 'τίνος ὑμῶν ... εἴληφα ... ἢ τίνος εἴληφα ἐξίλασμα' (whose-of-yours have-I-taken? whose ransom?). Pauline-self-vindication patterns the prophetic-Samuel farewell-speech. Pauline-financial-integrity recurs 1 COR 9:12-18, 1 TH 2:5-10, 2 COR 12:14-18.

ACT 22:14.notes: Acts 3:14 combines ἅγιον and δίκαιον in องค์บริสุทธิ์และชอบธรรม. Acts 7:52 has องค์ผู้ชอบธรรม and 22:14 พระผู้ชอบธรรม. Isaiah 53:11 uses δίκαιον. Greek Psalm 15:10 (English 16:10) uses ὅσιον and supplies a thematic parallel.

ACT 22:16.notes: Ananias urges Paul to receive baptism, wash away his sins and call on his name. Acts 9:18 reports Paul’s baptism without naming the baptizer. The allusion to calling on the Lord’s name recalls Joel 3:5 in the Hebrew and Greek editions (2:32 in common English numbering). Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 quote Joel, while Acts 22:16 uses a participle and the pronoun “his.”

ACT 22:21.notes: Paul reports being sent to distant nations. The commission recalls Isaiah 49:6, where the Greek τέθεικά σε introduces the servant’s appointment. Acts 13:47 quotes the light for the nations passage. Luke 2:32 echoes its light imagery in Simeon’s own wording. Jeremiah 1:5 appoints a prophet to nations, and 1:7 speaks of going wherever God sends him.

ACT 22:6.notes: Theophanic-light-from-heaven motif, parallel to ACT 9:3, ACT 26:13. The sudden bright light around Saul echoes the Sinai-theophany cloud-and-fire (LXX Exo 19:16-18, 24:17 the glory of YHWH "as devouring fire") and the Ezekielian merkabah-vision (LXX Eze 1:4 a great cloud with fire flashing, 1:27-28 the radiant kavod-glory of YHWH on the throne). ACT 22:6 amplifies this with the noon-detail (περὶ μεσημβρίαν), heightening the supernatural-character vs. solar-light. Cf. 2 COR 4:6 — Paul his own theological-reflection on the Damascus-light as creation-light theophany.

ACT 22:8.notes: Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἰησοῦς — Jesus self-identification formula. The absolute "I am" construction echoes LXX Exo 3:14 ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν divine-self-identification, the same formula used Christologically in JHN 6:35, 8:58 etc. Parallel to ACT 9:5 + ACT 26:15 (all three Damascus-road retellings). The theological freight is Christological-identity — the risen Christ identifies himself with the YHWH-formula.

ACT 23:3.notes: Acts calls Ananias a whitewashed wall. Ezekiel 13:10–15 portrays a coated wall that collapses under judgment and uses ἀλείφω for coating. Matthew 23:27 describes whitewashed tombs using κονιάω, the verb in Acts. The comparison with Ezekiel is thematic and the shared verb with Matthew does not establish literary dependence.

ACT 23:5.notes: DIRECT CITATION with gegraptai introduction. Greek matches LXX EXO 22:28 archonta tou laou sou ou kakos ereis near-verbatim (only word-order: SBLGNT-NT puts kakos after ereis; LXX before). The OT prohibition addresses the same situation Paul has just violated - speaking-evil-of-a-ruler-of-the-people. Paul's submission to Torah-discipline even when defending himself models ROM 13:1-7 (subject-to-authorities) and 1 PE 2:23 (Christ hos loidoroumenos ouk antelodorei).

ACT 23:9.notes: Luke 23:4, 14 and 22 likewise report a finding of no guilt. Acts 5:38–39 warns about opposing God. These are thematic allusions. The wording and speakers differ. SBLGNT has some scribes of the Pharisee party ask what if a spirit or angel spoke to Paul. NA28 punctuates the words as a question. Robinson–Pierpont reads “the scribes” and adds μὴ θεομαχῶμεν, “let us not fight against God.” In the shorter reading the speakers’ next words cannot be reconstructed.

ACT 24:15.notes: Paul's two-fold-resurrection formula 'of the just and the unjust' (anastasis ... dikaion te kai adikon) echoes the LXX form of DAN 12:2 'and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake — some to everlasting life and others to everlasting shame and contempt.' DAN 12:2 is the OT's clearest two-fold-resurrection text and the foundational source for the Pharisaic doctrine Paul affirms (cf. ACT 23:6, 23:8, 24:21, 26:6-8). The Greek does not match LXX-DAN-12:2 verbatim — Paul uses anastasis (resurrection-noun) and the dikaios/adikos pair rather than DAN's egeirthesontai (will be raised) and the zoe-aionios/oneidismos-aionios pair. Allusion, not citation. The Pharisaic-Sadducean split on this doctrine was foregrounded in ACT 23:6-8; Paul here insists 'they themselves accept' it — overstating slightly since Sadducees rejected resurrection. JHN 5:28-29 is the parallel Johannine formulation.

ACT 26:13.notes: Paul's λαμπρότης ('brightness, beyond the brightness of the sun') Damascus light echoes the eschatological 'Sun of Righteousness with healing in his wings' (LXX MAL 3:20 = MT MAL 4:2). The same Lukan word-family (λάμπω) appears in LK 1:78 (ἀνατολή 'sunrise from on high') drawing on the Malachi imagery. Allusion, not citation — Paul invokes the Sun-of-Righteousness type to identify the Damascus encounter as the eschatological-messianic dawn breaking into his life. SBLGNT-MT both attest. Per RULES §0 evangelical-Protestant typological reading: the Damascus Christ IS the Sun of Righteousness.

ACT 26:17.notes: Christ's commissioning of Paul fuses two prophetic-call topoi: (1) JER 1:8/1:19 'I am with you to deliver you' (the divine-promise-of-deliverance to a prophet sent into hostile reception) — Paul's 'rescuing you from the people [Jews] and from the Gentiles' picks up this Jeremianic deliverance-formula. (2) ISA 49:6 'I will make you a light to the nations' — the Servant-of-the-LORD as commissioned to the ἔθνη. The combined-source pattern (Jer + Isa servant-songs) is consistent with how Acts elsewhere fuses prophetic call-narratives (cf. ACT 13:47 directly cites ISA 49:6). Allusion not citation — no verbatim LXX reproduction.

ACT 26:18.notes: The five-fold mission summary (open blind eyes, dark→light, Satan→God, forgiveness, inheritance among sanctified) draws on a cluster of LXX servant-songs and prophetic-eschatological texts: ISA 42:7 (open blind eyes, bring out from prison), ISA 42:16 (lead the blind by ways they have not known, darkness to light), ISA 9:2 (people walking in darkness see great light), ISA 35:5 (eyes of blind shall be opened), ISA 61:1 (proclaim release to captives — Lukan favorite, LK 4:18). For 'inheritance among the sanctified' (κλῆρον ... ἡγιασμένοις): DAN 12:13 LXX 'you shall stand for your κλῆρος at the consummation of the days' + LEV 11:44 LXX 'you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy' as the holiness-foundation. The verse compresses the OT prophetic mission-vocabulary into a single Christian commissioning. Per evangelical-Protestant tradition (RULES §0): typological-fulfillment rendering of Servant-Song mission in the apostolic mandate.

ACT 26:20.notes: Paul's 'deeds worthy of repentance' (ἄξια τῆς μετανοίας ἔργα) echoes the Isaianic prophetic ethic — repentance must produce ethical deeds. ISA 1:16-17 LXX ('cease your evil ... learn to do good, seek justice, correct oppression') is the prototypical OT 'fruits of repentance' text. The phrase echoes John the Baptist's preaching at LK 3:8 / MT 3:8 directly (ποιήσατε ... ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας) — the Baptist himself drawing on the Isaianic ethic. Allusion via the John-the-Baptist intertext: Paul positions his message in continuity with John's prophetic preaching, which itself stood in continuity with Isaiah. Triple-layered intertext (Isa → John → Paul). No verbatim LXX reproduction; thematic-vocabulary echo.
