ACT 26:23.notes: The triadic Christ-suffer / first-from-resurrection / proclaim-light-to-people-and-Gentiles formula compresses the Isaianic Servant-Song + early Christian kerygma. ISA 53:3 (man of sorrows, acquainted with grief) + ISA 53:11 (servant justifies many) for παθητός 'subject to suffering.' For 'first from the resurrection of the dead' πρῶτος ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν: PSA 16:10 LXX (will not abandon to Hades) is the Petrine-Pauline resurrection-prooftext (cf. ACT 2:25-31, 13:35), implicitly drawing also on DAN 12:2's general-resurrection framework with Christ as the inaugurating πρῶτος (cf. 1CO 15:20 ἀπαρχή; COL 1:18 πρωτότοκος). For φῶς ... τῷ τε λαῷ καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσιν 'light to the people [Israel] and the Gentiles': ISA 49:6 (servant as 'light to the nations / salvation to the ends of the earth') — the same passage cited in ACT 13:47 and LK 2:32 (Simeon's Nunc Dimittis). The combined-source kerygmatic structure echoes 1CO 15:3-4 'died ... raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.'

ACT 28:26.notes: Acts 28:26 cites Isaiah 6:9. In Acts the destination πρὸς τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον follows Πορεύθητι. Greek Isaiah puts τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ after the active imperative εἰπόν. ἀκοῇ is a dative noun and βλέποντες a participle. The Thai repetition echoes Matthew 13:14.

ACT 28:27.notes: The Isaiah 6:10 citation continues the divine speech begun in the commission. The passive ἐπαχύνθη leaves the agent unstated. Acts uses เกรงว่า for μήποτε, whereas Matthew 13:15 has เพื่อมิให้. The first-person promise of healing belongs to the quoted speaker.

ACT 28:28.notes: LUKAN INCLUSIO + Isaianic-Servant-allusion. The phrase σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ (the salvation of God, neuter substantive) is a distinctively-Lukan vocabulary item — appears 4× in NT, all in Luke-Acts: LUK 2:30 (Simeon's Nunc Dimittis: εἶδον οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου τὸ σωτήριόν σου, ὃ ἡτοίμασας...), LUK 3:6 (Baptist citing ISA 40:5: ὄψεται πᾶσα σὰρξ τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ), here ACT 28:28 (Paul to Roman Jews: τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπεστάλη τοῦτο τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ), and EPH 6:17 (περικεφαλαίαν τοῦ σωτηρίου in armor metaphor — Pauline). The four Luke-Acts uses form an inclusio: opens with Simeon promising the salvation will be 'a light to the Gentiles and glory to your people Israel' (LUK 2:32 — citing ISA 49:6 'φῶς ἐθνῶν...εἰς σωτηρίαν ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς'); closes with Paul confirming 'the salvation of God HAS BEEN SENT to the Gentiles, and they WILL hear.' Acts 13:47 already cited ISA 49:6 directly in the same Pauline-mission context. The inclusio is Lukan theological closure: the Gentile-mission is the fulfillment of Simeon's prophecy and Isaiah's Servant Songs.

ACT 2:11.greek_matches: lexical parallel in Greek Psalm 70:19; thematic parallel in Exodus
ACT 2:11.notes: Acts calls the message τὰ μεγαλεῖα τοῦ θεοῦ, God’s great deeds. Greek Psalm 70:19 (Thai Psalm 71:19) does use μεγαλεῖα. The words ὁ ποιῶν θαυμάσια μόνος are in Greek Psalm 71:18 (English Psalm 72:18). Greek Exodus 15:11 uses ποιῶν τέρατα. These songs praise God’s deeds; Acts leaves the deeds heard by the crowd unspecified.

ACT 2:14.notes: PROPHETIC-OPENING-FORMULA: ἐνωτίσασθε τὰ ῥήματά μου 'give ear to my words' is a classic LXX-prophetic speech-opening. Joel 1:2 LXX (ἐνωτίσασθε ... πάντες οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὴν γῆν) is the closest — particularly apt since Peter is about to cite Joel 2. Also echoes Isa 1:2 LXX (ἄκουε οὐρανέ ... ἐνωτίζου γῆ) and Deut 32:1 LXX (πρόσεχε οὐρανέ ... ἀκουέτω γῆ τὰ ῥήματα ἐκ στόματός μου). Peter — the Galilean fisherman — now speaks with LXX-prophetic diction, a mark of Spirit-transformation. Formulaic-echo allusion.

ACT 2:17.notes: DIRECT CITATION of Joel 2:28 MT / Joel 3:1 LXX. Peter's citation matches LXX closely but introduces ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις 'in the last days' (LXX reads μετὰ ταῦτα) — a deliberate editorial-adjustment aligning Joel with the Isa 2:2 / Mic 4:1 eschatological frame. Also adds λέγει ὁ θεός ('God says'). Peter interprets Pentecost as the inauguration of the 'last days' Spirit-outpouring. Young-men/old-men + sons/daughters parallelism breaks age/gender/social barriers of OT prophetic access.

ACT 2:18.notes: Joel names both male and female servants in Hebrew and in Greek. In Acts, μου follows each word for servant, and Peter ends the verse with “they will prophesy.” Greek Joel 3:2 has neither of these possessives on the servants and ends with the outpouring of the Spirit. Hebrew and Greek Joel 3:2 correspond to Joel 2:29 in many English Bibles.

ACT 2:19.notes: DIRECT CITATION Joel 2:30 MT / Joel 3:3 LXX. Apocalyptic-cosmic signs. The signs were not visible at Pentecost itself — Peter cites the full Joel oracle because Pentecost (Spirit-outpouring) is part one, and the cosmic signs await eschatological completion. Inaugurated-eschatology framework.

ACT 2:2.notes: Exodus 19:16–19 describes thunder, lightning, cloud, a trumpet blast, smoke and fire at Sinai. Acts describes a sound like a rushing wind. Wind is part of the comparison in Acts; Exodus does not name it in this scene. Genesis 2:7 and Ezekiel 37:9 provide further comparisons for breath and life.

ACT 2:20.notes: DIRECT CITATION Joel 2:31 MT / Joel 3:4 LXX. Textual point: LXX ἐπιφανῆ 'manifest/resplendent' differs from MT הנורא 'dreadful/awesome' — Peter follows LXX. The 'Day of the Lord' (ἡμέραν κυρίου) is OT technical prophetic term for divine-judgment-day; κύριος here = YHWH per OT-context. Solar/lunar signs echo broader prophetic-apocalyptic tradition (Isa 13:10; Ezek 32:7-8; Amos 8:9; Luke 21:25 Jesus' Olivet Discourse).

ACT 2:21.notes: DIRECT CITATION Joel 2:32a MT / Joel 3:5a LXX — the interpretive-climax of Peter's sermon. 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.' Κύριος in Joel = YHWH; Peter will interpret κύριος as Jesus in v.36 (implicit divine-Christ identification). Paul cites the identical verse at Rom 10:13 as the Jew-Gentile universal-salvation formula. The universal (πᾶς) anticipates v.39 ('the promise is for you and your children and all who are far off').

ACT 2:24.notes: ὠδῖνας τοῦ θανάτου 'birth-pangs/agonies of death' directly echoes LXX Ps 17:5-6 (MT 18:4-5). The LXX translator rendered MT חבלי 'cords' (of Sheol) as ὠδῖνες 'birth-pangs' — either confusing חבל 'cord' with חבל 'pang' or deliberately semantic-shifting. Luke exploits the LXX-phrase for theological purpose: Jesus' resurrection loosed the 'birth-pangs' (implying a new-birth typology) of death. LXX-lexeme echo, thematic rather than direct citation.

ACT 2:25.notes: DIRECT CITATION Ps 16:8 MT / Ps 15:8 LXX, begins the Ps 16:8-11 block (vv. 25-28). Peter's hermeneutical claim (εἰς αὐτόν, 'about Him'): David spoke these words about the Messiah. The 'I will not be shaken' (μὴ σαλευθῶ) grounds the 'death could not hold Him' claim of v.24. Κύριος = YHWH in OT-quotation.

ACT 2:26.notes: DIRECT CITATION Ps 16:9 MT / Ps 15:9 LXX. Three-fold Hebrew-poetic parallelism (heart / tongue / flesh). Peter will exegete 'my flesh will dwell in hope' in vv. 29-32 — the key phrase for his resurrection-of-Messiah argument.

ACT 2:27.notes: DIRECT CITATION Ps 16:10 MT / Ps 15:10 LXX — the verse that Peter's exegesis turns on (re-cited at v.31). LXX διαφθοράν 'corruption' translates MT שחת which can mean either 'pit' or 'corruption'. Peter's argument requires the LXX-'corruption' reading: David DID see the pit (v.29 tomb) but only the Messiah avoided corruption. LXX text-critical dependence is crucial to the pesher-argument.

ACT 2:28.notes: DIRECT CITATION Ps 16:11 MT / Ps 15:11 LXX, concludes the vv. 25-28 block. The resurrection-implication: God revealing 'paths of life' to the Holy One whose flesh rests without seeing corruption = resurrection from death. Completes Peter's first scriptural proof.

ACT 2:3.notes: Acts compares what appeared with fire (ὡσεὶ πυρός). Hebrew Isaiah 5:24 uses the image of a tongue of fire consuming stubble. The Rahlfs Greek Isaiah describes stubble consumed by a burning coal and mentions a flame, without using γλῶσσα.

ACT 2:30.notes: COMPOSITE ALLUSION: (1) Ps 132:11 MT / Ps 131:11 LXX (ὤμοσεν κύριος τῷ Δαυὶδ ... ἐκ καρποῦ τῆς κοιλίας σου θήσομαι ἐπὶ τὸν θρόνον σου) — Luke's ἐκ καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος is near-verbatim echo (ὀσφύος replaces LXX κοιλίας). (2) 2 Sam 7:12-13 — Nathan's oracle establishing the Davidic covenant ('I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom'). Peter weaves both OT texts — the Psalms oath and the Samuel covenant — into a single dynastic-promise argument fulfilled in Messianic enthronement-via-resurrection.

ACT 2:31.notes: RE-CITATION of Ps 16:10 MT / Ps 15:10 LXX (first citation at v.27). Peter shifts from David's first-person ('my') to third-person ('He') to explicitly apply the text to Christ. The 'flesh did not see corruption' is the crux of the resurrection argument — Jesus' body did not decay because it was raised; David's did decay because it wasn't. See v.27 note for full LXX-text-critical details.

ACT 2:34.notes: DIRECT CITATION Ps 110:1 MT / Ps 109:1 LXX — one of the most-cited OT verses in the NT (Matt 22:44; Mark 12:36; Luke 20:42-43; Heb 1:13; 1 Cor 15:25; Eph 1:20; Col 3:1; 1 Pet 3:22). Peter's argument: David calls the Messiah 'my Lord,' implying the Messiah is greater than David, implying the Messiah is divine. The two-κύριος structure (εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου) lets Peter's sermon land the v.36 climax: Jesus is κύριος alongside God, so Joel 2:32's 'call on the name of the Lord' applies to Jesus.

ACT 2:35.notes: RE-CITATION of Ps 110:1 LXX (continuation of v.34 quotation — the ἕως-until clause). The enemies-as-footstool metaphor signals complete subjugation. 1 Cor 15:25-28 develops this as the Son's mediatorial reign until the final enemy (death) is defeated.

ACT 2:39.notes: COMPOSITE ALLUSION: (1) Isa 57:19 LXX — εἰρήνη εἰρήνη τοῖς μακρὰν καὶ τοῖς ἐγγύς 'peace peace to those far and those near' — the far/near language of eschatological-peace-inclusion. Paul picks this up explicitly at Eph 2:13, 17 as Jew/Gentile reconciliation. (2) Joel 2:32b LXX (ὅσους κύριος προσκέκληται) 'whom the Lord summons' — the continuation of the Joel quotation-block. Peter at this point likely meant 'far' primarily as Diaspora Jews; Luke, writing with Acts 10's retrospect, lets the language do double-duty with the Gentile-inclusion reading.

ACT 2:40.notes: σκολιᾶς γενεᾶς 'crooked generation' echoes Deut 32:5 LXX (γενεὰ σκολιὰ καὶ διεστραμμένη) — Moses' Song of condemnation of the perverse exodus-generation. Peter frames the current unbelieving-Israel in the same rebellious-generation typology. Paul will later reuse the Deut 32 echo at Phil 2:15 (ἐν μέσῳ γενεᾶς σκολιᾶς καὶ διεστραμμένης).

ACT 2:6.notes: BABEL-REVERSAL: συνεχύθη at ACT 2:6 uses the exact LXX verb from Gen 11:7-9 (συγχέωμεν ... συνέχεε κύριος ... τὴν γλῶσσαν πάσης τῆς γῆς). At Babel, God confounded (συγχέω) languages to scatter the nations; at Pentecost, the crowd is confounded (συνεχύθη) precisely because the languages are now united — the nations hear their own tongues from Galilean mouths. Deliberate typological inversion: Babel scattered; Pentecost regathers; diversity now serves unity in the Spirit. Lexical-verb echo, not direct quotation.

ACT 3:13.notes: DOUBLE OT ANCHORING: (1) 'God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' echoes Ex 3:6, 15 LXX — God's self-identification to Moses at the burning bush. Jesus cited the same formula to defend resurrection at Luke 20:37 (ὡς λέγει κύριον τὸν θεὸν Ἀβραὰμ καὶ θεὸν Ἰσαὰκ καὶ θεὸν Ἰακώβ). (2) 'his Servant ... glorified' — παῖς + δοξάζω echoes Isa 52:13 LXX (ἰδοὺ συνήσει ὁ παῖς μου ... ὑψωθήσεται καὶ δοξασθήσεται 'behold my servant will understand ... will be exalted and glorified'). Peter's verb ἐδόξασεν picks up δοξασθήσεται — signaling Jesus as the Isaianic Servant now glorified post-resurrection. Composite covenant-renewal language.

ACT 3:14.notes: MESSIANIC TITLES: ὁ ἅγιος καὶ δίκαιος as a Lucan Christological title. (1) ὁ δίκαιος echoes Isa 53:11 LXX δικαιῶσαι δίκαιον ('to justify the righteous one') — the Suffering Servant. Stephen (Acts 7:52) and Ananias (Acts 22:14) use 'the Righteous One' for Jesus as Lucan signature Christological title. (2) ὁ ἅγιος echoes Ps 16:10 LXX (τὸν ὅσιον σου — 'your holy one') — already cited by Peter at Acts 2:27 Christologically. Luke builds Christological titles cumulatively across Acts. Doublet-intensification with implicit Messianic reference per uW TN.

ACT 3:18.notes: Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 report Jesus speaking the opening cry of Psalm 22. Luke 23:46 instead records his prayer entrusting his spirit to the Father, drawing on Psalm 31:5. Acts 3:18 speaks of the prophets collectively without identifying a single text. Isaiah 52:13–53:12 is one comparison for the theme of suffering.

ACT 3:19.notes: SIN-BLOTTING METAPHOR: ἐξαλειφθῆναι ὑμῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας echoes LXX sin-blotting idiom. (1) Isa 43:25 LXX ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἐξαλείφων τὰς ἀνομίας σου ('I am he who blots out your transgressions'); (2) Ps 51:9 LXX (Ps 50:11 LXX) ἐξάλειψον πάσας τὰς ἀνομίας μου ('blot out all my iniquities' — Davidic confession). The ἐξαλείφω metaphor originates in erasing written records (cf. Col 2:14 ἐξαλείψας ... τὸ χειρόγραφον for erasing the debt-certificate). Lexical-idiom echo from LXX into Peter's homiletic-Greek.

ACT 3:20.notes: TIMES-OF-REFRESHING ESCHATOLOGY: καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ κυρίου composite-invokes OT restoration-era motifs. (1) Isa 32:15-17 LXX — Spirit poured from on high, resulting in peace and righteousness (future messianic-era respite). (2) Isa 57:18-19 LXX — God's comfort to the afflicted, 'peace to the far and near' (already cited at Acts 2:39). (3) Num 6:25 LXX ἐπιφάναι κύριος τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ('may the Lord make his face shine') + Ps 16:11 LXX πλήρωμα εὐφροσύνης ἐν τῷ προσώπῳ σου — the face-of-the-Lord presence-metaphor. Thematic-idiomatic allusion, not direct citation.

ACT 3:21.notes: UNIVERSAL RESTORATION: χρόνοι ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων invokes OT new-creation + restoration themes. (1) Isa 65:17 LXX (ἔσται γὰρ ὁ οὐρανὸς καινὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ καινή — new heavens + new earth); (2) Isa 66:22 same new-creation vision; (3) Mal 4:5-6 (LXX 3:22-23) — Elijah comes 'to restore' (ἀποκαταστήσει) all before the day of the Lord. Matt 17:11 uses the cognate verb ἀποκαταστήσει of Elijah's restorative work. The lexical-family (ἀποκατάστασις / ἀποκαθίστημι) is Malachi-rooted for eschatological restoration. Thematic-composite allusion.

ACT 3:22.notes: PROPHET-LIKE-MOSES CITATION: Direct quotation of Deut 18:15 with textual-variation. SBLGNT: κύριος ὁ θεὸς (no pronoun); Deut 18:15 LXX itself: κύριος ὁ θεός σου (2sg); some NT mss: ἡμῶν (ULT) or ὑμῶν (BSB translation). Peter applies Deut 18:15 Christologically — Jesus IS the prophet-like-Moses. Second Temple Judaism held this as a live messianic expectation (John 1:21, 6:14, 7:40). Stephen repeats the same citation at Acts 7:37, confirming Lucan programmatic use. Hebrews 3:1-6 develops Jesus-greater-than-Moses from this starting point.

ACT 3:23.notes: Deuteronomy 18:19 supplies the warning about failing to listen to the prophet. Leviticus 23:29 and Numbers 15:30 provide parallels for being cut off from the people. Hebrew שמע concerns hearing or heeding; כרת supplies the cutting-off language. The Community Rule (1QS IX.11) anticipates a prophet and anointed figures of Aaron and Israel. That line supplies no cutting-off penalty.

ACT 3:25.notes: ABRAHAMIC BLESSING CITATION: Direct quotation of Gen 22:18 LXX (ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν τῷ σπέρματί σου πάντα τὰ ἔθνη τῆς γῆς); parallel tradition Gen 12:3 LXX (ἐνευλογηθήσονται ἐν σοὶ πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς) and Gen 26:4 LXX (to Isaac). Paul cites the same verse at Gal 3:8, 3:16 with the Christological-singular interpretation ('seed' = Christ). Peter's use here anticipates Paul's theological move — the Abrahamic-blessing-to-all-nations finds fulfillment in Jesus the singular-seed (πατριαί = 'families/nations/people-groups' per uW metonymy). Universal-inclusion inclusio with Acts 2:39.

ACT 3:26.notes: SERMON-CLOSING COMPOSITE: τὸν παῖδα αὐτοῦ echoes Isa 52:13 LXX (ὁ παῖς μου — the Servant title, inclusio with v.13 + v.26 framing the sermon's Christology). εὐλογοῦντα ὑμᾶς echoes the Gen 22:18 blessing from v.25 — the Abrahamic-blessing mechanism is now concrete: Jesus-the-Servant, sent to Israel first, blessing by enabling repentance. Composite thematic echo closing the sermon's OT-arc.

ACT 3:8.notes: LAME-LEAP MESSIANIC SIGN: Luke deploys ἅλλομαι in the triple participle περιπατῶν καὶ ἁλλόμενος καὶ αἰνῶν — the exact verb at Isa 35:6 LXX (τότε ἁλεῖται ὡς ἔλαφος ὁ χωλός 'then shall the lame leap like a deer'). Isa 35 is the classic messianic-age-of-healing passage (blind see, deaf hear, lame leap, mute sing) cited by Jesus at Luke 7:22 as the sign that he is the Coming One. Luke shows the messianic-healing continuing through the apostles — the lame man at the Beautiful Gate is another fulfillment-instance. Lexical-echo + semantic-fulfillment, not direct quotation.

ACT 4:11.notes: Psalm 118:22 (LXX 117:22) — direct citation, MODIFIED. SBLGNT reads ὁ λίθος ὁ ἐξουθενηθεὶς ὑφ’ὑμῶν τῶν οἰκοδόμων, ὁ γενόμενος εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας. Peter substitutes ἐξουθενέω 'despise' for the LXX's ἀποδοκιμάζω 'reject (after testing)' used in the synoptic-gospel citations (MAT 21:42, MRK 12:10, LUK 20:17). The substitution is pesher-style modification: personalizes the council's contempt with a stronger word. Note the vocative 'ὑφ’ὑμῶν τῶν οἰκοδόμων' (by YOU, the builders) — Peter applies the rejected-stone role directly to the council members. οἰκοδόμος (agent-noun) is NT hapax (distinct from the οἰκοδομοῦντες participle in the synoptic citations). Ps 118 = final Hallel-psalm (113-118) sung at Passover — Peter's citation carries the Hallel's festal-vindication resonance. This same verse becomes programmatic Christian Messianic-Stone rhetoric: 1 Pet 2:6-7 clusters with Isa 28:16 + Isa 8:14; Rom 9:32-33 (same cluster).

ACT 4:12.notes: Joel 2:32 LXX (= 3:5 in MT/LXX numbering): πᾶς ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται ('everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved'). Peter cited this verse explicitly at ACT 2:21 in the Pentecost sermon. ACT 4:12 makes the Christological identification definite: the ὄνομα (name) that saves = the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth specifically. Lexical-echo cluster ὄνομα + σωθῆναι ('name' + 'be saved') connects the two Petrine sermons. The allusion is structurally programmatic for Acts: what Joel promised, the apostolic preaching delivers — and the Lord-of-the-name is now explicitly identified as Jesus (cf. ACT 2:36 where Peter concludes the Pentecost sermon with that very identification).

ACT 4:24.notes: Acts addresses God directly with σὺ ὁ ποιήσας. Greek Psalm 145:6 (English Psalm 146:6) has the accusative τὸν ποιήσαντα and lists the sea without another καί. In Greek Exodus 20:11 the list including καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν matches Acts, but its introductory clause has the finite verb ἐποίησεν with κύριος as subject.

ACT 4:25.notes: Psalm 2:1 LXX verbatim: Ἱνατί ἐφρύαξαν ἔθνη καὶ λαοὶ ἐμελέτησαν κενά. Introduced with 'God spoke by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of David your servant' — a foundational NT prooftext for Scripture as Spirit-inspired (2 Pet 1:21, 2 Tim 3:16). Ps 2 is THE primary Davidic messianic psalm, the most-cited OT psalm in the NT (Acts 4:25-26; Acts 13:33 [Ps 2:7 applied to resurrection]; Heb 1:5; Heb 5:5; Rev 2:26-27; Rev 12:5; Rev 19:15). Original historical context = royal enthronement psalm responding to vassal-king rebellion at a new Davidic accession. NT hermeneutic = messianic fulfillment, the ultimate 'rebelling nations' = those who oppose the Messiah. φρυάσσω NT hapax 'rage/snort-in-fury' (classical: horses rearing/snorting in battle); μελετάω 'devise/plot'. The believers identify the persecuting council as the very 'nations who rage' — themselves as the Messianic-king side.

ACT 4:26.notes: Psalm 2:2 LXX verbatim: παρέστησαν οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ τοῦ κυρίου καὶ κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ. Completes the Ps 2:1-2 quotation begun at 4:25. Original OT context: κύριος = YHWH, χριστός = the anointed Davidic king (OT-royal-anointing sense, not yet the NT-Christology title). v.27 makes the Christological application explicit: Herod + Pilate + Gentiles + Israel = the rebelling coalition; Jesus = the Anointed. παρίστημι 'take one's stand' = military idiom for 'line up for battle' (cf. LXX Jdt 6:14). The believers' pesher: the unlikely alliance (Herod-Jewish-tetrarch + Pilate-Roman-procurator + Gentile-soldiers + Jewish-crowd) against one man is Ps 2:2's prophetic template fulfilled.

ACT 4:34.notes: Deut 15:4 LXX: οὐκ ἔσται ἐν σοὶ ἐνδεής ('there will be no needy among you') — Acts 4:34 has οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐνδεής τις ἦν ἐν αὐτοῖς. The LXX-lexical match ἐνδεής (NT hapax) is diagnostic — Luke deploys the exact Septuagint word to frame the Jerusalem-church's voluntary-redistribution as the eschatological fulfillment of the Mosaic sabbath-year ideal (Deut 15:1-18 prescribes the seventh-year-release of debts + the-no-needy-among-you principle). The allusion links the Christian community's economic-ethics to the Jubilee-Sabbath vision (Lev 25 + Deut 15). The point is not Marxism but covenant-equity: the community embodies Israel's restored covenantal-economics by voluntary redistribution. κτήτωρ 'owner' also NT hapax, further emphasizing the lexical-distinctiveness of the verse.

ACT 5:2.notes: Joshua 7:1 and Acts 5:2 use related Greek wording for keeping something back. Joshua 7:20–26 recounts confession, recovery of the goods and stoning in the valley. In Acts 5:5 Ananias falls down and dies on hearing Peter. Sapphira falls after Peter speaks in 5:9–10.

ACT 5:30.notes: Peter describes Jesus being hanged on a tree, language that recalls Deuteronomy 21:22–23. Galatians 3:13 quotes the curse explicitly. Acts 5:30 does not quote the curse or report what reason the council gave for putting Jesus to death.

ACT 5:31.notes: RIGHT-HAND EXALTATION + SAVIOR-FORGIVENESS COMPOSITE. (a) τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ ὕψωσεν echoes PSA 110:1 LXX 109:1 — the most-cited OT text in the NT — already invoked in Peter's Pentecost sermon (ACT 2:33-35) and Stephen's vision (ACT 7:55-56); here triple Lucan kerygma-use. (b) ἀρχηγὸν καὶ σωτῆρα thematically echoes PSA 16:10 LXX 15:10 τὸν ὅσιόν σου (cited at ACT 2:27) — the Righteous/Holy One vindicated by resurrection is now the Savior who grants repentance. (c) μετάνοιαν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν echoes ISA 55:7 'Let the wicked forsake his way ... for he will abundantly pardon'. Apostolic-kerygma weave of three threads into one confessional sentence.

ACT 5:32.notes: TWO-OR-THREE-WITNESSES MOTIF. The 'we-and-the-Spirit-are-witnesses' pattern parallels the Torah legal-requirement of multiple witnesses (DEU 19:15 ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων καὶ ἐπὶ στόματος τριῶν μαρτύρων σταθήσεται πᾶν ῥῆμα). Peter structures his witness-claim as legally-compliant by Torah standards: the apostles are witnesses, AND the Holy Spirit is witness — meeting the two-witness threshold even in the Sanhedrin's own legal framework. Rhetorical-theological double-edge: the council that sits in judgment is itself being witnessed-against.

ACT 5:41.notes: PROPHET-SUFFERING REJOICE-IN-DISHONOR motif. κατηξιώθησαν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος ἀτιμασθῆναι is the practical-fulfillment of Jesus' Lucan beatitude LUK 6:22-23 ('blessed are you when men hate you ... for the prophets' reward is great'). The prophet-suffering paradigm itself traces to ISA 53:3 (ἠτιμάσθη καὶ οὐκ ἐλογίσθη — the Suffering Servant dishonored and not esteemed), JER 15:15 (Jeremiah bearing reproach for YHWH's sake), PSA 69:9 ('the reproaches of those who reproach you fell on me'). The apostolic rejoicing reframes dishonor as honor through participation in Servant-prophet destiny.

ACT 5:9.notes: TEST-THE-LORD-AT-MERIBAH motif. πειράζω + πνεῦμα/θεόν echoes Israel's wilderness testing-sin at Massah/Meribah (EXO 17:2-7 'You shall not test the LORD your God'; DEU 6:16; PSA 95:8-11 LXX 94:8-11 'Harden not your hearts as at Meribah'; PSA 106:14; HEB 3:7-11 expounds Psa 95). Peter applies the wilderness-testing paradigm to Ananias and Sapphira: lying to the Holy Spirit in the covenant community is the new-covenant equivalent of testing YHWH in the wilderness. Same sin-pattern, same judgment-principle.

ACT 6:15.notes: MOSES FACE-SHINING ALLUSION. Stephen's face 'like the face of an angel' (πρόσωπον ἀγγέλου) deliberately echoes Moses' post-Sinai shining-face (EXO 34:29-35 δεδόξασται ἡ ὄψις τοῦ χρώματος τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ — LXX). The narrative IRONY is pointed: the false-witnesses in ACT 6:11,14 have just charged Stephen with blaspheming Moses, but the Sanhedrin looks at him and sees Moses' own glorified-face. Luke the narrator thereby settles the charge — Stephen stands in the Moses-prophet succession, not against it. The Moses-typology then intensifies through Stephen's speech (ACT 7:20-44) where Moses is structured as rejected-then-vindicated-deliverer paralleling Jesus. 'Face like an angel' was also Jewish-idiom for divine-presence-marking (2 Esdras 7:97; 1 Enoch 62:15-16; Dan 10:5-6) — converging-backgrounds strengthen the Moses-allusion.

ACT 7:14.greek_matches: 75 in Greek Genesis and Exodus; 70 in Greek Deuteronomy
ACT 7:14.notes: Acts gives seventy-five. Rahlfs Greek Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 also give seventy-five, while Greek Deuteronomy 10:22 gives seventy. Greek Genesis 46:20 includes five additional descendants in Joseph’s family, and 46:27 counts nine on Joseph’s side in Egypt. Hebrew Genesis 46:26 counts sixty-six who came with Jacob and 46:27 gives seventy for the whole household. Agreement on the number alone cannot establish which passage Stephen used.

ACT 7:17.notes: 'The people multiplied' — Stephen echoes Exo 1:7 LXX (ηὐξήθησαν καὶ ἐπληθύνθησαν) doublet. Transition-formula from Joseph-era to Moses-era.

ACT 7:18.notes: The Pharaoh 'who did not know Joseph.' Stephen's Greek matches Exo 1:8 LXX near-verbatim (differs only by ἄχρι οὗ vs. δὲ connective). New-king + ignorant-of-Joseph setup for Egyptian oppression.

ACT 7:19.notes: Pharaoh's 'dealing shrewdly' (κατασοφίζομαι HAPAX here, exact match with Exo 1:10 LXX where Pharaoh says 'let us deal shrewdly with them') + infant-exposure decree reflecting Exo 1:22 (Pharaoh's kill-the-male-infants order). Stephen's NT-unique κατασοφίζομαι is borrowed directly from Exo 1:10 LXX.

ACT 7:28.notes: The Israelite's rejection-of-Moses formula: 'Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?' Verbatim from Exo 2:14 LXX. Stephen quotes the exact words that Exodus itself records, then at v.35 quotes them a third time to frame Moses-the-rejected-redeemer.

ACT 7:3.notes: God's call of Abraham. Stephen quotes Gen 12:1 LXX abbreviated (omits 'and from your father's house' because he telescopes Terah's death to after Abraham's Haran stay — see v.4 compression). Foundational to Stephen's argument that God called Abraham outside the promised land, i.e., God is not location-bound.

ACT 7:30.notes: Burning-bush theophany. Stephen's phrasing 'angel appeared in a flame of fire of a bush' closely follows Exo 3:2 LXX (ὤφθη αὐτῷ ἄγγελος Κυρίου ἐν πυρὶ φλογὸς ἐκ τοῦ βάτου). The angel-equals-God equation runs through vv.30-35.

ACT 7:32.notes: In Exodus 3:6 God identifies himself to Moses by naming the patriarchs. Acts 7:32 and Mark 12:26 express the identification without a finite verb. Matthew 22:32 has εἰμι. Luke 20:37 reports how Moses names the Lord, and 20:38 explicitly contrasts the dead and the living. The Gospel passages discuss resurrection. Here Stephen recounts Moses’s encounter at the bush.

ACT 7:33.notes: 'Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground.' Stephen renders Exo 3:5 LXX near-verbatim.

ACT 7:34.notes: Acts and Greek Exodus 3:7 both have ἰδὼν εἶδον: an aorist participle followed by a finite aorist verb. This Greek construction represents the Hebrew infinitive absolute followed by a finite verb. For what God heard, Greek Exodus 3:7 has κραυγή (“cry”), and Acts has στεναγμός (“groaning”), a noun also used at Romans 8:26.

ACT 7:37.notes: Moses's prophet-like-me prophecy. Stephen's citation matches Peter's earlier use at ACT 3:22 — both use Deut 18:15 as proof-text for Jesus-as-the-prophet-like-Moses. Abbreviated — omits 'him you shall hear' extender.

ACT 7:40.notes: The Israelites' demand of Aaron at the golden-calf incident. Stephen's citation of Exo 32:1 LXX near-verbatim. The rejection-of-Moses lexical-parallel to v.27: the Israelites reject God's chosen deliverer by preferring idols.

ACT 7:41.notes: Acts 7:40 uses the aorist ἐγένετο for what happened to Moses. Greek Exodus 32:1 and 32:23 have the perfect γέγονεν. Acts 7:41 describes making the calf with one verb, ἐμοσχοποίησαν. Greek Exodus 32:4 describes it with ἐποίησεν and the noun μόσχον. A rare word’s occurrence here does not tell us who coined it.

ACT 7:42.notes: Amos's rhetorical question about wilderness-sacrifices. Part 1 of the Amos 5:25-27 LXX quotation continuing into v.43. Stephen reads the Amos prophecy as indicting Israel's wilderness-era worship: formal sacrifices covered inner idolatry.

ACT 7:43.notes: Amos 5:26-27 LXX. Stephen replaces 'beyond Damascus' (LXX Amos 5:27) with 'beyond Babylon' — either a deliberate theological-update (framing the exile to its fuller Babylonian fulfillment, 586 BCE) or following a variant LXX-tradition. The LXX names Molech and Rephan as Israel's idols (both NT-HAPAX here); the MT has Sikkuth and Kiyyun — a major LXX-vs-MT lexical divergence that Stephen's NT-Greek citation preserves by following LXX. 3 hapax in this verse (Μολόχ, Ῥαιφάν, ἐπέκεινα).

ACT 7:44.notes: The tabernacle-made-per-pattern formula. Stephen's κατὰ τὸν τύπον ὃν ἑωράκει echoes Exo 25:40 LXX (κατὰ τὸν τύπον τὸν δεδειγμένον σοι ἐν τῷ ὄρει). Contrasts with v.43: pagan tabernacle (Molech) vs. true tabernacle (God's pattern).

ACT 7:45.notes: Acts 7:45 uses ἐξῶσεν for God driving out the nations. Greek Deuteronomy 7:1 uses ἐξαρεῖ and shares the expression “from before” someone. Greek Psalm 43:3 (Hebrew 44:3, English 44:2) has ἐξωλέθρευσεν and ἐξέβαλες. The passages describe related actions using different verbs.

ACT 7:46.notes: David seeks a dwelling for the God of Jacob in SBLGNT. NA28 reads “for the house of Jacob,” identifying Jacob’s household instead. Greek Psalm 131:5 (Hebrew and English 132:5) has σκήνωμα τῷ θεῷ Ιακωβ, corresponding to the SBLGNT wording. The Psalm provides a verbal parallel; it does not settle how the two readings arose.

ACT 7:48.notes: The Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands. Stephen's thesis echoes Solomon's own dedication-prayer at 1 Kgs 8:27 LXX: 'Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; much less this house that I have built!' Stephen invokes OT-Israel's own theological self-awareness to refute the charge he speaks against the temple.

ACT 7:49.notes: Greek Isaiah 66:1 introduces the speech with “Thus says the Lord.” Acts 7:49 places “says the Lord” between the questions. Where Isaiah has ποῖος τόπος (“what kind of place”), Acts has τίς τόπος (“what place”). Isaiah 66:2 states that God’s hand made these things; Acts 7:50 expresses that claim as a question.

ACT 7:5.notes: The Abrahamic land-and-seed promise. Stephen summarizes the complex of land-promise passages (Gen 12:7 first giving; 13:15 reiteration; 15:18 covenant-cutting; 17:8 covenant-of-circumcision) plus the enslavement-then-deliverance prophecy of Gen 15:13. Stephen's point: God promised land-to-descendants BEFORE Abraham had any descendants.

ACT 7:50.greek_matches: LXX declaration adapted as a question
ACT 7:50.notes: Greek Isaiah 66:1 introduces the speech with “Thus says the Lord.” Acts 7:49 places “says the Lord” between the questions. Where Isaiah has ποῖος τόπος (“what kind of place”), Acts has τίς τόπος (“what place”). Isaiah 66:2 states that God’s hand made these things; Acts 7:50 expresses that claim as a question.

ACT 7:51.notes: Stephen's triple-accusation: 'stiff-necked' (Exo 32:9, 33:3, 33:5, 34:9, Deut 9:6, 9:13, 31:27 — the classic OT indictment of Israel's stubbornness, particularly at golden calf) + 'uncircumcised hearts/ears' (Lev 26:41, Jer 4:4, 6:10, 9:25-26, Ezek 44:7-9 — covenant-disobedience metaphor) + 'resist the Spirit' (Isa 63:10 'they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit'; LXX Num 27:14 for ἀντιπίπτω). 3 hapax in this verse (σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος, ἀντιπίπτω) — densely-packed OT-indictment vocabulary.

ACT 7:53.notes: In Greek Deuteronomy 33:2 the phrase σὺν μυριάσιν Καδης is followed by a distinct clause locating angels with the Lord at his right hand. That scene provides possible background for Acts 7:53. Acts says the hearers received the law εἰς διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων. Galatians 3:19 describes the law as ordained through angels, and Hebrews 2:2 speaks of a word spoken through angels.

ACT 7:56.notes: Son of Man standing at God's right hand. The 'Son of Man' title directly invokes Dan 7:13 LXX (ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου), Jesus's own favored self-designation. The ONLY NT occurrence of 'Son of Man' outside the Gospels (+ REV 1:13, 14:14). Stephen's confession uses Jesus's own Messianic title — making his vision a direct-Messianic claim rejected by his hearers.

ACT 7:6.notes: Acts 7:6 retains enslavement and mistreatment, including the verb κακόω for mistreatment. Greek Genesis 15:13 also has a separate clause with ταπεινόω, to humble, which Acts omits. Both passages give four hundred years. Acts uses different words for the foreign land.

ACT 7:7.notes: Composite citation — Stephen blends Gen 15:14 (κρινῶ ἐγώ, 'I will judge') with Exo 3:12 (λατρεύσουσίν μοι ἐν τῷ τόπῳ τούτῳ, 'they will serve me in this place'). τόπος 'place' is deliberately ambiguous — LXX Exo 3:12 specifies 'this mountain' (Sinai); Stephen's generic τόπος sets up the argument at v.49 that God is not bound to any τόπος (temple).

ACT 8:23.notes: Acts uses χολὴν πικρίας, with “bitterness” in the genitive. Greek Deuteronomy 29:17 pictures a root growing ἐν χολῇ καὶ πικρίᾳ, joining the two nouns in the dative. Greek Isaiah 58:6 uses the singular σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας in the command to loose every bond of injustice. This two-word expression recurs in Acts.

ACT 8:26.notes: ANGELIC-COMMISSIONING FORMULA echoes OT prophet-commissioning idioms: 1 KINGS 17:9 LXX (angel-of-the-Lord directs Elijah to Zarephath), 2 KINGS 1:3 LXX (angel-of-the-Lord directs Elijah to meet the messengers of Ahaziah). The ἄγγελος κυρίου + Ἀνάστηθι imperative + directional-travel-command pattern is OT-prophet-template now applied to Philip-the-evangelist. Not verbal-quotation; genre-pattern background establishing Philip in the prophet-lineage.

ACT 8:27.notes: EUNUCH-INCLUSION — DEUT-TO-ISAIAH REVERSAL: Deut 23:1 LXX (οὐκ εἰσελεύσεται θλαδίας οὐδὲ ἀποκεκομμένος εἰς ἐκκλησίαν κυρίου — 'no one emasculated shall enter the assembly of the Lord') barred physical eunuchs from full-Israel-assembly. But ISA 56:3-5 LXX promises the eschatological-reversal: the eunuch who keeps the covenant shall be given 'within my house and my walls a name better than sons and daughters'). The Ethiopian eunuch's conversion and baptism in vv.36-38 (and his rejoicing-departure in v.39) fulfills the Isa-56 promise. Luke's characterization of the eunuch as a God-fearer who had come to worship at Jerusalem (v.27c) sets up the Deut-restriction-reversal: the eunuch who could only worship peripherally now receives full-Christ-incorporation. Thematic-fulfillment, programmatic for Acts' inclusive-covenant-vision.

ACT 8:32.notes: DIRECT OT-CITATION: ὡς πρόβατον ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἤχθη καὶ ὡς ἀμνὸς ἐναντίον τοῦ κείραντος αὐτὸν ἄφωνος, οὕτως οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ — exact verbatim-match with LXX Isa 53:7 (minor accent-variation only). The passage being read by the Ethiopian eunuch in his chariot. Philip takes this as his starting-point (v.35 ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τῆς γραφῆς ταύτης) to preach Jesus as the Suffering-Servant. SERVANT-SONG cluster: the NT's most-explicit identification of Jesus with the Isaiah-53-Servant. Parallels: LUK 22:37 direct-citation ISA 53:12; 1 PET 2:22-25 ISA 53 application. Philip's exegesis here is programmatic for apostolic Christology.

ACT 8:33.notes: DIRECT OT-CITATION continued from v.32: ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη· τὴν γενεὰν αὐτοῦ τίς διηγήσεται; ὅτι αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ αὐτοῦ — exact LXX Isa 53:8 (variant from MT: the LXX interprets מֵעֹצֶר וּמִמִּשְׁפָּט לֻקָּח as 'in his humiliation his judgment was-taken-away' making the Servant the victim-of-injustice rather than merely afflicted). The LXX-ambiguous τὴν γενεὰν αὐτοῦ τίς διηγήσεται reads as 'who will-describe his generation/descendants?' — our translation takes the descendants-sense primary (since ISA 53:10 LXX ὄψεται σπέρμα promises seed, which the NT applies to the risen Christ's many spiritual-offspring). Philip's preaching from here produces the eunuch's baptism in vv.36-38.

ACT 8:7.notes: Acts 8:7 names people who were paralyzed and people who were lame. Isaiah 35:6 pictures the lame person leaping. Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22 name the lame walking among other signs. None of these comparisons has the same pair as Acts. Acts 5:16 reports healing of people troubled by unclean spirits without describing a cry.

ACT 9:14.notes: "Those who call on your name" — ἐπικαλουμένους τὸ ὄνομά σου. The phrase echoes LXX Joel 3:5 (= English Joel 2:32) "πᾶς ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται" — "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." This verse was already cited explicitly at ACT 2:21 (Peter at Pentecost) and is reused by Paul at ROM 10:13. Here at ACT 9:14 (Ananias speaking) the ἐπικαλούμενοι pattern identifies the Christian community by the Joel-prophecy designator — "those-who-call-on-the-name." The allusion is technical-identifying, not fresh-citation. Same phrase recurs at ACT 9:21 (Damascus crowd describing believers) and 22:16 (Ananias baptizing Saul: "καὶ ἐπικάλεσαι τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ"). The Thai render "ร้องออกพระนาม" preserves the Joel-echo across occurrences.

ACT 9:15.notes: The Lord tells Ananias to go and describes Saul as his chosen instrument. Greek Isaiah 49:6 has τέθεικά σε, and Greek Jeremiah 1:5 also uses τίθημι in naming a prophet to the nations. Acts 9:15 shares the theme of a mission to the nations without using that verb. Acts 27:24 promises an appearance before Caesar; the narrative ends without describing the audience.

ACT 9:3.notes: Theophanic light-from-heaven motif. The sudden bright light around Saul echoes the Sinai-theophany cloud-and-fire (LXX Exo 19:16-18, 24:17 the glory of YHWH "as devouring fire") and the Ezekielian merkabah-vision (LXX Eze 1:4 a great cloud with fire flashing, 1:27-28 the radiant kavod-glory of YHWH on the throne). Not a verbal citation; Luke uses theophanic-tradition vocabulary to frame the Christophany as a genuine divine-glory encounter. Paul himself will later echo this at 2 Cor 4:6 "God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" — direct personal-reflection on his Damascus-road experience as creation-light theophany.

ACT 9:5.notes: Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἰησοῦς — Jesus self-identification formula. The absolute "I am" construction (ἐγώ εἰμι + predicate) echoes the LXX Exo 3:14 divine-self-identification (ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν "I am the existing-one"). This is the same formula used by the Johannine-Jesus for his absolute "I AM" sayings (JHN 6:35, 8:58, 10:11, etc.). Luke is not directly quoting LXX Exo 3:14 here; rather, the ἐγώ εἰμι self-disclosure pattern is intertextually charged — the risen Christ identifies himself with the ἐγώ εἰμι formula that LXX Exo 3:14 uses for YHWH himself. Allusion rather than citation; the theological freight is Christological-identity.

GAL 1:15.notes: Greek Isaiah 49:1 shares the wording about the mother's womb and the calling. Jeremiah 1:5 speaks of God knowing and consecrating Jeremiah before birth and appointing him to the nations, a comparison with Paul's commission to the Gentiles in Galatians 1:16. The passages illuminate a prophetic calling through different verbal and thematic connections.

GAL 2:16.notes: Greek Psalm 142:2 (143:2 in common English and Thai numbering) says no living person is justified before God, addressing him as ‘you.’ Galatians speaks of all flesh, adds the reference to works of law, and omits ‘before you.’ Romans 3:20 similarly has all flesh and retains ‘before him.’

GAL 3:10.notes: Greek Deuteronomy 27:26 names every person, uses the future ἐμμενεῖ with ἐν, and speaks of all the words of this law. Galatians omits ἄνθρωπος, uses present ἐμμένει, and describes what is written in the book of the law. Compare the book and writing language at Deuteronomy 28:58, 61. Deuteronomy 27:26 itself remains the source of the curse.

GAL 3:11.notes: Paul omits μου from LXX (HOI dikaios ek pisteos mou zēsetai) → ho dikaios ek pisteos zēsetai. Same citation: Rom 1:17; Heb 10:38. The thesis-verse of Pauline justification doctrine.

GAL 3:12.notes: Leviticus 18:5 in Greek uses the neuter plural relative ἃ in ἃ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς. Galatians has ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς, with the doer expressed through the article and participle. Romans 10:5 takes up the same Torah text in its own sentence.

GAL 3:13.notes: Paul changes LXX kekatēramenos hupo theou pas kremamenos epi xulou → epikataratos pas ho kremamenos epi xulou (matches v.10 epikataratos for cognate-echo; drops hupo theou). Applied to Christ's crucifixion: he bore the law's curse-pronouncement substitutionarily.

GAL 3:16.notes: Genesis 13:15 in Greek has the exact phrase καὶ τῷ σπέρματί σου, “and to your offspring.” In Genesis 13:16 the same singular noun refers to descendants collectively. Paul identifies the one offspring with Christ in this verse. He applies the singular to a group in Galatians 3:29. The related Abrahamic promise texts supply the wider context.

GAL 3:20.notes: theos heis estin echoes the Shema (Deut 6:4 LXX kurios ho theos hēmōn kurios heis estin). Paul applies the monotheistic confession not as polemic against polytheism but as supporting argument: God acting alone (without mediator) — as in the Abraham promise — implies one-party-divine-guarantee, contrast with the two-party Sinai covenant (which required mediator).

GAL 3:28.notes: The opening ในพระคริสต์นั้น supplies the setting from the closing clause “in Christ Jesus.” Greek repeats οὐκ ἔνι without a locative phrase in the three contrasts. The final pair uses καί, reflected in ชายและหญิง, an allusion to Genesis 1:27. First Corinthians 12:13 and Colossians 3:11 offer parallels for the social contrasts without that creation wording. Baptism in verse 27 supplies context, but does not establish that these words belonged to an earlier baptismal formula. Tregelles has ἅπαντες where SBLGNT, WH, NA28 and RP have πάντες, all the readers.

GAL 3:6.notes: Genesis 15:6 in Greek has ἐπίστευσεν Αβραμ, with the verb before Abram. Galatians introduces the citation with καθὼς and places Abraham’s later name first: Ἀβραὰμ ἐπίστευσεν. Both texts use the passive for reckoning. The Thai makes God the one who reckons Abraham's faith as righteousness and marks the quoted passage with double quotation marks.

GAL 3:8.notes: Genesis 12:3 in Greek promises blessing ‘in you’ for all the families of the earth. Genesis 18:18 has ‘in him’ and ‘all the nations of the earth.’ Galatians combines ‘in you’ with ‘all the nations’ and omits ‘of the earth.’ The promise is presented as good news announced beforehand to Abraham.

GAL 4:22.notes: Summary reference to the Hagar/Sarah / Ishmael/Isaac narrative complex. Paul does not quote a specific verse; he summarizes the well-known Genesis story for the allegorical typology of vv.22-31.

GAL 4:27.notes: After his citation introduction, Paul follows Greek Isaiah 54:1 from εὐφράνθητι through τὸν ἄνδρα. The Isaiah text continues with εἶπεν γὰρ κύριος, outside the excerpt. The Thai in Isaiah and Galatians follows the Hebrew and Greek respectively, explaining differences in the imperatives and the absence of a final speaker attribution here.

GAL 4:30.notes: Greek Genesis 21:10 uses two demonstratives for ‘this slave woman’ and a simple οὐ. Galatians omits the demonstratives, strengthens the negative with μή, and replaces ‘my son Isaac’ with ‘the free woman's son.’ SBLGNT uses the future κληρονομήσει; Robinson–Pierpont has a subjunctive. Paul applies the statement to the dispute over inheritance; the quotation itself prescribes no general policy for removing church members.

GAL 5:14.notes: The citation gives the neighbor-love command of Leviticus 19:18. Jesus speaks it in Matthew 22:39 and Mark 12:31. In Luke 10:27 the legal expert answers Jesus. Galatians uses เจ้า and ตนเอง, Leviticus uses เจ้า and ตัวเอง, and Romans 13:9 and James 2:8 use ท่าน and ตนเอง. These differences in address and reflexive wording convey the same command.

GAL 6:7.notes: Sowing-and-reaping proverbial-formula echoing OT wisdom-tradition. Job 4:8 (those who sow trouble reap the same), Prov 22:8 (sows injustice reaps calamity), Hos 8:7 (sows the wind reaps the whirlwind), Hos 10:12-13 (sow righteousness, reap steadfast love). Paul applies the universalizing-moral-axiom to flesh-vs-Spirit sowing in v.8.

JHN 10:11.notes: 'I am the good shepherd' echoes the OT messianic-shepherd promise (EZE 34:11-16, 23-24 'I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David'; PSA 23 'YHWH is my shepherd'). Strong allusion-cluster, not direct citation. Jesus's claim weaponizes the EZE 34 indictment of corrupt Israelite shepherds against the present religious leadership.

JHN 10:16.notes: 'There will be one flock and one shepherd' near-quotes EZE 37:24 'David my servant shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd' (cf. EZE 34:23 same theme). The ἄλλα πρόβατα ('other sheep not of this fold') extends the promise beyond ethnic Israel — Gentile inclusion in messianic-flock prophecy.

JHN 10:34.notes: ἐγὼ εἶπα Θεοί ἐστε — direct quotation of LXX PSA 81:6 (= MT 82:6) 'I have said, you are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you.' Jesus uses this in qal-vahomer argument: if Scripture calls human judges 'gods,' the Father-sanctified-and-sent Son can certainly be called Son-of-God without blasphemy.

JHN 10:36.notes: ἡγίασεν ('sanctified, set apart') of the Father's act toward Jesus echoes priestly-consecration patterns: EXO 28:41 (Aaron and his sons consecrated to priesthood); JER 1:5 ('before I formed you in the womb I sanctified you, I appointed you a prophet to the nations'). Jesus's sanctified-and-sent designation patterns the OT consecration-for-divine-mission motif while transcending it (Father-Son sanctification rather than human priest/prophet).

JHN 11:27.notes: ὁ εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἐρχόμενος ('the One coming into the world') in Martha's confession echoes the prophet-like-Moses promise of DEU 18:15 'I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers ... and put my words in his mouth.' Standard 1st-cent. Jewish messianic expectation; cf. JHN 6:14 ('the prophet who is to come into the world'); JHN 1:21 (questioning of John the Baptist about 'the Prophet').

JHN 11:52.notes: 'Scattered children of God gathered into one' echoes the OT regathering-from-exile motif: EZE 36:24 ('I will take you from the nations and gather you'); DEU 30:3-5 (regathering-of-the-dispersed promise); ISA 11:12 ('he shall assemble the dispersed of Israel'). The Johannine extension: the regathering scope is universalized to include Gentiles ('children of God' = broader than ethnic Israel) — the atonement scope is universal-yet-particular.

JHN 12:13.notes: ὡσαννά + εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου — direct citation of PSA 118:25-26 (the Hallel psalm, recited at Passover). 'Hosanna' = Hebrew הוֹשִׁיעָה־נָּא 'save-please now'. The crowd's triumphal-entry acclamation. Same citation appears at MRK 11:9-10, MAT 21:9, LUK 19:38 (Synoptic parallels).

JHN 12:15.notes: The approaching king and the young donkey recall Zechariah 9:9. John abbreviates and adapts the wording. In particular, πῶλον ὄνου, ลูกลา, is John’s wording for the young animal. “Do not fear” also recalls the reassurance to Zion in Zephaniah 3:16. Zechariah opens with a call to rejoice. John’s line brings these motifs together.

JHN 12:38.notes: Κύριε τίς ἐπίστευσεν τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν — direct LXX citation of ISA 53:1 (opening of the Suffering Servant chapter). Same verse cited at ROM 10:16. John's contextual application: the unbelief of Israel was prophesied; Jesus's rejection fits the Servant-Messiah pattern.

JHN 12:40.notes: Τετύφλωκεν αὐτῶν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ... ἐπώρωσεν αὐτῶν τὴν καρδίαν — paraphrastic citation of ISA 6:10 (the hardening-prophecy from Isaiah's commission). Same verse cited variously at MRK 4:12, MAT 13:14-15, LUK 8:10, ACT 28:26-27. The Johannine version is closer to the MT than the LXX in some details. Theologically grounds the unbelief-of-Israel pattern.

JHN 13:18.notes: Jesus adapts Psalm 41:10 in the Hebrew and Thai numbering (41:9 in common English editions, 40:10 in Greek). Greek Psalms uses the eating verb ἐσθίω, plural loaves and a noun for a heel action. John uses τρώγων, singular bread and “raised his heel.” RP reads “with me” where the selected text has “my bread.” The Thai preserves the heel and explains the hostile action with ทำการต่อต้านเรา. The psalm speaks of a trusted companion without naming Ahithophel.

JHN 13:19.notes: ἐγώ εἰμι (absolute, no predicate) — Jesus's signature divine-self-identification echoing EXO 3:14 LXX 'ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν' (the divine name revealed to Moses) and ISA 43:10 'ἐγώ εἰμι' (the prophetic absolute-I-AM cluster). Same formula at JHN 4:26, 6:20, 8:24, 8:28, 8:58, 18:5-8.

JHN 14:27.notes: 'Peace I leave with you' echoes the Aaronic priestly-blessing of NUM 6:24-26 ('the LORD bless you and keep you ... and give you peace'). Christ as the eternal high-priest dispenses the priestly-blessing-peace. Also prefigures the resurrection-greeting 'εἰρήνη ὑμῖν' (JHN 20:19, 21, 26).

JHN 14:8.notes: Philip's request 'show us the Father' echoes Moses's theophany-petition in EXO 33:18 ('show me your glory'). The OT pattern of seeking-divine-vision is fulfilled in Christ — the Father is being seen in the Son's face (per v.9). Implicit-allusion that orients Philip's request as a continuation of OT theophany-petitions.

JHN 15:25.notes: “They hated me without cause” recalls either Psalm 35:19 or Psalm 69:5 in Hebrew and Thai numbering (69:4 in common English editions). Greek Psalms 34:19 and 68:5 use the participle μισοῦντες. John uses a finite verb, ἐμίσησαν. Thai Psalm 35:19 uses โดยไร้สาเหตุ and Psalm 69:5 uses โดยไม่มีเหตุ, also used here. Both psalms describe undeserved hostility.

JHN 15:3.notes: Allusion to PSA 119:9 ('How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word') — cleansing-via-word theme. Christ's word as the means by which the disciples are 'already clean' parallels the Psalm's word-as-purifier. Echoes also EPH 5:26 'washing of water with the word' (NT-internal, not OT-claim).

JHN 17:12.notes: Jesus speaks of the fulfillment of Scripture without naming a particular verse. Psalm 41:10 in Hebrew and Eremos numbering (English 41:9) is a likely connection, especially because John 13:18 quotes the close companion’s betrayal. Psalm 109:8 is another comparison used in Acts 1:20 in connection with Judas’s replacement. The prayer itself does not quote that psalm. SBLGNT’s ᾧ refers to the name given to Jesus; Robinson–Pierpont has οὓς, referring to the people given to him.

JHN 17:6.notes: Allusion-cluster to the YHWH-name-revelation tradition: EXO 3:14 (the I-AM-WHO-I-AM Sinai-call name-disclosure), EXO 33:19 (YHWH proclaims his name to Moses on the cleft of the rock), EXO 34:5-7 (YHWH-name-and-attributes proclamation). Christ's ‘I have revealed Your name to those You have given me’ takes up the OT-pattern of YHWH's-self-revelation-via-the-Name and applies it to his earthly ministry — Christ as the eschatological-fulfillment of the Sinai-name-revelation.

JHN 18:1.notes: John names the Kidron and describes a garden without naming it. Judas knew the place because Jesus often met there with the disciples (18:2). Matthew 26:36 names Gethsemane and relates prayer there on this occasion. David also crossed the Kidron while fleeing in 2 Samuel 15:23, a possible narrative echo.

JHN 19:24.notes: DIRECT CITATION of PSA 22:18 LXX (= LXX 21:19): διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτιά μου ἑαυτοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμόν μου ἔβαλον κλῆρον. PSA 22 is the most-cited-Psalm in the Passion-narratives — its-lament-pattern (vv.1, 7-8, 16, 18) finds detail-by-detail fulfillment at the cross. Christ's suffering is patterned-on the righteous-sufferer-Davidic typology.

JHN 19:28.notes: Fulfillment of PSA 22:15 ‘my strength is dried up like a potsherd; my tongue sticks to my jaws’ + PSA 69:21 ‘for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.’ Christ's ‘I thirst’ saying explicitly framed by John as Scripture-completion (ἵνα τελειωθῇ ἡ γραφή). The two-Psalms-of-righteous-sufferer cluster in cross-narratives.

JHN 19:29.notes: Allusion to EXO 12:22 LXX — hyssop (ὕσσωπος) used to apply Passover-lamb-blood to doorposts at the original Exodus. The hyssop-detail (otherwise odd to mention) preserves the Passover-typology. Christ as true Passover-Lamb (cf. 1 COR 5:7); the hyssop that-once-applied-blood now-touches-the-Lamb-himself.

JHN 19:36.notes: DIRECT CITATION (compound): EXO 12:46 LXX + NUM 9:12 LXX (Passover-lamb stipulation: ὀστοῦν οὐ συντρίψετε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ ‘you shall not break a bone of it’) + PSA 34:20 (LXX 33:21) (righteous-sufferer-bones-protected: ‘he keeps all his bones, not one of them is broken’). The compound-citation establishes Christ as both true-Passover-Lamb and righteous-sufferer of the Psalms — the not-breaking-of-bones (because Christ-already-dead before-soldiers-arrived) fulfills both typologies simultaneously.

JHN 19:37.notes: DIRECT CITATION of ZEC 12:10. Greek ἐξεκέντησαν (‘they-pierced’) reflects the MT דָּקָרוּ rather than the mainstream LXX rendering κατωρχήσαντο (‘they-mocked-or-trampled’) — JHN's quotation aligns with the Aquila/Symmachus/Theodotion correction-toward-MT. PHRASE-LOCK with REV 1:7 same-Zechariah-citation in eschatological-context — dual fulfillment: soldiers/onlookers see-pierced-Christ now, all-people see-pierced-Christ at parousia.

JHN 19:38.notes: Allusion to ISA 53:9 — ‘they made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death.’ Joseph of Arimathea is described as wealthy (MAT 27:57); Christ-buried in the rich-man's-tomb fulfills the prophecy after-being-crucified-with-criminals. The cross + tomb-pair completes the ISA 53:9 dual-fulfillment.

JHN 19:9.notes: Allusion to ISA 53:7 — the silent-suffering-servant: ‘he was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.’ Christ's-silence before Pilate fulfills the Suffering-Servant typology. The silence-as-eloquence motif central to Servant-Song fulfillment.

JHN 1:11.notes: His own people did not receive Him — alludes to Isa 53:3 'he was despised and rejected by men' (Suffering Servant). Establishes the rejection-pattern that climaxes at the cross.

JHN 1:14.notes: The verb ἐσκήνωσεν, “dwelt” or “pitched his tent,” and the mention of glory allude to God’s presence with Israel. Hebrew Exodus 25:8 says God will dwell among the people. Greek Exodus 25:8 says “I shall appear among you.” Greek Exodus 40:34–35 speaks of the tent, σκηνή, being filled with the Lord’s glory.

JHN 1:17.notes: Law given through Moses formula — alludes to the giving of the Decalogue and the Mosaic Torah. No direct quotation; allusive reference to the OT framework that Jesus-Christ-grace-and-truth supersedes.

JHN 1:18.notes: No one has seen God — alludes to Exod 33:20 'no one shall see me and live' (also 1 Tim 6:16). Establishes the divine-invisibility-by-nature theology that Christ overcomes by exegeting/revealing the Father.

JHN 1:23.notes: John the Baptist applies Isaiah 40:3 to himself in his answer. Greek Isaiah says to prepare the Lord’s way and to make straight the paths. John gives a single imperative, Εὐθύνατε, to make the Lord’s way straight. Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3 and Luke 3:4 give the two imperatives in the narrator’s quotation.

JHN 1:29.greek_matches: shared lamb noun and related sacrificial images
JHN 1:29.notes: Greek Isaiah 53:7 describes a sheep (πρόβατον) led to slaughter and a lamb (ἀμνός) silent before the shearer. Isaiah 53:4 has φέρει for bearing our sins, while John uses αἴρων. Exodus 12:5 allows a sheep or goat from the flock. In Genesis 22:8 Abraham speaks of a sheep, and a ram appears in 22:13. These are possible sacrificial and thematic backgrounds for John’s title. None supplies the entire expression.

JHN 1:34.greek_matches: shared chosen title and Spirit motif
JHN 1:34.notes: The title ὁ ἐκλεκτὸς τοῦ θεοῦ may allude to Isaiah 42:1 and its Spirit motif. Hebrew Isaiah opens “Behold my servant.” Greek Isaiah names Jacob as God’s servant and Israel as “my chosen one,” ὁ ἐκλεκτός μου. The expression in John is consequently related but distinct.

JHN 1:36.notes: The Baptist says “Look, the Lamb of God” in the hearing of two disciples. At 1:29 John gives a similar declaration the following day without identifying its audience as the earlier delegation. Papyrus 66 continues in verse 36 with ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου, “who takes away the sin of the world.” SBLGNT, followed by the Thai, ends with the title. The Passover lamb and Isaiah’s lamb are possible allusions in both verses; the comparison with Genesis 22:8 also appears at 1:29.

JHN 1:47.notes: No δόλος in Nathanael — alludes to Gen 27:35 LXX (Isaac to Esau: 'your brother came with deceit, μετὰ δόλου, and took your blessing'). Jacob (renamed Israel) was characterized by δόλος; Nathanael is the inverse-Jacob, the renewed-Israel-without-deceit. Sets up v.51's Jacob's ladder allusion (Gen 28:12).

JHN 1:51.notes: Genesis 28:12 supplies the angels ascending and descending on Jacob’s ladder. Ezekiel 1:1 provides a comparison with opened heavens, and Daniel 7:13–14 with one like a son of man. Mark 1:10 says the heavens are torn open, while Matthew 3:16 says they opened. John’s ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου makes the Son of Man the focus of the movement. Thai เหนือ locates it over him. The identification of Jesus as the ladder is an interpretation of the image.

JHN 20:1.notes: Allusion to GEN 1:3 (creation-light). The pre-dawn ‘still-dark’ + first-day-of-week echoes the original-creation-week's first-day light-emerges-from-darkness pattern. Christ's-resurrection inaugurates new-creation paralleling original-creation. The JHN narrative-pattern of cosmic-symbolism (light/darkness, creation/new-creation) supports this typological reading.

JHN 20:12.notes: Allusion to EXO 25:18-22 — the two cherubim on the mercy-seat of the Ark of the Covenant (one at each end). The two angels at head and feet of the empty grave-slab parallels the cherubim flanking the mercy-seat. Christ's empty grave as eschatological-mercy-seat where atonement is completed and witnessed. The cherubim-mercy-seat is where God ‘meets’ Israel (EXO 25:22) — now the empty-tomb is where the risen Christ meets the new-Israel.

JHN 20:22.notes: DIRECT VERBAL ALLUSION — same rare Greek verb ἐμφυσάω (NT-hapax here) appears in LXX GEN 2:7 (God breathes life into Adam: ‘ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ πνοὴν ζωῆς’) and LXX EZK 37:9 (Spirit-breath into the dry bones: ‘ἐμφύσησον εἰς τοὺς νεκροὺς τούτους καὶ ζησάτωσαν’). Christ's-breathing-the-Spirit on disciples enacts a new-creation moment paralleling original-Adam-creation + new-Israel-from-dry-bones. The verbal-allusion is deliberate Johannine signaling. New-Adam Christology (1 COR 15:45).

JHN 20:9.notes: John says that the other disciple saw and believed. The verb has no expressed object. Verse 9 connects the disciples’ lack of scriptural understanding with γάρ, “for.” It says Jesus must rise from the dead without naming a passage. Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53:10 and Hosea 6:2 offer thematic comparisons. John does not identify them as his source.

JHN 2:16.notes: Conceptual allusion to Zech 14:21 (no merchant/Canaanite in the house of the LORD of hosts). The wording is not a quotation but an evocation of the eschatological-purification motif (cf. Mal 3:1-4 "the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple"). Jesus enacts in real time what Zech 14:21 prophesies for the Day of the LORD. ADDED TO NT_OT_CITATIONS for John 2 (Eremos translation 2026-04-26).

JHN 2:17.greek_matches: direct quotation with a verbal variant
JHN 2:17.notes: John 2:17 uses the future form καταφάγεται. Rahlfs prints the aorist κατέφαγέν με in Psalm 68:10, and the Hebrew of Psalm 69:10 also describes the zeal as having consumed the speaker. A future form is also attested in the Greek Psalter. The difference between the printed editions does not establish how John came to use the future. Psalm 69:10 in Hebrew numbering corresponds to 69:9 in common English numbering.

JHN 3:13.notes: Jesus' οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν ('no one has ascended into heaven') echoes Prov 30:4 LXX τίς ἀνέβη εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν ('who has ascended into heaven?') — the rhetorical-question denying human-ability-to-climb-to-heaven for divine knowledge. Cf. Deut 30:12 'who will go up to heaven for us...?' Jesus' point: only the One-who-descended-from-heaven (himself) has the heavenly knowledge to communicate. Greek does not match LXX wording — paraphrase-reuse of the rhetorical structure with explicit-Christological resolution. Implicit Christology: Jesus is the Wisdom-from-on-high that Prov 30:4's question implicitly seeks.

JHN 3:14.notes: Jesus references Moses lifting the bronze serpent on a pole in the wilderness — Israelites bitten by fiery serpents could look at the bronze-snake-on-pole and live (Num 21:8-9). Jesus draws a typological parallel to his own crucifixion-lifting: ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. The καθὼς...οὕτως simile-formula. Wisdom of Solomon 16:6-7 (deuterocanonical, not authoritative for our project but historically informative) already moralized the serpent-incident. Greek does not match LXX wording verbatim — paraphrase-typology, not direct quotation. Christological-key for the Johannine ὑψόω motif (8:28; 12:32, 34).

JHN 3:5.notes: Jesus' phrase γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ πνεύματος (born of water and Spirit) alludes to Ezekiel 36:25-27 — God's new-covenant promise: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean ... I will put my Spirit within you.' The water-cleansing + Spirit-indwelling pairing is the OT eschatological-restoration theme. Per uW figs-metaphor: most natural reading. Jesus rebukes Nicodemus in v.10 for not recognizing 'these things' as a teacher of Israel — the Ezek 36 echo is the implicit-OT-substrate Nicodemus should-have-known. Also resonant with Jer 31:31-34 (new covenant on the heart) and Ezek 37:1-14 (dry bones revived by Spirit).

JHN 4:10.notes: ὕδωρ ζῶν ('living water') metaphor — draws on the prophetic-tradition of God-as-fountain-of-living-waters (JER 2:13 'they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters'; JER 17:13 'spring of living waters'), the eschatological-temple-river (EZEK 47:1-12), and the Jerusalem-as-source-of-living-waters in messianic age (ZECH 14:8 'on that day living waters shall flow out from Jerusalem'). Jesus identifies HIMSELF as the source — the prophetic-promised-spring is Christ. Recurs at JHN 7:38-39 where the Evangelist explicitly identifies the living-water as the Spirit.

JHN 4:14.notes: πηγὴ ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον ('spring of water leaping up to eternal life') — alludes to ISA 12:3 'with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation' (eschatological joy-spring) and ISA 58:11 'you shall be like a watered garden, like a spring whose waters do not fail.' The Spirit-given inner-spring of Johannine theology fulfills both Isaianic images.

JHN 4:19.notes: Samaritan messianic expectation — the Tahebh ('restorer'), grounded in DEUT 18:15-19 (the Mosaic-prophet expectation: 'a prophet like me from your midst'). When the Samaritan woman calls Jesus 'prophet' (προφήτης), her conceptual framework places him on the Tahebh-trajectory: the eschatological-Mosaic-prophet who would restore Samaritan-Israel. Jesus' coming 'I AM' (v.26) accepts and transcends this framework.

JHN 4:26.notes: Ἐγώ εἰμι (I AM) — first explicit Johannine I-AM-self-disclosure (predicate-less form). Resonates with LXX EXO 3:14 ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν ('I am the existing one' — divine-name revelation to Moses) and the Isaianic ἐγώ εἰμι formulae (ISA 41:4 'I AM the first and the last'; 43:10 'before me no god was formed'; 43:25 'I, I am he who blots out your transgressions'; 46:4 'I am he, I will carry you'; 51:12 'I, I am he who comforts you' — all anarthrous ἐγώ εἰμι in LXX, divine-self-identification). The bare ἐγώ εἰμι in JHN 4:26 carries surface-Messianic-identification (answering the woman's expectation) AND deeper-divine-name resonance (especially explicit at JHN 8:58 'before Abraham was, I am'). First in the Johannine I-AM disclosure-cluster.

JHN 4:5.notes: Jacob's gift of the field at Shechem to Joseph — patriarchal land-grant tradition. GEN 48:22 records Jacob giving Joseph 'one portion above your brothers' (a Shechem land-grant, the Hebrew shechem ambiguous between place-name and 'shoulder/portion'). JOSH 24:32 records Joseph's bones interred at Shechem in 'the parcel of ground that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor.' Johannine narrative-allusion grounding the well-locale's covenant-history.

JHN 5:17.notes: Jesus' claim "my Father is working until now and I am working" engages the Jewish exegesis of Gen 2:2-3 (God's Sabbath-rest from creation): rabbinic theology acknowledged that God's providential work continued even on Sabbath; Jesus claims the same prerogative as a deity-claim (recognized as such in v.18). Cf. Philo, On the Cherubim 87-90; Genesis Rabbah 11.10.

JHN 5:18.notes: The leaders' move to kill Jesus for blasphemy (calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God) invokes Lev 24:16 LXX (death-penalty for blasphemy of the Name). The legal basis for the persecution-program that culminates at the cross is laid here.

JHN 5:21.notes: The combination of "raises the dead" + "makes alive" (ἐγείρει τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ ζῳοποιεῖ) draws on the OT divine-prerogative formula. Deut 32:39: "I kill and I make alive" (LXX ἀποκτενῶ καὶ ζῆν ποιήσω). 1 Sam 2:6: "YHWH kills and makes alive" (Hannah's prayer). 2 Kings 5:7: "Am I God to kill and make alive?" Jesus claims this exclusively-divine prerogative for the Son.

JHN 5:22.notes: Universal-judgment delegated from Father to Son matches Daniel 7:13-14: "to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him." The eschatological-judgment role assigned to the Son-of-Man figure is the basis for v.27's explicit citation.

JHN 5:27.greek_matches: related title and grant of authority
JHN 5:27.notes: Daniel 7:13–14 depicts one like a son of man receiving dominion. Old Greek Daniel explicitly uses ἐξουσία for authority; Theodotion includes rule, honor and kingdom and then describes enduring authority. John specifically says authority to execute judgment. The anarthrous predicate “Son of Man” is grammatically possible in its own right. The connection with Daniel is an allusion.

JHN 5:29.notes: The double-resurrection language (ἀνάστασις ζωῆς / ἀνάστασις κρίσεως) directly echoes Dan 12:2 LXX: πολλοὶ τῶν καθευδόντων ἐν γῆς χώματι ἐξεγερθήσονται, οὗτοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον καὶ οὗτοι εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν καὶ εἰς αἰσχύνην αἰώνιον. The substantive shift from "life vs shame" to "life vs judgment" is Johannine theological clarification: the OT "shame and contempt" is an anthropological description; John's "judgment" names the divine-juridical reality behind it.

JHN 5:3.notes: John lists blind people, lame people and people with withered limbs (คนแขนขาลีบ). Isaiah 35:5–6 describes blind, deaf, lame and speech-impaired people. Blindness and lameness provide a thematic parallel. Isaiah has no counterpart to ξηρῶν here. The chapter footer explains the longer reading about waiting for the water and the angel.

JHN 5:31.notes: Jesus invokes the two-witness rule of Deut 19:15: "a single witness shall not suffice... only on the evidence of two witnesses or three witnesses shall a charge be established." Self-testimony alone is legally invalid; Jesus then enumerates the additional witnesses (the Father v.32, John the Baptist v.33, the works v.36, the Father directly v.37, the Scriptures v.39, Moses v.46).

JHN 5:37.notes: Jesus addresses these hearers directly about never hearing the Father’s voice or seeing his form (รูป). Deuteronomy 4:12 recalls hearing a voice without seeing a likeness. In Greek Numbers 12:8 ἐν εἴδει describes how God speaks to Moses, while what Moses sees is τὴν δόξαν κυρίου, the Lord’s glory. Hebrew Numbers speaks of the LORD’s form. Exodus 24:10 also describes an encounter involving several people. These parallels do not establish a universal claim that Moses alone saw God.

JHN 5:44.notes: τὸν μόνον θεόν ("the only God") echoes the Shema (Deut 6:4 LXX: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστιν). Ironic indictment: the leaders pride themselves on monotheism but do not actually seek the only-God's honor — true devotion to the only-God includes honoring his Son (cf. v.23).

JHN 5:46.notes: "Moses wrote about me" includes (1) direct prophecy (Deut 18:15-19 "a prophet like me from your brothers"); (2) typology (Passover lamb Exod 12; bronze serpent Num 21:9 = JHN 3:14; Manna Exod 16 = JHN 6); (3) covenant-trajectory (Gen 3:15, Gen 49:10, Num 24:17). The Pentateuch's Christological-witness is the cumulative weight Jesus invokes.

JHN 5:5.notes: The 38-year duration of the man's illness parallels Israel's 38-year wilderness span between Kadesh-Barnea and the Zered-crossing (Deut 2:14). Johannine numeric-echo: the paralytic typifies Israel-under-judgment awaiting messianic rescue.

JHN 6:14.notes: The crowd's identification of Jesus as 'the Prophet' (ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον) draws on Deut 18:15-19 (the Mosaic-prophet promise: 'YHWH your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your midst, from your brothers'). The bread-from-heaven sign + the mountain-setting + the Passover-context all reinforce the new-Moses typology.

JHN 6:19.notes: They have rowed twenty-five or thirty stadia, about 4.6–5.6 km at 185 m per stadion. The route is not specified precisely enough to locate the boat at the center. Job, speaking about God in 9:8, describes him walking on the sea. Psalm 77:19 and Habakkuk 3:15 provide related sea imagery. Calling this the fifth sign reflects a common way of counting the signs.

JHN 6:20.notes: Jesus' absolute Ἐγώ εἰμι (no predicate) on the storm-tossed sea evokes the divine 'I AM' formula: Exod 3:14 LXX (ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν), Isa 41:4 (κἀγὼ ἐγώ εἰμι), Isa 43:10 (ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι), Isa 51:12. The placement (post-storm, post-walking-on-water) makes the divine-allusion deliberate. First absolute I-AM in JHN; sets up the predicative I-AMs that follow (vv.35, 41, 48, 51 'I AM the bread of life').

JHN 6:31.notes: The crowd quotes Scripture about the manna. Psalm 78:24 (Greek 77:24) closely parallels the giving of bread from heaven. Exodus 16:4 and 16:15 tell of that provision. αὐτοῖς names the recipients, “to them”; the giver is the unexpressed subject of ἔδωκεν. Jesus names Moses and his Father in verse 32. The crowd’s own line does not explicitly identify Moses as the giver.

JHN 6:35.notes: The 'never hunger / never thirst' double-promise (οὐ μὴ πεινάσῃ καὶ...οὐ μὴ διψήσει πώποτε) echoes Isa 49:10 (Servant-Song: 'they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them') and Isa 55:1-3 (covenantal-banquet invitation: 'come, all who thirst, come to the waters; come, eat without money'). The first I-AM-with-predicate in John builds on these eschatological-banquet motifs.

JHN 6:4.notes: Passover-frame: John deliberately situates the bread-feeding + bread-of-life discourse in proximity to Passover (cf. JHN 2:13, 11:55) — preparing the reader to hear the v.51 claim ('the bread which I will give is my flesh...for the life of the world') in the Exod 12 paschal-lamb register. The substitutionary-atonement Christology of JHN 1:29 (Lamb of God) is structurally framed by the three Johannine Passovers.

JHN 6:41.notes: The repeated บ่น in verses 41 and 43 renders γογγύζω. It echoes the wilderness complaints about food. Greek Exodus 16:2 and 16:8 use forms of the related compound διαγογγύζω; 16:8 also has the noun γογγυσμός.

JHN 6:45.notes: Jesus quotes Isaiah 54:13 with adaptation. Greek Isaiah reads καὶ πάντας τοὺς υἱούς σου διδακτοὺς θεοῦ, “and all your sons taught by God.” John reads Καὶ ἔσονται πάντες διδακτοὶ θεοῦ, “and all will be taught by God.” John gives a finite verb and no longer specifies “your sons.”

JHN 6:9.notes: Andrew's report of the boy's 'five barley loaves and two fish' echoes Elisha's miracle of multiplying twenty barley loaves to feed 100 (2 Kgs 4:42-44 — Elisha-feeding, with similar 'how can this feed so many?' incredulity from the servant, and the same barley + multiplication + leftovers pattern). John's signal: Jesus is the prophet-greater-than-Elisha; cf. v.14 'this is truly the Prophet who is to come.'

JHN 7:19.notes: Jesus indicts the leadership for plotting murder while claiming to keep Moses' law — implicit reference to the Sixth Commandment (Decalogue framing). The argument is qal va-chomer: those who claim Mosaic-fidelity are themselves breaking the most fundamental Mosaic-prohibition.

JHN 7:22.notes: Circumcision-rite institution. GEN 17:10-14 establishes the rite with Abraham (the πατέρες/Patriarchs reference); LEV 12:3 specifies the 8th-day timing. Jesus references 'from the patriarchs' (Genesis frame) rather than 'from Moses' (Leviticus frame), correctly noting the rite's pre-Mosaic origin.

JHN 7:24.notes: Right-judgment formula. Jesus' command 'do not judge by appearance, but judge with right judgment' echoes the OT-judicial-impartiality commands: LEV 19:15 ('do not show partiality... judge your neighbor in righteousness'); DEU 1:16-17 + 16:18-20 (judges to be impartial).

JHN 7:37.notes: Tabernacles water-pouring rite. Per Mishnah Sukkah 4.9, the water drawn from Siloam was carried in procession to the altar while ISA 12:3 ('with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation') was sung. Jesus' invitation 'if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink' lands at the climax of this rite. Wider echoes: ISA 55:1 ('come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters'); EXO 17:6 + NUM 20:8-11 (water from rock at Massah/Meribah — wilderness-water-tradition).

JHN 7:38.notes: 'As Scripture said: rivers of living water will flow' — composite-thematic citation with no single OT verse matching verbatim. The cluster: EZK 47:1-12 (river from temple healing the Dead Sea); ZEC 14:8 (living waters from Jerusalem in messianic age); ISA 12:3 (wells of salvation — the Tabernacles rite citation); ISA 44:3 (Spirit poured on offspring); ISA 58:11 (like a watered garden); JOL 3:18 (fountain from house of YHWH watering valley of Shittim); PSA 78:16 + 105:41 (waters from rock). The whose-belly question (αὐτοῦ) — modern critical consensus reads it as the believer's; we follow that reading. v.39 makes plain: 'living water = Holy Spirit.'

JHN 7:40.notes: 'The Prophet' (definite ὁ προφήτης) refers to the eschatological Mosaic-prophet promised at DEU 18:15-18 ('The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers — to him you shall listen'). This was a distinct messianic-figure expectation in Second Temple Judaism, sometimes identified with the Christ, sometimes seen as a separate eschatological figure.

JHN 7:42.notes: The crowd asks about the Messiah’s descent from David and origin in Bethlehem. These expectations recall the Davidic promise (2 Samuel 7:12–13; Psalm 132:11) and the Bethlehem ruler of Micah 5:2. John reports what the crowd says. Matthew and Luke narrate a birth in Bethlehem. Luke 3:23 names Joseph and Heli without calling its genealogy Mary’s.

JHN 7:51.notes: Nicodemus' due-process appeal invokes Mosaic judicial-procedure: DEU 1:16-17 (judge fairly between brothers); DEU 17:6 (capital case requires two-or-three witnesses); DEU 19:15 (single-witness insufficient); EXO 23:1 (no false report). The leadership is rushing-to-condemn without hearing Jesus directly — proto-mob-trial in violation of these procedures.

JHN 7:52.notes: Counterexample to the leadership's claim 'no prophet rises out of Galilee.' 2KI 14:25 — Jonah (the prophet sent to Nineveh) was from Gath-Hepher in tribal-Zebulun = Galilee. ISA 9:1-2 ('Galilee of the Gentiles ... the people walking in darkness have seen a great light') is THE prophecy of light-from-Galilee, fulfilled in Jesus' Galilean ministry (cf. MAT 4:13-16 explicit-citation). The leadership in their rush-to-judgment commits a Scripture-knowledge fail. Their own 'search-and-see' imperative ironically condemns them.

JHN 8:12.notes: ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου — composite allusion: (a) EXO 3:14 LXX 'ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν' divine-name echo; (b) EXO 13:21-22 wilderness pillar of fire (Sukkot context — see John 7-8); (c) ISA 9:2 'people walking in darkness have seen a great light'; (d) ISA 42:6 + 49:6 'a light to the nations' Servant Song theology. Cultural backdrop: post-Sukkot Jerusalem with the Court-of-Women menorahs still in mind.

JHN 8:17.notes: Jesus quotes the Mosaic two-witness rule. DEU 19:15 is the foundational text ('on the testimony of two or three witnesses every charge shall be established'); also DEU 17:6 (capital cases require 2+ witnesses), NUM 35:30 (homicide requires 2+ witnesses). Jesus invokes the rule to justify his self-testimony alongside the Father's — the two witnesses required by Mosaic law are met.

JHN 8:24.notes: FIRST ABSOLUTE ἐγώ εἰμι in JHN 8 (cluster with vv.28, 58). Composite allusion: (a) EXO 3:14 LXX 'ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν' YHWH self-name; (b) ISA 43:10 LXX 'ἵνα γνῶτε καὶ πιστεύσητε ... ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι' — the verbal closest match: 'know / believe / I am' triplet; (c) ISA 43:25, 45:18, 51:12 — Deutero-Isaiah's repeated 'I am he' divine self-declarations. Jesus claims for himself the response that Isaiah commands toward YHWH.

JHN 8:28.notes: Jesus speaks of the lifting up of the Son of Man, ได้ยกบุตรมนุษย์ขึ้น. John 3:14 uses ὑψόω to compare this with Moses and the serpent. Greek Numbers 21:8–9 describes placing or setting the serpent on a standard with other verbs. Greek Isaiah 52:13 uses ὑψωθήσεται of the servant. The connection with Numbers comes through John’s comparison, and the wording of Isaiah supplies a verbal parallel. The following เราเป็น repeats the expression of 8:24.

JHN 8:35.notes: Slave-vs-son house-membership contrast. GEN 21:10 Sarah's word: 'Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac.' Slaves can be sold/freed/displaced; sons retain permanent place. Pauline parallel: GAL 4:21-31 develops the same allegory.

JHN 8:41.notes: The Jewish leaders' counter-claim 'ἕνα πατέρα ἔχομεν τὸν θεόν / we have one Father, God' echoes the OT covenantal Father-language: ISA 63:16 'You, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name'; MAL 2:10 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?'; DEU 32:6 'Is he not your father, who created you?' The leaders invoke an authentic OT theme but use it as a self-justifying weapon — Jesus's reply (vv.42-44) shows that genuine God-paternity produces love-of-Christ, which the leaders lack.
