JHN 8:44.notes: Jesus says the devil was a murderer from the beginning and calls him a liar. Genesis 3 depicts the serpent’s deception, Genesis 4:8 the killing of Abel, and Wisdom 2:24 the entry of death through the devil’s envy. First John 3:12 recalls Cain, and 3:15 uses the same term for murderer. John’s Gospel does not identify a single Genesis incident as the exclusive referent.

JHN 8:5.notes: The scribes/Pharisees cite the Mosaic adultery-death-penalty composite. LEV 20:10 prescribes death for both adulterer and adulteress without specifying method; DEU 22:22 reaffirms; DEU 22:23-24 specifies stoning for the betrothed-virgin offender and her partner. The trap selectively cites the stoning provision while procedurally skipping the both-parties-to-be-executed requirement.

JHN 8:51.notes: θάνατον οὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα / 'shall never see death' — echoes PSA 89:48 'What man can live and not see death?' (a rhetorical lament about universal mortality). Jesus's 'never see death' is the Gospel inversion: the question Psalm 89 raises as a lament receives its answer in eschatological life through the Son. The Jewish leaders' v.52 retort ('Abraham died, the prophets died') misses that Jesus speaks of spiritual / eternal death (cf. REV 20:14).

JHN 8:56.notes: John uses ἀγαλλιάομαι for Abraham’s rejoicing, translated ปลื้มยินดี here and ปีติยินดี of Mary in Luke 1:47. Abraham’s laughter at the promise of Isaac in Genesis 17 and the provision on the mountain in Genesis 22 offer possible backgrounds. Neither passage describes a vision of Jesus’ day. Jesus says that Abraham saw his day and rejoiced without identifying the occasion.

JHN 8:58.notes: THIRD AND CLIMACTIC ABSOLUTE ἐγώ εἰμι in JHN 8 (cluster with vv.24, 28). The verb-tense disjunction is the grammatical hammer: γενέσθαι (aorist infinitive 'to come into being') vs. εἰμί (present 'I am'). Echoes EXO 3:14 LXX 'ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν' YHWH self-name and the Deutero-Isaiah 'I am he' cluster (43:10, 13, 25). The audience reaction in v.59 (immediate stoning attempt under LEV 24:16 blasphemy law) confirms they heard the divine-name claim — arguably the most explicit deity-claim in any of the gospels.

JHN 8:7.notes: Jesus's 'let him without sin cast the first stone' weaponizes DEU 17:7 'the hand of the witnesses shall be first against him to put him to death' — applies the law's witness-must-cast-first rule with surgical precision against the accusers' standing.

JHN 9:24.notes: δὸς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ — Hebrew juridical adjuration formula commanding a witness to confess truth as worship-of-God. JOSH 7:19 LXX: δὸς δὴ δόξαν σήμερον τῷ κυρίῳ θεῷ Ισραηλ καὶ δὸς τὴν ἐξομολόγησιν. Pharisees use the formula ironically — invoking truth-telling-as-worship while demanding the man recant his testimony.

JHN 9:35.notes: Jesus's signature self-designation 'Son of Man' (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) systematically echoes DAN 7:13 LXX 'ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐρχόμενος' — the apocalyptic divine-human authority figure who receives dominion from the Ancient of Days. This Johannine instance, like the rest in John (1:51, 3:13-14, 5:27, 6:27, 6:53, 6:62, 8:28, 12:23, 12:34, 13:31), draws its weight from the Daniel 7 echo.

LUK 10:1.notes: The sending of the seventy-two (or seventy per MS variant) echoes Num 11:16-25 (Moses appointing 70 elders to share the Spirit and burden of leadership). Num 11:26-27 adds Eldad and Medad who prophesied in the camp outside the tent, possibly bringing the count to 72. If Luke reads 72 (SBLGNT/NA28), the number also matches LXX Gen 10's 72 nations-of-the-world (vs. MT's 70), framing the mission as anticipation of universal/Gentile mission. Either number carries typological significance — Jesus as the new Moses commissioning Israel-representing-and-extending envoys.

LUK 10:15.notes: Greek Isaiah 14:13–15 contrasts a boast about ascending to heaven with descent to Hades, using καταβήσῃ. Luke addresses Capernaum in the second person. His SBLGNT has the passive καταβιβασθήσῃ, “you will be brought down,” while Westcott–Hort and NA28 have καταβήσῃ. Matthew 11:23 in SBLGNT has καταβήσῃ. Luke does not rank towns by the number of miracles performed there.

LUK 10:18.notes: Lightning-fall imagery of Satan evokes Isa 14:12 LXX (πῶς ἐξέπεσεν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὁ Ἑωσφόρος ὁ πρωὶ ἀνατέλλων — 'How has fallen from heaven the morning-star'), read from 2nd-century CE onward as Satan's primordial fall. Also connects to Jewish apocalyptic tradition (1 Enoch 86, 88; Rev 12:7-9). ἐθεώρουν imperf = Jesus sees Satan's cosmic-defeat actualized proleptically in the 72's exorcisms.

LUK 10:19.notes: Authority to tread on snakes-and-scorpions echoes Ps 91:13 LXX (Psalm 90:13 LXX): ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδα καὶ βασιλίσκον ἐπιβήσῃ, καὶ καταπατήσεις λέοντα καὶ δράκοντα. Jesus extends the psalmist's promise-of-protection to his missionaries. Note the Ps 91 inclusio: Satan quoted Ps 91:11-12 in Luke 4:9-11 to tempt Jesus; Jesus now rightly applies the following verse (91:13) to his delegates' mission. Possible secondary-echo of Gen 3:15 (seed crushing serpent's head).

LUK 10:20.notes: 'Names written in heaven' echoes the OT book-of-life tradition: Exod 32:32 (Moses: 'blot me out of your book'); Ps 69:28; Dan 12:1 ('everyone whose name is found written in the book'); Mal 3:16 ('a book of remembrance was written before him'). The motif is elaborated in Rev 3:5, 13:8, 20:12-15, 21:27 (the Lamb's book-of-life); Phil 4:3. Jesus redirects the 72's joy from exorcistic-power to eschatological-security.

LUK 10:27.notes: The knowledgeable man combines Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. Rahlfs’s Deuteronomy names heart, soul and strength (δύναμις). Luke gives heart, soul, strength (ἰσχύς) and mind. Mark 12:30 also gives four in a different order, and Matthew 22:37 gives three. Leviticus explicitly repeats “you shall love”; Luke connects “your neighbor as yourself” with καί and leaves the verb understood. Thai naturally repeats love.

LUK 10:28.notes: FULFILLMENT/PRINCIPLE-ALLUSION. 'Do this and you will live' paraphrases Lev 18:5 LXX (καὶ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς). Paul cites the same verse at Rom 10:5 and Gal 3:12 as the principle of law-righteousness. Jesus agrees formally with the lawyer's Torah-answer; the Samaritan-parable then exposes whether the lawyer can actually DO it.

LUK 10:33.notes: The Samaritan-as-exemplary-neighbor enacts Lev 19:18 love-of-neighbor in a way that reverses first-century Jewish assumptions about who qualifies as 'neighbor.' Rabbinic debates variously limited πλησίον to fellow-Israelite; Jesus' parable redefines neighbor through action rather than ethnic or religious category-membership. The Samaritan (ethnically-religiously other) is the one who fulfills the commandment the priest and Levite (ethnically-religiously insider) fail to fulfill. See Luke 10:27 for the primary citation.

LUK 10:34.notes: The Samaritan binds the wounds, pouring on oil and wine. The present participle ἐπιχέων describes action accompanying κατέδησεν. Isaiah 1:6 mentions wounds, oil and bandages (καταδέσμους) but no wine. The allusion is thematic. Luke says the man was placed on the Samaritan’s animal and brought to an inn.

LUK 11:20.greek_matches: finger of God with different case and articles
LUK 11:20.notes: The magicians say “the finger of God” in Exodus 8:15 in the Hebrew and Rahlfs numbering (English 8:19), with nominative δάκτυλος θεοῦ. Luke uses instrumental ἐν δακτύλῳ θεοῦ. Exodus 31:18 has τῷ δακτύλῳ τοῦ θεοῦ and Deuteronomy 9:10 has ἐν τῷ δακτύλῳ τοῦ θεοῦ for writing the tablets. Matthew 12:28 says “Spirit of God.” The parallels show related expressions without determining which Gospel wording came first.

LUK 11:22.notes: The 'stronger-one overcoming the strong-man and dividing his spoils' echoes Isa 53:12 LXX (αὐτὸς ἁμαρτίας πολλῶν ἀνήνεγκεν... διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸς κληρονομήσει πολλοὺς καὶ τῶν ἰσχυρῶν μεριεῖ σκῦλα — 'he will divide the spoils with the strong'). Divine-warrior imagery from Isa 49:24-25 ('will the captives of a warrior be taken? But thus says the LORD: even the captives of the warrior shall be taken') also resonates. Jesus applies divine-warrior-victor imagery to his own exorcism-ministry of liberating those held by Satan. Parallels Matt 12:29 / Mark 3:27.

LUK 11:29.notes: Introduces the 'sign of Jonah' motif developed in vv.30-32. OT referent = the book of Jonah as a whole. Jesus frames his generation's demand for a sign through the lens of Jonah's ministry — developed in v.30 as typological-equivalence. Parallels Matt 12:39, 16:4, Mark 8:12 (Mark truncates without interpretation).

LUK 11:30.notes: Luke's interpretation of the 'sign of Jonah' is Jonah's PREACHING to Nineveh (Jon 3) as typological-parallel to Jesus' preaching-to-this-generation. Distinct from Matt 12:40's three-days-in-fish typological-interpretation (which Luke does NOT include). Luke's reading suits his Gentile-mission theology: Jonah's word-to-pagans is paradigmatic-precedent for the Son-of-Man's word to his own Israel. Both Jonah-interpretations are authentic-synoptic-tradition preserved in parallel forms.

LUK 11:31.notes: Queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon (1 Kgs 10:1-13 / 2 Chr 9:1-12) — a paradigm-Gentile-seeker of divine-wisdom. Her eschatological-rising-to-condemn-this-generation damns-by-contrast: foreign-queen crossed-great-distance to hear Solomon's wisdom; Jesus' contemporaries reject the greater-wisdom speaking-to-them-directly. Parallels Matt 12:42. 'Ends of the earth' idiom echoes OT distance-formula (cf. Deut 28:49, Isa 5:26).

LUK 11:32.notes: Ninevites' repentance at Jonah's preaching (Jon 3) paradigm-Gentile-repenters. Eschatological-rising-to-condemn-this-generation by-contrast: pagan-Ninevites repented at the preaching-of-a-reluctant-prophet; Jesus' contemporaries reject the preaching of 'one-greater-than-Jonah.' Parallels Matt 12:41. Paired with v.31 as double-Gentile-testimony-against-Israel's-unresponsiveness.

LUK 11:40.notes: The ἄφρων ('fool') vocative echoes wisdom-literature condemnation of those-who-reject-God's-ways. Ps 14:1 LXX (13:1 LXX) εἶπεν ἄφρων ἐν καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ· Οὐκ ἔστιν θεός ('the fool has said in his heart, there is no God') — same lexeme, same theological weight. Also Prov 1:7, 22-32 on fools rejecting wisdom. Jesus applies the wisdom-literature-condemnation of fools to the Pharisees — a sharp-rhetorical reversal since the Pharisees claimed wisdom-and-piety. The rhetorical-question 'did not the One who made the outside make the inside' echoes wisdom-creation-theology (Ps 139:13-16, Prov 20:12).

LUK 11:49.notes: 'I will send them prophets' is an OT prophetic-sending FORMULA attested across the Deuteronomistic-history and the prophetic corpus. 2 Chr 36:15-16 summarizes: 'the LORD... sent persistently to them by his messengers... but they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words, and scoffing at his prophets.' Cf. Jer 7:25 (ἀπέστειλα πρὸς ὑμᾶς πάντας τοὺς δούλους μου τοὺς προφήτας ἡμέρας καὶ ὄρθρου), Jer 25:4, 2 Kgs 17:13. Luke's 'wisdom of God said' presents this recurring-OT-formula as spoken-by-personified-divine-Wisdom. Matt 23:34 attributes the saying directly to Jesus without invoking 'wisdom.' Luke's addition 'and apostles' (ἀποστόλους) extends the Deuteronomistic-sending-formula forward to the New-Covenant apostolic-mission — a Luke-Acts distinctive framing.

LUK 11:50.notes: ἐκζητηθῇ τὸ αἷμα 'blood be sought-out/required' is technical-legal Hebraic language for divine-avenging of murder — Gen 9:5 LXX καὶ γὰρ τὸ ὑμέτερον αἷμα τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν ἐκζητήσω ('for your blood of your lives I will require/seek-out'), the foundational post-Flood principle for human-bloodshed accountability. Extended to righteous-prophets' blood in 2 Kgs 9:7, Gen 42:22, Ps 9:12(11), Ezek 33:6. Jesus applies this foundational-principle to cumulative-blood-guilt of rejected-prophets falling on this-generation.

LUK 11:51.notes: FROM FIRST TO LAST MURDER IN THE JEWISH CANON. Abel = Gen 4:8-10 (first murder in Genesis, first book of Tanakh). Zechariah-ben-Jehoiada = 2 Chr 24:20-22 (killed in temple-court by King Joash's order — 'between altar and house' per 2 Chr 24:21). In the Jewish canonical-ordering, 2 Chronicles is the LAST book; so 'from Abel to Zechariah' = the entire biblical-history of murdered-innocents from first-to-last. This presupposes Jesus reading Scripture in the Tanakh-ordering. Matt 23:35 adds patronym 'son of Berechiah' (possibly conflating with prophet-Zechariah, Zech 1:1); Luke preserves the simpler attribution. ADDED in parallel with Matt 23:35.

LUK 12:14.notes: Luke’s question shares τίς, κατέστησεν and the phrase beginning ἐφ’ with Exodus 2:14. Greek Exodus asks about appointing a ruler and a δικαστής. Luke’s selected text has κριτής and μεριστής, judge and divider. Robinson–Pierpont reads δικαστήν in Luke. Acts 7:27 and 7:35 also recall the Exodus question with δικαστήν.

LUK 12:15.notes: οὐκ ἐν τῷ περισσεύειν τινὶ ἡ ζωὴ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων echoes Eccl 5:10 (5:9 LXX) ἀγαπῶν ἀργύριον οὐ πλησθήσεται ἀργυρίου — wealth does not supply life or fulfillment. Sirach 31:1-11 extends this wisdom tradition on wealth's inadequacy for life-sustenance. The aphorism's form is sapiential-proverbial.

LUK 12:16.notes: The rich-fool parable resonates with OT wisdom-echoes on foolish-rich-man dying-and-leaving-wealth-to-unknown-heir. Eccl 2:18-21 (Qoheleth hates his toil because he must leave it to one who comes after him who-may-be-a-fool); Eccl 5:13-15 (hoarded riches harm the owner; he takes nothing with him at death); Prov 11:28 (ὁ πεποιθὼς ἐπὶ πλούτῳ αὐτοῦ οὗτος πεσεῖται — the one trusting in his riches will fall); Ps 49:16-20 LXX (do not fear when a man becomes rich, for he will take nothing when he dies). Lukan-distinctive parable assimilates this entire wisdom-tradition.

LUK 12:19.notes: φάγε πίε εὐφραίνου imperative-string evokes Eccl 8:15 LXX (τοῦ φαγεῖν καὶ τοῦ πιεῖν καὶ τοῦ εὐφρανθῆναι, Qoheleth's observation about life-under-sun) AND Isa 22:13 LXX (φάγωμεν καὶ πίωμεν αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνῄσκομεν — which Paul cites at 1 Cor 15:32 as paradigm-of-hedonism-if-no-resurrection). The rich-fool's self-address assimilates the Qoheleth-formula without its הֶבֶל-qualification, collapsing into pagan-Epicurean carpe-diem-without-wisdom. Luke's v.20 God-speech then realizes the Isaiah-tomorrow-we-die threat literally.

LUK 12:20.notes: ἄφρων-vocative + διελογίζετο ἐν ἑαυτῷ (v.17) echoes Ps 14:1/53:1 LXX εἶπεν ἄφρων ἐν καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ — the biblical fool speaks-to-himself-ignoring-God. The rich-farmer IS the Psalmic fool, and God's direct-address via ἄφρων names the diagnosis. Wis 15:8 provides a Second-Temple parallel for ἀπαιτέω (demand-back) of soul-as-entrusted-capital returned to Creator.

LUK 12:24.notes: Lukan-distinctive κόρακες (where Matt 6:26 has generic τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ). Ravens were unclean by Lev 11:15 / Deut 14:14. OT feeding-tradition: 1 Kgs 17:4-6 (ravens feed Elijah at Cherith); Job 38:41 LXX τίς δὲ ἡτοίμασεν κόρακι βοράν; Ps 147:9 LXX διδόντι τοῖς κτήνεσι τροφὴν αὐτῶν καὶ τοῖς νεοσσοῖς τῶν κοράκων. Luke's κόρακας picks up the Psalmic/Wisdom tradition of God-feeding-unclean-ravens as evidence of universal divine care. A-fortiori: if God feeds unclean birds, how much more his covenant-children.

LUK 12:27.notes: The queen sees Solomon’s wisdom, house and court in 1 Kings 10:4–5 and 2 Chronicles 9:3–4. These accounts supply background for royal splendor. Their Greek does not say she saw his glory. Luke’s ἐν πάσῃ τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ also appears in Matthew 6:29. The surrounding wording differs, including Luke’s singular and Matthew’s plural verbs for toiling and spinning.

LUK 12:32.notes: τὸ μικρὸν ποίμνιον invokes the OT shepherd-flock motif: Ezek 34 (God as Shepherd over false-shepherds, gathering scattered flock); Isa 40:11 LXX ὡς ποιμὴν ποιμανεῖ τὸ ποίμνιον αὐτοῦ (the coming-Lord as tender shepherd); Ps 100:3 LXX πρόβατα νομῆς αὐτοῦ. 'Little-flock' carries the covenant-flock weight while acknowledging the numerically-small Jesus-movement of c. 30 CE. Father's εὐδόκησεν (gnomic-aorist) frames the kingdom-gift as enduring-divine-pleasure.

LUK 12:35.notes: Luke’s command about girded waists recalls preparations for departure in Exodus 12:11. Rahlfs has αἱ ὀσφύες ὑμῶν περιεζωσμέναι. Luke places ὑμῶν before the article and adds ἔστωσαν. The Greek participle describing the girded waists is shared. Luke then speaks of lamps burning.

LUK 12:40.notes: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἔρχεται combines Dan 7:13 Son-of-Man-coming (ἰδοὺ μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐρχόμενος) with the thief-unexpectedness-metaphor. Parousia-imminence-without-calendar draws on Danielic expectation of decisive-Son-of-Man-in-glory, reframed for ongoing-disciple-vigilance.

LUK 12:49.notes: πῦρ motif linking Jesus' ministry to OT fire-of-judgment. Mal 4:1 (3:19 MT) ἰδοὺ ἡμέρα ἔρχεται καιομένη ὡς κλίβανος — imagery picked up by John the Baptist at Luke 3:16-17. Isa 66:15-16 eschatological fire-judgment on flesh. Luke 3:16 already pairs fire with Holy-Spirit-baptism (πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πυρί), integrating Pentecost-flame-imagery Acts 2:3 into the Luke-Acts narrative theology. Here πῦρ primarily indicates division-crisis (v.51 διαμερισμόν) and possibly eschatological judgment, with the paradox that the fire-bringer must first endure baptism-of-suffering (v.50).

LUK 12:5.notes: τὴν Γέενναν < Hebrew גֵּי־הִנֹּם Valley-of-Hinnom, where Ahaz/Manasseh sacrificed children to Molech (2 Chr 28:3; 33:6); Josiah desecrated it (2 Kgs 23:10); Jeremiah prophesied it would become valley-of-slaughter (Jer 7:31-32; 19:5-7). By second-temple era a burning refuse-dump, whence the metonym for eschatological fiery-judgment. Isa 66:24 LXX πῦρ ... οὐ σβεσθήσεται undergirds the unquenchable-fire-imagery. Luke preserves the Greek transliteration γέεννα; our Thai renders as นรก for reader-comprehension with the Hinnom-etymology documented in the verse-summary.

LUK 12:53.notes: Explicit citation of Mic 7:6 LXX υἱὸς ἀτιμάζει πατέρα, θυγάτηρ ἐπαναστήσεται ἐπὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτῆς, νύμφη ἐπὶ τὴν πενθεράν αὐτῆς. Luke EXPANDS Micah's asymmetric oppositions into SYMMETRIC bidirectional pairs (father-vs-son AND son-vs-father, mother-vs-daughter AND daughter-vs-mother, mother-in-law-vs-daughter-in-law AND daughter-in-law-vs-mother-in-law), heightening mutual alienation. Micah 7 diagnosed pre-exilic Israel's covenant breakdown; Jesus applies the same diagnostic to Messianic-era dividedness. Matt 10:35-36 preserves Micah's asymmetric pattern; Luke's symmetric form is distinctive.

LUK 12:56.notes: Jesus addresses the crowds introduced in 12:54. The vocative plural ὑποκριταί calls them hypocrites, while 12:1 uses the related abstract noun ὑπόκρισις for hypocrisy. Isaiah 1:3 supplies a thematic parallel in the failure to recognize.

LUK 12:8.notes: ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ Ἀνθρώπου ὁμολογήσει ἐν αὐτῷ ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ Θεοῦ evokes Dan 7:13-14 LXX where the Son-of-Man enters the divine-court with myriads-of-attendants (Dan 7:10 θρόνοι ἐτέθησαν ... χίλιαι χιλιάδες ἐλειτούργουν αὐτῷ). Jesus switches from first-person to third-person Son-of-Man self-reference, maintaining the Danielic-title resonance while allowing ambiguity for outsiders. Court-room-witness frame (ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀγγέλων) mirrors Dan 7's heavenly-tribunal.

LUK 13:1.notes: Pilate mixing Galileans' blood with their sacrifices evokes the OT motif of innocent blood defiling holy space: 2 Kings 16:3 (Ahaz's Molech child-sacrifices), Ps 79:3 LXX (they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them), Jer 2:34 (on your skirts is found the lifeblood of the guiltless poor), Ezek 22:3-4 (city that sheds blood defiles itself). Luke frames the atrocity in prophetic-judgment register: blood-guilt is the covenantal-catastrophe that precipitates judgment on the whole people — setting up Jesus's repent-or-perish call.

LUK 13:14.notes: The synagogue ruler's 'six days for work' (Ἓξ ἡμέραι εἰσὶν ἐν αἷς δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι) echoes the Decalogue's fourth commandment: Exod 20:9 ἓξ ἡμέρας ἐργᾷ καὶ ποιήσεις πάντα τὰ ἔργα σου / Deut 5:13 ἓξ ἡμέρας ἐργᾷ. The citation is appealed to in order to criticize Jesus's Sabbath-healing; Jesus in response will reframe the Sabbath by appeal to Exodus-liberation-theology (Deut 5:15).

LUK 13:16.notes: Jesus's argument for Sabbath-healing-as-liberation rests on a cluster: Deut 5:15 (the Deuteronomic Sabbath grounded in Exodus-deliverance — the day of memory-of-slavery-ended); Isa 58:6 LXX λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας... ἀπόστελλε τεθραυσμένους ἐν ἀφέσει (the fast God chooses: to LOOSE the bonds of wickedness, to SET-FREE the oppressed — lexical-echo with ἔδησεν/λυθῆναι); Isa 61:1 LXX κηρύξαι αἰχμαλώτοις ἄφεσιν (proclaim release to captives — Luke 4:18 Nazareth-manifesto programmatic-text); Gen 17:7 (Abrahamic-covenant extends to descendants — 'daughter of Abraham' invokes covenant-inclusion). Jesus recasts Sabbath as the DAY OF RELEASE — fulfilling rather than violating the commandment.

LUK 13:19.notes: Mustard-seed-becomes-tree with birds-nesting-in-branches deliberately echoes the empire-as-cosmic-tree imagery: Dan 4:12, 21 LXX (Nebuchadnezzar's tree, birds of heaven dwelt in its branches, all flesh fed from it); Ezek 17:23 LXX (Messianic cedar under which every bird of every kind will dwell — direct background for the messianic-kingdom-as-tree reading); Ezek 31:6 (pharaoh-cedar with birds nesting in branches); Ps 104:12 LXX (birds of heaven dwell by waters and sing among the branches). The imperial-tree metaphor is co-opted for God's kingdom — subverting Daniel's Babylonian-tree reading.

LUK 13:21.notes: Three seahs of flour (ἀλεύρου σάτα τρία) matches the amount Sarah prepared for the three divine visitors at Mamre (Gen 18:6 LXX τρία μέτρα σεμιδάλεως). The hospitality-association suggests the hidden-leaven-transformation as new-Abrahamic-household-making: the kingdom silently transforms a community the way Sarah's baking fed the divine encounter. Hyperbolically large quantity (≈22 liters) matches the extravagance of Abraham's welcome.

LUK 13:25.notes: The householder's 'I do not know you' (οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς) uses covenantal-knowing vocabulary: Amos 3:2 LXX ὑμᾶς ἔγνων ἐκ πασῶν φυλῶν τῆς γῆς (only you have I known from all families of the earth — covenantal-knowing = covenantal-recognition). Jer 24:5-10 (God 'knows' the good figs and rejects the bad). The formula is echoed in Matt 25:12 (ten-virgins parable) and Matt 7:23 (Lord-Lord pleaders). 'Do-not-know' is not memory-gap but covenantal-rejection.

LUK 13:27.notes: Luke’s citation echoes Greek Psalm 6:9 (English 6:8) in the command ἀπόστητε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ. Luke addresses ἐργάται ἀδικίας. The psalm has οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν. Matthew 7:23 shares the psalm’s latter wording but opens with ἀποχωρεῖτε.

LUK 13:28.notes: Luke uses the noun βρυγμός, gnashing, with “of teeth.” Greek Psalm 111:10 (English 112:10) uses the related verb βρύξει. Matthew 8:12 has Luke’s weeping-and-gnashing expression. The rich food of the feast in Hebrew Isaiah 25:6 is expressed differently in Rahlfs Greek: drinking wine and anointing with perfume. Isaiah provides a banquet parallel for the following verse.

LUK 13:29.notes: Jesus names east, west, north and south. Greek Psalm 106:3 (English 107:3) lists east, west, north and the sea. Greek Isaiah 49:12 names north, sea and the land of the Persians, where Hebrew has the land of Sinim. Isaiah 43:5–6 and Malachi 1:11 provide further comparisons for a far-reaching gathering or worship. Luke does not specify the identity of each group coming to eat.

LUK 13:32.notes: Hosea 6:2 describes a group rising on the third day. The vision in Ezekiel 37:3–14 describes restoration to life but gives no third-day timetable. Jesus speaks of completing his work. The comparison of Herod to a fox conveys a judgment of him, but the saying does not explain which characteristics of the animal were intended.

LUK 13:33.notes: 'It is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem' alludes to the Jerusalem-prophet-murder tradition: 2 Chr 24:20-22 (Zechariah ben-Jehoiada stoned in the temple court — the final OT martyr, cited by Jesus in Matt 23:35 / Luke 11:51 as the CANONICAL-BRACKET with Abel); Jer 26:20-23 (Uriah the prophet executed in Jerusalem under Jehoiakim). The pseudepigraphic Martyrdom-of-Isaiah continues this tradition (Isaiah sawn-asunder). Jesus's irony: Jerusalem is the EXPECTED place for prophet-murder — 'of course my death will happen there.'

LUK 13:34.notes: Hen-gathering-chicks-under-wings simile draws on the extensive OT wings-of-refuge cluster: Deut 32:11 LXX (eagle covers her nestlings, spreads her wings, takes them up); Ruth 2:12 (under whose wings you have come to take refuge); Ps 17:8 (hide me under the shadow of your wings); Ps 36:7 LXX (children of men take refuge under the shadow of your wings); Ps 57:1; Ps 61:4 (I will take refuge in the shelter of your wings); Ps 91:4 (he will cover you with his feathers, under his wings you will find refuge). Jesus assumes YHWH-as-mother-bird role, a strong Christological move. Prophet-killing echoes 2 Chr 24:20-22. Parallel to Matt 23:37 (near-verbatim logion).

LUK 13:35.notes: The BSB reads “left to you desolate.” The selected Greek and NA28 omit ἔρημος here, while Robinson–Pierpont includes it. Matthew 23:38 also includes the adjective. The Thai follows the shorter Luke text. The blessing quotes the first half of Greek Psalm 117:26 (Hebrew and common English 118:26). Jeremiah 12:7 provides a further parallel for a forsaken house.

LUK 13:6.notes: Fig-tree-in-vineyard parable draws on the established Israel-as-fig-tree imagery: Hos 9:10 (I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness, like first-ripe fruit on the fig tree); Mic 7:1 (no first-ripe fig my soul craved); Jer 8:13 (no grapes on the vine, no figs on the fig tree, their leaves withered); Joel 1:7 (he has laid waste my vine, splintered my fig tree). The vineyard-frame is borrowed from Isa 5:1-7 Song-of-the-Vineyard (Israel as God's vineyard bearing only wild grapes). Jesus compresses the cluster into a single parable of patience-before-judgment.

LUK 14:14.notes: Jesus speaks of the resurrection of the righteous. In Greek Daniel 12:2 the Old Greek uses ἀναστήσονται and Theodotion ἐξεγερθήσονται of sleepers rising. Luke uses the noun ἀνάστασις and offers a related promise to the host. The verse gives no schedule of separate resurrections.

LUK 14:15.notes: The guest's beatitude 'Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God' (μακάριος ὅστις φάγεται ἄρτον ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ) invokes the Second-Temple-era eschatological-banquet hope rooted in Isa 25:6 LXX (καὶ ποιήσει κύριος σαβαωθ πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἐπὶ τὸ ὄρος τοῦτο πίονται εὐφροσύνην, πίονται οἶνον, χρίσονται μύρον = 'The LORD of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain [a feast of fat things, feast of wine...]'). Cross-refs: 1 Enoch 62:14, 2 Baruch 29:4-5, Luke 13:29, Matt 8:11, 22:1-14, Rev 19:9 all develop this Messianic-banquet motif. The guest's confidence will be parabolically subverted (vv.16-24) — popular-Israel presumption of inclusion gives way to Jesus's warning that many presumed-inside find themselves outside.

LUK 17:18.notes: ἀλλογενής (NT f=1) is a near-technical LXX-term for 'foreigner/Gentile-of-another-people' — ~100x in LXX (Gen 17:27, Exod 12:43, Lev 22:10, Num 1:51, Deut 17:15 etc.), typically for those excluded from sacred-precincts or sacral-privileges. The word is famously inscribed on the Jerusalem Temple's Soreg-wall warning-inscription (two extant copies) prohibiting Gentile-entry: ΜΗΘΕΝΑ ΑΛΛΟΓΕΝΗ ΕΙΣΠΟΡΕΥΕΣΘΑΙ. Jesus's choice of this word for the grateful Samaritan is pointedly-ironic: the man institutionally-excluded-from-Temple-worship is the one who actually gave-glory-to-God (the very purpose of Temple-worship). Prefigures Luke's Acts-narrative of gospel going to ἔθνη/Gentiles.

LUK 17:26.notes: Jesus invokes Noah-typology (vv.26-27): the days-of-Noah as a time of routine normalcy before sudden catastrophic judgment, paralleled to the days-of-the-Son-of-Man. Per Matt 24:37-39 synoptic-parallel this is an established apocalyptic Jesus-tradition. Theological point: eschatological-catastrophe comes suddenly upon the routine-absorbed generation, as it did in Noah's day.

LUK 17:27.notes: εἰσῆλθεν Νῶε εἰς τὴν κιβωτόν + ἦλθεν ὁ κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἀπώλεσεν πάντας echoes the Gen 7:7-23 LXX flood-destruction narrative. κιβωτός ('ark') and κατακλυσμός ('flood') are the LXX technical-terms for these (Gen 7:1-23 LXX passim). Synoptic-parallel: Matt 24:38-39.

LUK 17:28.notes: Jesus opens Lot/Sodom-typology (vv.28-30) paralleling the Noah-typology of vv.26-27. The list of six routine activities (eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building) characterizes Sodom's prosperous-normalcy right up to the destruction. Genesis 18-19 provides the narrative base for Sodom/Gomorrah as the paradigm of sudden-divine-judgment on wicked-prosperity.

LUK 17:29.notes: ἔβρεξεν πῦρ καὶ θεῖον ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ directly echoes LXX Gen 19:24: καὶ κύριος ἔβρεξεν ἐπὶ Σόδομα καὶ Γόμορρα θεῖον καὶ πῦρ παρὰ κυρίου ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('and the Lord rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord from heaven'). Luke's verb ἔβρεξεν + nouns θεῖον + πῦρ + prep ἐκ/ἀπ' οὐρανοῦ preserve the LXX diction. The fire-and-sulfur-from-heaven becomes NT paradigm for eschatological-judgment (cf. ISA 34:9-10 LXX, REV 14:10, 19:20, 20:10). Luke shows characteristic LXX-dependent vocabulary here.

LUK 17:32.notes: Brief one-verse imperative 'remember Lot's wife' presupposes audience-knowledge of Gen 19:26 (καὶ ἐπέβλεψεν ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω καὶ ἐγένετο στήλη ἁλός — 'his wife looked back and became a pillar of salt'). Note the DELIBERATE verbal-echo: v.31 warns μὴ ἐπιστρεψάτω εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω ('do not turn-back to the things behind') — Gen 19:26 LXX ἐπέβλεψεν εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω ('she looked back to the things behind'). Same phrase εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, echoing across the two verses by design. Jesus structures the Lot-typology with careful LXX-phraseology.

LUK 17:37.notes: Job 39:27 names an eagle and a vulture in its Greek form. Verse 30 describes the birds being found wherever the dead are, οὗ δ᾽ ἂν ὦσι τεθνεῶτες. Luke has “body” (σῶμα) and ἐπισυναχθήσονται, while Matthew 24:28 has “carcass” (πτῶμα) and συναχθήσονται. The similar sayings use distinct words. The birds’ gathering at a body supports the Thai reference to vultures.

LUK 18:20.notes: Luke lists adultery, murder and theft in that order. Rahlfs’s Greek Deuteronomy 5:17–19 also has that order, but its commands use οὐ plus the future, while Luke uses μή plus the subjunctive. Deuteronomy places honoring parents earlier, in 5:16; Luke ends his list with that command. Matthew 19:18 in SBLGNT begins with murder. Mark 10:19 also includes a warning against defrauding.

LUK 18:31.notes: Jesus says that everything written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled. He does not name a passage. Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Zechariah 12:10 and Daniel 7:13–14 are listed as possible thematic backgrounds, concerning suffering, piercing and the Son-of-Man figure.

LUK 18:7.notes: God’s chosen ones cry to him day and night. Psalm 22:3 in Hebrew numbering (English 22:2, Greek 21:3) has יוֹמָם and וְלַיְלָה, “by day” and “by night.” Psalm 88:2 in Hebrew (English 88:1, Greek 87:2) also relates crying and night. The Psalms compare sustained prayer without quoting Luke’s whole expression.

LUK 19:10.notes: Allusion to Ezek 34:16 LXX τὸ ἀπολωλὸς ζητήσω ('I will seek the lost'). In Ezek 34 YHWH promises to personally shepherd Israel after the failed human shepherds. Jesus' mission-statement takes on the divine-shepherd role. The lexical pair ζητέω + ἀπολωλώς is the Ezekiel-signature. Not direct-citation (no ὅτι-formula or γέγραπται marker) but long-recognized allusion. Connects to Luke 15's three lost-parables.

LUK 19:38.notes: Luke adapts Greek Psalm 117:26 (English 118:26) by explicitly identifying the one who comes as the king, ὁ βασιλεύς. The greeting is followed by peace in heaven and glory in the heights. Luke 2:14 also pairs glory and peace, there locating peace on earth.

LUK 19:40.notes: Allusion to Hab 2:11 — 'the stone will cry out from the wall.' In Habakkuk the stones cry as witness against oppressors; Jesus redeploys the image for stones crying in praise of Messiah. Creates ironic-bookend with v.44 ('they will not leave stone upon stone in you'): stones praising (v.40) and stones falling (v.44) frame the rejection-of-Messiah scene.

LUK 19:41.notes: Prophetic-weeping echoes. Jer 9:1 LXX 'τίς δώσει τῇ κεφαλῇ μου ὕδωρ καὶ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς μου πηγὴν δακρύων; καὶ κλαύσομαι' (who will give water to my head and fountain of tears to my eyes, and I will weep). Isa 22:4 'let me alone, I will weep bitterly.' Both set the paradigm of prophetic-lament over Jerusalem's coming destruction that Jesus enacts at Luke 19:41. Not direct-citation; conceptual-allusion grounded in the shared prophet-weeping-over-Jerusalem trope. Reinforces that Jesus' tears are prophetic-compassionate, not emotional-collapse.

LUK 19:43.notes: Rahlfs Isaiah 29:3 describes surrounding the city and then says βαλῶ περὶ σὲ χάρακα, “I will cast up a rampart around you.” Luke has the same siege noun χάρακα in a different construction. Ezekiel 4:2 supplies another siege comparison. Luke identifies the agents as Jerusalem’s enemies.

LUK 19:44.notes: ἐδαφίζω ('dash to ground') echoes Ps 137:9 LXX (136:9 LXX) of dashing Babylonian babies on rocks — the captivity-lament. Also Hos 10:14, Nah 3:10 similar razing-to-ground. τέκνα σου ἐν σοί applies the metaphor to Jerusalem's inhabitants (inversion: Jerusalem, formerly victim, is now the target of the same fate). Secondary connection: the ἐπισκοπή-theme recapitulates Luke's visitation-inclusio (1:68, 1:78, 7:16, now 19:44).

LUK 19:46.notes: Isaiah 56:7 calls the temple a house of prayer for all nations. Luke introduces “my house” with καὶ ἔσται and abbreviates the rest. Matthew 21:13 also lacks “for all nations,” while Mark 11:17 retains it. Jeremiah 7:11 asks whether the house has become a den of robbers, σπήλαιον λῃστῶν. Luke applies that expression in a statement.

LUK 19:9.notes: Allusion to the Abrahamic covenant (Gen 17). 'Son of Abraham' language draws on Second-Temple debate over who counts as covenant-member (cf. LUK 3:8 John Baptist; 13:16 daughter of Abraham; JHN 8:39). Jesus affirms Zacchaeus as genuine covenant-member against the Pharisaic exclusion of tax collectors — repentance-evidenced-by-fruit defines Abrahamic descent more than mere lineage.

LUK 1:10.notes: Gabriel appeared to Daniel 'at the time of the evening sacrifice' (Dan 9:20-21) — tight parallel to Gabriel appearing to Zechariah during incense offering.

LUK 1:13.notes: Pre-natal angelic name-giving parallels Isaac (Gen 17:19) and Samson (Judg 13). Biblical marker of exceptional divine purpose.

LUK 1:14.notes: Joy at miraculous-birth echoes Hannah's exultation at Samuel's birth.

LUK 1:15.notes: Gabriel predicts that John will drink no wine or strong drink and will be filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb. Numbers 6:3 gives abstinence in the context of a Nazirite vow. In Judges 13:4 it is Samson’s mother who is told to abstain, and 13:5 explicitly calls her child a Nazirite. Rahlfs Judges B 13:4 uses μέθυσμα, where Numbers and Luke have forms of σίκερα. Jeremiah 1:5 adds a thematic parallel of a prenatal calling. Luke does not explicitly call John a lifelong Nazirite.

LUK 1:16.notes: 'Turning sons of Israel back to the Lord' echoes Deuteronomic/prophetic repentance-idiom (Deut 30:2, Mal 3:7, Hos 3:5).

LUK 1:17.greek_matches: adapted Elijah promise and related messenger motif
LUK 1:17.notes: Luke adapts Malachi’s promise concerning Elijah (English 4:5–6, Rahlfs 3:22–23). Greek Malachi has a finite verb of restoration and singular “father” and “son.” Luke uses the infinitive “to turn,” plural fathers and children, and a different second clause about the disobedient and the understanding of the righteous. Malachi 3:1 also describes a messenger preparing a way; in Luke John prepares a people.

LUK 1:18.notes: Zechariah's kata ti gnosomai echoes Abraham's question to YHWH in Gen 15:8 LXX. But Zechariah is rebuked while Abraham was granted covenant-confirmation.

LUK 1:19.greek_matches: same named messenger in different scenes
LUK 1:19.notes: Gabriel stands before God and was sent to tell Zechariah this good news. Daniel 8:16 and 9:21 also name Gabriel. Daniel 9:21 places that encounter at the evening offering, while Luke 1:10–11 gives the hour of incense without specifying morning or evening. These are narrative comparisons. This is Luke’s first use of εὐαγγελίζομαι; Matthew 11:5 also uses it.

LUK 1:25.greek_matches: close verbal echo of Rachel’s speech
LUK 1:25.notes: Elizabeth speaks about the Lord in the third person. Her words echo Rachel’s in Genesis 30:23. The Greek Genesis has the finite ἀφεῖλεν, while Luke uses the infinitive ἀφελεῖν and adds “among people.” Both use ὄνειδος for reproach. Rachel names Joseph in the next verse, Genesis 30:24. Hannah’s distress in 1 Samuel 1:5–7 is a thematic comparison.

LUK 1:27.notes: Emphatic parthenos repetition sets up the virginal-conception theology rooted in Isa 7:14.

LUK 1:28.notes: Chaire + 'Lord-is-with-you' formula echoes Zephaniah's daughter-of-Zion-rejoice (Zep 3:14-15) and the Gideon-commissioning-formula (Judg 6:12 LXX). TEXTUAL VARIANT: Byz adds eulogemene su en gynaixin from v.42 assimilation — SBLGNT omits, we follow.

LUK 1:30.notes: heures charin para to theo is LXX idiom for the privileged-elect (Noah Gen 6:8, Moses Exod 33:12-17, David 2 Sam 15:25).

LUK 1:31.notes: The messenger announces conception, the birth of a son and his naming. Similar announcements occur at Genesis 16:11 and Judges 13:3. Rahlfs Isaiah 7:14 has ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει and names Immanuel. Luke addresses Mary with συλλήμψῃ and gives the name Jesus. Matthew 1:23 explicitly quotes Isaiah, while Matthew 1:21 shares Luke’s naming formula for Jesus.

LUK 1:32.notes: The allusion to 2 Samuel 7:12–14 recalls God’s promise to establish the throne of David’s offspring and to be a father to him. Luke calls the child Son of the Most High and says God will give him David’s throne. Psalm 2:7 supplies a further royal sonship parallel.

LUK 1:33.notes: Luke promises an everlasting reign and says with one negative, οὐκ, that the kingdom will have no end. Compare the enduring kingdom in Daniel 7:14 and throne in 2 Samuel 7:13. The Isaiah 9:6 LXX allusion (9:7 in common English numbering) pairs David’s throne with peace without limit.

LUK 1:35.notes: The Exodus 40:35 allusion shares the overshadowing verb. Exodus has the cloud as subject with an imperfect verb, while Luke has the power of the Most High with a future verb. Numbers 9 describes the cloud covering the tent with different vocabulary. “Come upon” specifies no downward path. The Greek allows either “the holy one to be born” or “the one to be born will be called holy.” The Thai องค์บริสุทธิ์ที่จะทรงประสูติ follows the first construction.

LUK 1:37.notes: The allusion to Genesis 18:14 reworks a question about God’s promise to Sarah. Greek Genesis uses μή and παρὰ τῷ θεῷ without πᾶν. Luke has a negative statement with οὐκ and πᾶν ῥῆμα. SBLGNT reads παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, while Robinson–Pierpont has the dative. The Thai expresses divine possibility broadly. Verse 38 repeats ῥῆμα in Mary’s response to the message.

LUK 1:38.notes: doule + humble-servant language anticipates Magnificat's fuller quotation of 1 Sam 1:11 (Hannah's vow).

LUK 1:41.notes: The allusion to Genesis 25:22 shares a verb of movement. Greek Genesis uses plural imperfect ἐσκίρτων of the children within Rebekah. Luke has a singular verb for Elizabeth’s baby and a separate predicate for Elizabeth being filled with the Holy Spirit. Verse 44 identifies joy. ดิ้นไหว describes the movement without specifying its force.

LUK 1:42.notes: eulogemene su en gynaixin echoes Judg 5:24 LXX (Deborah's blessing on Jael — enemy-breaker typology). 'Fruit of your womb' echoes Deuteronomic blessing Deut 28:4.

LUK 1:43.notes: Elizabeth's 'why should the mother of my Lord come to me?' echoes David's 'how shall the ark of the Lord come to me?' (2 Sam 6:9) — Mary-as-new-Ark typology.

LUK 1:45.notes: 'Blessed is she who believed' places Mary in Abrahamic-faith-paradigm (Gen 15:6) and Psalm-beatitude-formula (Ps 1:1).

LUK 1:46.notes: Mary declares that her soul magnifies the Lord. Greek Psalm 33:4 (English 34:3) invites others to magnify the Lord together, using a plural imperative. Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2:1 is a thematic model. Rahlfs there says that Hannah’s heart was strengthened, using different words from Mary.

LUK 1:47.notes: Habakkuk 3:18 has two verbs of rejoicing. Luke’s verb corresponds to the first, and his phrase “in God my Savior” resembles the phrase with the second. Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2:1 is another thematic comparison.

LUK 1:48.notes: Hannah asks God to look upon the lowliness of his servant in 1 Samuel 1:11. Greek Samuel doubles the verb for looking and uses “your servant.” Mary describes an act already accomplished, in the third person, with “his servant.”

LUK 1:49.notes: Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her, using the dative μοι. Deuteronomy 10:21 speaks of great things done ἐν σοί, “among you.” Her praise of God’s holy name also echoes Greek Psalm 110:9 (English 111:9), which describes the name as both holy and fearsome.

LUK 1:5.notes: Priestly division of Abijah per 1 Chr 24:10; Elizabeth's name shares with Aaron's wife Elisheba (Exod 6:23) — doubly-priestly couple.

LUK 1:50.notes: Greek Psalm 102:17 (English 103:17) speaks of the Lord’s mercy from age to age upon those who fear him. Luke’s allusion has “his mercy,” measures time in generations and uses a dative for those who fear him.

LUK 1:51.notes: The allusion to Greek Psalm 88:11 (English 89:10) brings together God’s arm, pride and scattering. The psalm says God humbled the proud one and scattered his enemies. In Luke those scattered are the proud.

LUK 1:52.notes: The reversal of rulers and the lowly recalls Hannah’s song in 1 Samuel 2:7–8. Hannah speaks of bringing low, exalting and seating the needy with rulers. Mary speaks of removing rulers from thrones. Compare also Greek Psalm 112:7–8 (English 113:7–8) and the reversal in Ezekiel 21.

LUK 1:53.notes: Greek Psalm 106:9 (English 107:9) has the phrase ἐνέπλησεν ἀγαθῶν, “filled with good things.” The allusion changes the singular hungry soul into the plural hungry people. Mary then contrasts them with the rich sent away empty.

LUK 1:54.notes: Isaiah 41:8–10 addresses Israel as God’s servant and speaks of God taking hold of him. Greek Psalm 97:3 (English 98:3) says God remembered his mercy. Luke combines the related images with Israel as object of the verb for helping and an infinitive for remembering mercy.

LUK 1:55.notes: The allusion to Micah 7:20 links mercy for Abraham and an oath sworn to the ancestors. Genesis 17:7 and 22:17–18 provide the related promise concerning descendants. Luke explicitly includes Abraham’s offspring. “Forever” can characterize the enduring promise or the mercy extended to them.

LUK 1:6.greek_matches: related character descriptions and legal terms
LUK 1:6.notes: Luke calls both parents righteous and blameless. Greek Genesis 6:9 calls Noah righteous and complete (δίκαιος τέλειος), while Job 1:1 uses both ἄμεμπτος and δίκαιος. Deuteronomy 4:1 and 5:1 pair ordinances with judgments. Deuteronomy 6:1 includes commandments and ordinances in a longer list. These comparisons illuminate Luke’s wording without reproducing it.

LUK 1:68.notes: Zechariah opens with a familiar blessing of the Lord, the God of Israel. Greek Psalms 40:14 and 105:48 have ὁ θεὸς Ισραηλ, while 71:18 repeats ὁ θεός. Luke has τοῦ Ἰσραήλ and continues by naming God’s visit and redemption. These Greek Psalm verses correspond to 41:13, 106:48 and 72:18 in common English numbering. Exodus 3:16 also speaks of God visiting his people.

LUK 1:69.notes: Luke speaks of God raising a horn of salvation for us in the house of David. Greek Psalm 17:3 (English 18:2) calls God the horn of my salvation. In Greek Psalm 131:17 (English 132:17) God says he will make a horn sprout for David. Hannah’s song also speaks of an anointed one’s horn in 1 Samuel 2:10. Luke draws on related images without quoting any entire line.

LUK 1:7.notes: The opening καί connects the couple’s childlessness to the previous description, rendered แต่. καθότι introduces the reason, rendered เพราะ. Genesis 18:11 uses the same participle προβεβηκότες with genitive ἡμερῶν. Luke uses ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις αὐτῶν. The shared expression evokes Abraham and Sarah’s age.

LUK 1:71.notes: ek cheiros...misounton hemas quotes Ps 106:10 LXX (ek cheiros misountos).

LUK 1:72.notes: Remembering the holy covenant echoes Greek Psalm 105:45 (English 106:45), which uses a finite verb for remembering. The same psalm describes deliverance from enemies in verse 10. Exodus 2:24 also speaks of God remembering his covenant.

LUK 1:73.notes: The oath recalls Genesis 22:16–18. Zechariah refers to what God swore to Abraham. Genesis presents God swearing in the first person. The grant introduced here extends through verses 74–75 to deliverance and fearless service in holiness and righteousness.

LUK 1:76.notes: Zechariah’s prophecy contains an allusion to Isaiah 40:3, which commands several hearers to prepare a road. Luke uses an infinitive with plural roads. Malachi 3:1 has the sending of a messenger and language of watching the road. SBLGNT reads ἐνώπιον and Tregelles and Robinson–Pierpont read πρὸ προσώπου. Luke 3:4 explicitly introduces a quotation from Isaiah.

LUK 1:77.notes: Knowledge-of-salvation-through-forgiveness echoes new-covenant theme Jer 31:34 and Isaianic-servant atonement Isa 53:11.

LUK 1:78.notes: The dawn from on high recalls the rising sun of Greek Malachi 3:20 (English 4:2) and the light of Greek Isaiah 9:1 (English 9:2). Other passages use imagery of a star or a shoot for a coming ruler. These are possible echoes. SBLGNT, Westcott–Hort and NA28 read the future ἐπισκέψεται, while Tregelles and Robinson–Pierpont read the aorist ἐπεσκέψατο.

LUK 1:79.notes: Greek Psalm 106:10 (English 107:10) speaks of those sitting in darkness and death’s shadow. Luke places the words in a different order and grammatical case. Compare Greek Isaiah 9:1 (English 9:2) for light in darkness. Isaiah 59:8 has “a way of peace” that people do not know, while Luke speaks of being guided into it.

LUK 1:80.notes: John's wilderness-dwelling continues Elijah-typology (1 Kgs 19 Elijah in wilderness).

LUK 1:9.notes: Daily incense offering per Exod 30:7-8 — background for Zechariah's priestly service.

LUK 20:17.notes: Psalm 118:22 (LXX 117:22) verbatim quotation: λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας. Psalm 118 is the final Hallel-psalm (113-118), sung at Passover and Tabernacles — every hearer would recognize the line immediately. Messianic-interpretation of this verse predates Jesus: Targum Ps 118:22 identifies the rejected-stone with David/Messiah, and the stone-imagery is picked up throughout NT (Acts 4:11; Rom 9:33; 1 Pet 2:4-8 combines with Isa 28:16 + Isa 8:14 in a stone-testimonia-collection). Luke renders identical to MRK 12:10 synoptic-parallel and MAT 21:42. After the parable's indictment, the citation applies the stone-metaphor: the rejected-heir (parable) becomes the cornerstone (Psalm 118) — death becomes vindication.

LUK 20:18.notes: Daniel 2:34–35 describes the stone striking the image and wind carrying its fragments away. Theodotion Daniel 2:44 uses the exact form λικμήσει for the shattering of kingdoms. Luke uses it for the person on whom the stone falls. Greek Isaiah 8:15 has συντριβήσονται for people being broken, compared with Luke’s συνθλασθήσεται.

LUK 20:28.notes: Sadducee-citation of Levirate-marriage law (yibbum) from Deuteronomy 25:5-6 LXX: ἐὰν δὲ κατοικῶσιν ἀδελφοὶ ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ ἀποθάνῃ εἷς ἐξ αὐτῶν καὶ σπέρμα μὴ ᾖ αὐτῷ...ὁ ἀδελφὸς τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς εἰσελεύσεται πρὸς αὐτὴν καὶ λήμψεται αὐτὴν ἑαυτῷ γυναῖκα... Luke's wording is paraphrase, not verbatim LXX, but clearly invokes the Deut law. Sadducee-strategy: cite Pentateuch (their accepted canon) to construct a case whose resolution-requires resurrection, then claim the resurrection-leads-to-absurdity. Jesus responds (vv.34-38) not by reinterpreting Levirate-law but by showing resurrection-life is ontologically-different from earthly-marriage-life — the presupposition of the trap was wrong. Also connected to GEN 38:8 (Onan refusing Levirate) + RUT 4 (Boaz as kinsman-redeemer via Levirate-analogous-custom).

LUK 20:37.notes: Exodus 3:6 burning-bush theophany (LXX: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ θεὸς τοῦ πατρός σου, θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ καὶ θεὸς Ἰσαὰκ καὶ θεὸς Ἰακώβ). Jesus' quotation preserves the three patriarch-names and the θεός-thrice-repetition, while adapting the framing: he uses κύριον (Lord = YHWH euphemism) and restructures the first-person-divine-statement into a third-person-description-of-Moses'-language. Argumentum from verb-tense: God in Exodus-present says 'I AM' (not 'I WAS') the God of Abraham — requiring Abraham to be in present-existent-relation, hence resurrection. Rabbinic-precedent for this exegetical-move: b. Sanhedrin 90b (Rabbi Simai's proof from Exod 6:4 'to give them the land'); m. Sanhedrin 10:1 notes resurrection-from-Torah as required-belief. Jesus uses the Sadducees' accepted-canon (Pentateuch only) against them. Matches MRK 12:26 + MAT 22:32 synoptic-parallel citations.

LUK 20:42.notes: Luke quotes Greek Psalm 109:1 (English 110:1). The Psalm begins εἶπεν ὁ κύριος while Luke’s selected Greek has εἶπεν κύριος. Robinson–Pierpont includes the article. In the continuation Luke 20:43 and the Greek Psalm use ὑποπόδιον, “footstool.” Matthew 22:44 and Mark 12:36 instead use ὑποκάτω, “under.”

LUK 20:43.notes: Continuation of Ps 110:1 (LXX 109:1b): ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου. Footstool-image signifies total subjection of enemies (ANE royal-iconography, Egyptian pharaohs depicted with feet on enemy-necks). The 'until' (ἕως ἂν) marks the messianic enthronement-reign culminating in eschatological-victory. Footstool-motif recurs in NT: 1 Cor 15:25 (πάντας τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας), Heb 1:13 + 10:13 (ἕως τεθῶσιν οἱ ἐχθροὶ ὑποπόδιον). Matches MRK 12:36 + MAT 22:44 synoptic-parallel citations. Verse-division is editorial: in NA28/SBLGNT verse 43 continues the citation begun in v.42.

LUK 20:9.notes: The parable of the wicked tenants (Luke 20:9-19 || Mark 12:1-12 || Matt 21:33-46) draws its ἀμπελών-framework from Isaiah 5:1-7 (LXX vocabulary-cluster: ἀμπελῶνα ἐγενήθη τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ / φυτεύω / φραγμός / ληνός / πύργος). Isaiah casts Israel as God's vineyard which fails to yield justice (Isa 5:7 κρίσιν, 7:5 δικαιοσύνην); Jesus redirects the indictment from the vineyard-itself (Isaiah) to the tenant-leadership (parable). Audience would recognize the Isaianic-framework immediately. Luke's compact retelling (omitting Mark's φραγμός/ληνός/πύργος details) focuses exclusively on the tenant-conflict rather than the vineyard-structure, sharpening the leadership-indictment.

LUK 21:10.notes: ἐγερθήσεται ἔθνος ἐπ’ ἔθνος echoes LXX Isa 19:2 (ἐπεγερθήσεται Αἰγύπτιος ἐπ’ Αἰγύπτιον) + 2 Chron 15:6 (καὶ πολεμήσει ἔθνος πρὸς ἔθνος καὶ πόλις πρὸς πόλιν). Apocalyptic-chaos-formula for end-time political-convulsion. Same allusion operative at MRK 13:8 / MAT 24:7 synoptic-parallels.

LUK 21:11.notes: Isaiah 19:17 uses the singular φόβητρον for a cause of terror. Hosea 6:10 uses φρικώδη for something horrifying. It offers a thematic comparison but lacks Luke’s noun. Josephus, War 1.377, mentions pestilence, famine and earthquakes while discussing possible premonitory signs. He is not reporting that famine and pestilence happened together there.

LUK 21:15.notes: ἐγὼ γὰρ δώσω ὑμῖν στόμα καὶ σοφίαν echoes LXX Exod 4:12 (ἐγὼ ἀνοίξω τὸ στόμα σου καὶ συμβιβάσω σε ἃ μέλλεις λαλῆσαι) and Exod 4:15 (ἐγὼ ἀνοίξω τὸ στόμα σου καὶ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ καὶ συμβιβάσω ὑμᾶς ἃ ποιήσετε). Christological-claim: Jesus promises in his own person what YHWH promised Moses. High-christology compressed into a trial-preparation exhortation.

LUK 21:16.notes: παραδοθήσεσθε...ὑπὸ γονέων καὶ ἀδελφῶν echoes LXX Mic 7:6 (υἱὸς ἀτιμάζει πατέρα, θυγάτηρ ἐπαναστήσεται ἐπὶ τὴν μητέρα αὐτῆς, νύμφη ἐπὶ τὴν πενθερὰν αὐτῆς, ἐχθροὶ ἀνδρὸς πάντες οἱ ἄνδρες οἱ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ). Classic apocalyptic-motif of end-time family-dissolution. Luke expands Micah's three-pair family-conflict to a four-category list (parents, siblings, relatives, friends), broadening the betrayal-scope.

LUK 21:18.notes: The promise that even a hair will not perish recalls an idiom of protection. In Rahlfs–Hanhart, 1 Reigns 14:45 (1 Samuel) has εἰ πεσεῖται τῆς τριχὸς τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν in the people’s oath concerning Jonathan. Second Samuel 14:11 and 1 Kings 1:52 use related wording. Luke’s allusion uses ἀπόληται (“perish”), and verse 16 has already acknowledged that some disciples will die.

LUK 21:20.notes: ἤγγικεν ἡ ἐρήμωσις αὐτῆς echoes the Danielic 'βδέλυγμα τῶν ἐρημώσεων / abomination-of-desolation' vocabulary-cluster (LXX Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11). Luke REPLACES Mark 13:14 / Matt 24:15 direct-citation of 'τὸ βδέλυγμα τῆς ἐρημώσεως' with the plain-historical description 'armies-surrounding-Jerusalem' — translating the Danielic prophecy for Greco-Roman readers unfamiliar with the Hebrew-Bible allusion. ἐρήμωσις-vocabulary retained as subtle-echo.

LUK 21:22.greek_matches: days of vengeance and wider judgment themes
LUK 21:22.notes: Hosea 9:7 in Rahlfs says ἥκασιν αἱ ἡμέραι τῆς ἐκδικήσεως, “the days of vengeance have come.” Luke uses related wording in saying these are days of vengeance. Other prophetic texts associate judgment and recompense. Luke names no particular text in saying that all that is written will be fulfilled.

LUK 21:23.notes: ἔσται...ἀνάγκη μεγάλη ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς καὶ ὀργὴ τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ echoes the prophetic Day-of-the-Lord ὀργή-formula: Zeph 1:15 LXX (ἡμέρα ὀργῆς ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνη ἡμέρα θλίψεως καὶ ἀνάγκης); Ezek 7:19 (ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς κυρίου); Isa 10:5-6 (the Assyrian-rod-of-God's-wrath on disobedient-people). Luke's specific phrasing λαῷ τούτῳ (this people) localizes the covenantal-wrath to the Jewish-people in context of AD-70 Jerusalem-siege. Historical AD 70: Josephus War 5-6 corroborates famine-induced suffering concentrated on most-vulnerable (pregnant + nursing).

LUK 21:24.notes: Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἔσται πατουμένη ὑπὸ ἐθνῶν ἄχρι οὗ πληρωθῶσιν καιροὶ ἐθνῶν — the only occurrence of phrase καιροὶ ἐθνῶν 'times-of-the-Gentiles' in NT. OT-background cluster: Dan 8:13 LXX (ἕως πότε ... ἡ θυσία ... δοθήσεται εἰς καταπάτημα); Dan 12:7 (ἕως καιροῦ καὶ καιρῶν καὶ ἥμισυ καιροῦ); Ps 79:1 LXX 78:1 (ἐμίαναν τὸν ναὸν τὸν ἅγιόν σου ... ἐποίησαν Ιερουσαλημ εἰς ὀπωροφυλάκιον); Isa 63:18 (κατεπάτησαν τὸ ἁγίασμά σου); Zech 12:3 (τίθησιν Ἰερουσαλὴμ λίθον καταπατούμενον). Paul's πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν (Rom 11:25) is the missiological-theological parallel — possibly informed by Luke's formulation (or shared tradition).

LUK 21:25.notes: σημεῖα ἐν ἡλίῳ καὶ σελήνῃ καὶ ἄστροις...συνοχὴ ἐθνῶν...ἤχους θαλάσσης καὶ σάλου — composite Day-of-the-Lord vocabulary. OT sun/moon/stars sign-cluster: Isa 13:10 (Babylon-oracle: οἱ γὰρ ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ὁ Ὠρίων...οὐ δώσουσιν τὸ φῶς αὐτῶν); Isa 34:4 (Edom-oracle: τακήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν); Ezek 32:7-8 (Egypt-oracle: ὁ ἥλιος ἐν νεφέλῃ συγκαλύψω); Joel 2:10,30-31 (Day-of-the-Lord: ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ἡ σελήνη συσκοτάσουσιν); Joel 3:15 (same). OT sea-roaring tumult-cluster: Ps 46:2-3 MT = 45:3 LXX (ἠχήθησαν καὶ ἐταράχθησαν τὰ ὕδατα αὐτῶν); Isa 17:12-13 (ἠχὴ θαλασσῶν πολλῶν).

LUK 21:26.notes: Luke and Matthew 24:29 have a genitive expression for the powers of the heavens. Mark 13:25 instead has αἱ δυνάμεις αἱ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς. Luke says the powers will be shaken (σαλευθήσονται). Greek Haggai 2:6 uses σείσω with God as subject, while Greek Isaiah 34:4 says the sky will be rolled up (ἑλιγήσεται ὁ οὐρανός). Joel 2:10 likewise describes cosmic upheaval.

LUK 21:27.notes: The crowds see the Son of Man coming in a cloud, singular ἐν νεφέλῃ. Daniel 7:13 compares the figure to a son of man and speaks of clouds in the plural: Old Greek uses ἐπί, “upon,” and Theodotion μετά, “with.” Luke also mentions great power and glory and does not name a destination in this verse. The allusion does not delimit a verbatim quotation.

LUK 21:33.notes: ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται, οἱ δὲ λόγοι μου οὐ μὴ παρελεύσονται — christological-claim echoing LXX Isa 40:6-8 (πᾶσα σὰρξ χόρτος ... ἐξηράνθη ὁ χόρτος καὶ τὸ ἄνθος ἐξέπεσε· τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα); Isa 51:6 (ὁ οὐρανὸς ὡς καπνὸς ἐστερεώθη ... ἡ δὲ σωτηρία μου εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ἔσται); Ps 102:25-27 LXX 101:26-28 (τὰ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σού εἰσιν οἱ οὐρανοί ... αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμενεῖς). Jesus substitutes 'my words' for 'word of God / God himself' — implicit-divine-identity-claim. Synoptic-parallel MRK 13:31, MAT 24:35.

LUK 21:35.notes: Greek Isaiah 24:17 describes fear, pit and snare confronting the inhabitants of the earth, τοὺς ἐνοικοῦντας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Luke speaks of those sitting on the face of the whole earth. Isaiah 24:19 uses ἀπορίᾳ, and verse 20 puts drunkenness and carousing together and later uses κατίσχυσεν. Compare the related expressions in Luke 21:25,34,36 without treating the complete sentences as quotations.

LUK 21:36.notes: σταθῆναι ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου echoes LXX Ps 130:3 (Ps 129:3: ἐὰν ἀνομίας παρατηρήσῃς, κύριε κύριε, τίς ὑποστήσεται;). 'Stand' as judicial-idiom for 'be-declared-innocent-when-judged' (cf. Ps 1:5; Mal 3:2; Rev 6:17). Combined with Dan 7:13-14 echo at v.27 (Son of Man coming), the closing exhortation frames disciples' prayer-and-watchfulness as preparation for vindication-before the eschatological-Judge.

LUK 22:20.notes: The new covenant recalls Jeremiah 31:31 (Greek 38:31); covenant blood recalls Exodus 24:8 and Zechariah 9:11. Greek Exodus describes Moses sprinkling the people with κατεσκέδασεν. Luke uses ἐκχυννόμενον, poured out. Isaiah 53:12 supplies a thematic comparison of self-giving. Paul uses “for you” in his bread saying (1 Corinthians 11:24) and the new-covenant formula in his cup saying (11:25).

LUK 22:21.notes: ἡ χεὶρ τοῦ παραδιδόντος με μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης echoes LXX Ps 40:10 (Ps 41:9 MT: ὁ ἐσθίων ἄρτους μου ἐμεγάλυνεν ἐπ’ ἐμὲ πτερνισμόν 'the-one-eating-my-bread has-lifted-his-heel-against-me'). Same Ps-41 explicitly-cited at JHN 13:18 in parallel context. Betrayer-who-shares-bread motif. Lukan rendering preserves the table-fellowship-image without explicit-citation-marker.

LUK 22:30.notes: καθήσεσθε ἐπὶ θρόνων τὰς δώδεκα φυλὰς κρίνοντες τοῦ Ἰσραήλ echoes Dan 7:9-14 Son-of-Man receives kingdom + Dan 7:22 'judgment-was-given-to-the-saints-of-the-Most-High-and-the-time-came-and-the-saints-possessed-the-kingdom' + Dan 7:27 'the-kingdom-and-the-dominion-will-be-given-to-the-people-of-the-saints-of-the-Most-High.' Possible additional-allusion to Wis 3:8 (deuterocanonical, non-authoritative per RULES.md §0): κρινοῦσιν ἔθνη καὶ κρατήσουσιν λαῶν. Synoptic-parallel MAT 19:28 same promise but Matthew places it during Galilean ministry.

LUK 22:31.notes: ὁ Σατανᾶς ἐξῃτήσατο ὑμᾶς echoes LXX Job 1:9-12 + 2:4-6 where Satan requests permission from God to test Job (Job 1:11 ἀποστεῖλον τὴν χεῖρά σου καὶ ἅψαι πάντων ὧν ἔχει; 1:12 'all that he has is in your hand'). The mid-voice ἐξαιτέομαι preserves the asking-for-custody-from-another's-authority sense characteristic of the Job-prologue. Theological-point: Satan's access-to-tempt is LIMITED — requires divine-permission (Job-theodicy-frame). The Satan-Job-sifting pattern illuminates Jesus' warning-to-Peter: a bounded-test is coming, and Peter's faith is under divine-protective-prayer (v.32).

LUK 22:37.notes: Luke directly cites Isaiah 53:12 as Scripture to be fulfilled in Jesus. Luke uses μετὰ ἀνόμων, “with transgressors,” where Greek Isaiah uses ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις, “among the transgressors.” Luke 23:32 calls the two led away with Jesus κακοῦργοι, criminals; Mark 15:27 uses λῃσταί, robbers.

LUK 22:42.notes: παρένεγκε τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ — 'cup' as OT symbol-of-divine-wrath-and-judgment. LXX Isa 51:17 (τὸ ποτήριον τοῦ θυμοῦ 'cup-of-wrath'), 51:22 (τὸ ποτήριον τῆς πτώσεως 'cup-of-staggering'); Jer 25:15-16 (LXX 32:15-16: τὸ ποτήριον τοῦ οἴνου τοῦ ἀκράτου τούτου 'cup-of-the-unmixed-wine' = Yahweh's-wrath against nations); Ezek 23:32-33 (cup-of-astonishment); Ps 75:8 LXX 74:9 (ποτήριον ... οἴνου ἀκράτου). Jesus prays-that-the-cup-of-divine-wrath (which-sinners-deserve) would-pass-from-him — acknowledging he is about to drink it on their behalf. Foundational to substitutionary-atonement-theology. Synoptic-parallel MRK 14:36, MAT 26:39.

LUK 22:43.notes: ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ ἄγγελος ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ ἐνισχύων αὐτόν (textually-disputed, see RULES.md Tier-3 treatment) echoes the angelic-strengthening-of-servants-of-God motif: LXX Dan 10:18-19 (καὶ προσέθηκέ μοι καὶ ἥψατό μου ὡς ὅρασις ἀνθρώπου καὶ ἐνίσχυσέ με 'one-like-a-man touched me and strengthened me') and 1 Kgs 19:5-8 (angel-strengthens-Elijah under the broom-tree in his despair). Contrastive-echo to LUK 4:10-11 (Satan's taunt quoting Ps 91:11 'he-will-command-his-angels to-guard-you') — in Gethsemane, the angelic-guard materializes when the Son-of-God actually needs it, not at Satan's cynical prompt.

LUK 22:52.notes: Jesus' ὡς ἐπὶ λῃστήν-question points-forward to his crucifixion-between-two-λῃσταί (MRK 15:27, MAT 27:38; Luke has κακούργους 'criminals' at LUK 23:32-33). All three Synoptics invoke the Isa 53:12 'numbered-with-transgressors' fulfillment-frame. Luke uniquely makes the Isa 53:12 citation EXPLICIT at LUK 22:37 (see entry there); v.52 is the narrative-ratification of the citation — Jesus explicitly named the prophetic-lens under which his arrest unfolds. Cross-reference entry.

LUK 22:64.notes: In SBLGNT and NA28 the men cover Jesus and ask him to prophesy who struck him. Robinson–Pierpont also explicitly says that they were striking his face. Greek Isaiah 50:6 mentions beatings, slaps and spitting. The connection with the treatment of Jesus is thematic.

LUK 22:69.notes: The reference to sitting at God’s right hand echoes Psalm 110:1 (Greek 109:1); “Son of Man” recalls Daniel 7:13–14. Luke 20:41–44 uses the Psalm to ask how David calls the Christ his Lord. Luke 22:69 combines the images without Daniel’s clouds. “From now on” marks a new situation and leaves the precise timing of the scene open.

LUK 22:70.notes: Isaiah 43:10 includes ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι and 43:25 repeats ἐγώ εἰμι before naming God as the one who blots out transgressions. The Greek of 43:13 begins ἔτι ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς and lacks that self-identification formula. These passages offer possible comparisons. In Luke, Jesus answers the council’s question about being the Son of God; the formula alone does not specify the full force the speakers hear.

LUK 23:12.notes: KINGS-AND-RULERS-UNITED: Herod-Pilate reconciliation fulfills PSA 2:2 LXX παρέστησαν οἱ βασιλεῖς τῆς γῆς, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ τοῦ κυρίου καὶ κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ αὐτοῦ. Luke MAKES THE CITATION EXPLICIT in ACT 4:25-27 where Peter and the early church quote Psalm 2:1-2 and apply it directly to Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and peoples of Israel gathered against 'your holy servant Jesus.' This is one of the most explicit Luke-Acts OT-fulfillment-interpretations; the LUK 23:12 event is the narrative-anchor for the ACT 4:25-27 interpretation.

LUK 23:22.notes: SUFFERING-SERVANT INNOCENCE: Pilate's third declaration οὐδὲν αἴτιον θανάτου εὗρον ἐν αὐτῷ ('I have found no fault deserving death in him') echoes the Servant-Song's assertion in ISA 53:9 LXX: ἀνομίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν, οὐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτοῦ ('he committed no lawlessness, nor was deceit found in his mouth'). Luke's triple-repetition of this formula (vv.4, 14-15, 22) builds a cumulative-echo of the servant's innocence across the trial-scene. The verb εὑρίσκω 'find' appears in both texts, tying the Roman-judicial finding to the Isaianic prophetic declaration. One of several Isa-53-echoes woven through Luke's passion.

LUK 23:29.notes: BARREN-BLESSED INVERSION: Jesus's 'blessed are the barren' reverses the normal Jewish-blessing of childbearing, echoing HOS 9:14 (δὸς αὐτοῖς, κύριε· τί δώσεις αὐτοῖς; δὸς αὐτοῖς μήτραν ἀτεκνοῦσαν καὶ μαστοὺς ξηρούς 'give them, O LORD — what shall you give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts') — Hosea's judgment-oracle on idolatrous Israel, re-applied by Jesus to Jerusalem facing the 70 CE siege. During the siege, barrenness becomes mercy (no children to watch starve). Thematically parallels LUK 21:23 'woe to those who are nursing in those days.'

LUK 23:30.notes: Jesus adapts Hosea 10:8. In the Greek of Hosea the mountains are asked to cover and the hills to fall (πέσατε). Luke asks the mountains to fall (πέσετε) and the hills to cover. Revelation 6:16 also uses πέσετε, addressing mountains and rocks and adding a request to be hidden. Luke introduces the saying as words people will begin to say in distress.

LUK 23:31.notes: GREEN-TREE / DRY-TREE JUDGMENT: Jesus's riddle draws on EZK 20:47 LXX (21:3 in LXX numbering): Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἀνάπτω ἐν σοὶ πῦρ, καὶ καταφάγεται ἐν σοὶ πᾶν ξύλον χλωρὸν καὶ πᾶν ξύλον ξηρόν 'behold I kindle a fire in you, and it shall consume every green tree and every dry tree in you.' Ezekiel's original-oracle: God's judgment-fire consumes both righteous-and-wicked as indiscriminate-wrath. Jesus applies the green/dry-tree contrast a-fortiori: if the green-tree (innocent one, himself) faces this treatment, how much more the dry-tree (Jerusalem)? Some scholars also cite PRO 11:31 LXX (cited at 1 PET 4:18) as a parallel a-fortiori logic.

LUK 23:32.notes: NUMBERED WITH TRANSGRESSORS — NARRATIVE FULFILLMENT: Luke's introduction of the two criminals being led away with Jesus (ἤγοντο δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι κακοῦργοι δύο σὺν αὐτῷ) sets up the narrative-fulfillment of ISA 53:12 LXX (καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη) which Jesus himself cited one chapter earlier at LUK 22:37 (τοῦτο τὸ γεγραμμένον δεῖ τελεσθῆναι ἐν ἐμοί, Τὸ καὶ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη — 'this scripture must be fulfilled in me, "he was numbered with the transgressors"'). The ἕτεροι κακοῦργοι 'other-of-different-kind' (ἕτεροι NOT ἄλλοι, per uW figs-distinguish) marks Jesus as innocent-but-counted-with the criminals. Dovetails with v.33 (the actual crucifixion alongside them) to complete the fulfillment-scene.

LUK 23:33.notes: CRUCIFIED-BETWEEN-CRIMINALS — ISA 53:12 FULFILLMENT: the placement of the two criminals at Jesus's right and left (ὃν μὲν ἐκ δεξιῶν ὃν δὲ ἐξ ἀριστερῶν) visually fulfills the ISA 53:12 prophecy (καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη — 'numbered with the transgressors') that Jesus cited at LUK 22:37. All four gospels record this positioning (MRK 15:27; MAT 27:38; JHN 19:18). Mark adds an explicit fulfillment-formula (TR/Byz reading at MRK 15:28) quoting Isa 53:12, absent from SBLGNT/NA28 but witnessing early Christian recognition of this scene as Isa-53 fulfillment.

LUK 23:34.notes: The soldiers dividing the garments and casting lots in the second half of the verse echo Greek Psalm 21:19 (MT and Eremos Psalm 22:19; English Psalm 22:18). Luke has “his garments,” uses a participle for dividing, and in SBLGNT uses a plural for lots. The Psalm speaks in the first person. Compare Mark 15:24 and Matthew 27:35 for the scene. John 19:24 explicitly introduces the Psalm as Scripture fulfilled. The textual question about Jesus’s prayer at the start of Luke 23:34 is separate; see the verse note.

LUK 23:35.greek_matches: shared mockery verb and adapted challenge
LUK 23:35.notes: The rulers’ sneering echoes Psalm 22:8–9 in Hebrew and Eremos numbering (English 22:7–8; Greek 21:8–9). Luke and the Greek Psalm share the verb for mocking. In the Psalm the mockers speak of the Lord rescuing the sufferer. In Luke they challenge Jesus to save himself.

LUK 23:36.notes: SOUR-WINE OFFERED TO THE SUFFERER: soldiers offering ὄξος echoes PSA 68:22 LXX (69:21 MT): καὶ ἔδωκαν εἰς τὸ βρῶμά μου χολήν, καὶ εἰς τὴν δίψαν μου ἐπότισάν με ὄξος ('they gave gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar'). All four gospels apply this to the cross: MRK 15:36, MAT 27:48, LUK 23:36, JHN 19:29 (explicit ἵνα τελειωθῇ ἡ γραφή). Luke's narrative-sequencing places the vinegar-offering early in the crucifixion-scene as part of three-fold mockery (leaders-soldiers-criminal), whereas Mark/Matt place it near the death and John connects it to Jesus's thirst-cry. ὄξος is technically posca, the Roman-military ration-wine.

LUK 23:44.notes: Luke reports darkness from about the sixth to the ninth hour. This recalls Amos 8:9, which depicts the sun setting at midday. Passover falls near full moon, ruling out an ordinary solar eclipse, which requires new moon. The narrative provides no measurements for diagnosing the darkness. In 23:45 SBLGNT and NA28 have the dependent phrase τοῦ ἡλίου ἐκλιπόντος; Tregelles and Robinson–Pierpont read “and the sun was darkened.”

LUK 23:46.notes: Jesus addresses the Father and adapts Psalm 31:6 in Hebrew and Eremos numbering (English 31:5; Greek 30:6). Luke uses present παρατίθεμαι, “I entrust,” where the Greek Psalm has future παραθήσομαι. Matthew 27:50 uses ἀφῆκεν and John 19:30 παρέδωκεν when speaking of the spirit. Acts 7:59 is a related prayer with an imperative asking Jesus to receive Stephen’s spirit.

LUK 23:47.notes: Luke’s centurion praises God and calls Jesus δίκαιος, righteous or innocent. His words express an assessment here. A possible allusion to Isaiah 53:11 rests on the servant theme and δίκαιος: Greek Isaiah reads δικαιῶσαι δίκαιον εὖ δουλεύοντα πολλοῖς. Mark 15:39 has a centurion say υἱὸς θεοῦ. Matthew 27:54 has the centurion and those with him say θεοῦ υἱός.

LUK 23:49.notes: Luke describes Jesus’s acquaintances and women watching from a distance. Greek Psalm 37:12 says ἀπὸ μακρόθεν ἔστησαν, “they stood far off”; the selected Luke has μακρόθεν without ἀπό, while NA28 includes the preposition. Greek Psalm 87:9 uses accusative γνωστούς, cognate with Luke’s nominative γνωστοί. The possible echoes correspond to Hebrew and Eremos Psalms 38:12 and 88:9 (English 38:11 and 88:8).

LUK 23:52.notes: LEGAL-BACKGROUND (not a quotation): Joseph's request for Jesus's body reflects Jewish-law's same-day burial requirement for executed criminals per DEU 21:22-23 LXX: Ἐὰν δὲ γένηται ἔν τινι ἁμαρτία κρίμα θανάτου, καὶ ἀποθάνῃ, καὶ κρεμάσητε αὐτὸν ἐπὶ ξύλου, οὐ κοιμηθήσεται τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τοῦ ξύλου, ἀλλὰ ταφῇ θάψετε αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, ὅτι κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ θεοῦ πᾶς κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου ('if anyone is guilty of a capital crime and is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for anyone hanged on a tree is cursed by God'). Paul cites DEU 21:23 (cursed-hanged-on-tree) in GAL 3:13 applying it to Christ's redemptive-death. Joseph's initiative to request the body before sunset was both pious-observance of Deut 21:22-23 AND an act of honoring Jesus beyond the Roman-custom of leaving bodies to decay.

LUK 23:53.notes: Luke describes an unused tomb hewn in rock. Matthew 27:57–60 identifies Joseph as rich and calls the tomb his own. Isaiah 53:9 provides a possible thematic parallel. Greek Isaiah has δώσω, “I will give,” with ἀντί twice: the wicked in exchange for the burial and the rich in exchange for the death. The Hebrew-based rendering associates the servant’s grave with the wicked and his death with a rich man. These are distinct source formulations.

LUK 23:9.notes: Jesus gives Herod no answer. The scene may echo the silent servant in Isaiah 53:7. Greek Isaiah reads τοῦ κείροντος αὐτὸν ἄφωνος οὕτως οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὸ στόμα, with a present participle for the one shearing. Acts 8:32 has the different participle κείραντος. Luke 23 does not quote the Isaiah verse.

LUK 24:50.notes: Jesus raises his hands and blesses the disciples. Leviticus 9:22 records Aaron raising his hands to bless the people. Numbers 6:22–27 gives the words of the priestly blessing without specifying a gesture. The allusion offers a priestly comparison. Luke supplies neither a blessing formula nor a date here for the inauguration of the covenant.

LUK 24:51.notes: Luke describes Jesus parting from the disciples while blessing them. The included ascension clause says he was carried up into heaven. It leaves the agent unnamed. Mark 16:19 also recounts an ascension in the disputed longer ending. The cloud is explicit in Acts 1:9. Daniel 7:13 is a possible typological allusion: the Old Greek depicts coming upon clouds, and Theodotion depicts coming with clouds toward the Ancient of Days. Luke 24:51 mentions no cloud.

LUK 2:11.notes: Davidic covenant — messiah from David's line; 'city of David' locator reinforces. Psalm 2:2 'Lord's Anointed' also in view.

LUK 2:13.notes: stratia ourania = 'host of heaven' = tzva hashamayim; 1 Kgs 22:19 Micaiah's vision, Ps 103:21 LXX angelic praise. Ironic reversal: heavenly army announces peace, not war.

LUK 2:14.notes: Messianic peace + cosmic reconciliation themes. Also textual-variant context (eudokias vs eudokia) — following SBLGNT genitive = peace to men of divine favor.

LUK 2:21.notes: 8th-day circumcision per Abrahamic covenant (Gen 17:12) and Mosaic code (Lev 12:3).

LUK 2:22.notes: Post-partum purification (Lev 12) + firstborn-presentation (Exod 13:2) compressed in one Jerusalem trip.

LUK 2:23.notes: Luke introduces a composite citation of the law. Exodus 13:2 consecrates every firstborn and speaks of what opens the womb. Verse 12 distinguishes the males in its discussion of firstlings. Verse 15 recalls the death of Egypt’s firstborn and the redemption of Israel’s firstborn sons. Luke brings the language of the male womb-opener and consecration together.

LUK 2:24.notes: The citation of Leviticus 12:8 gives the alternative offering when the mother lacks the means for a lamb (ἀμνόν). The Greek law specifies δύο τρυγόνας or two young pigeons (νοσσούς). Luke expresses the first option as ζεῦγος τρυγόνων, a pair of turtledoves. The offering indicates what the family could bring on that occasion.

LUK 2:25.notes: 'Consolation of Israel' (paraklēsis tou Israēl) = Messianic technical expression tied to Isaianic consolation-of-Zion texts.

LUK 2:26.notes: 'the Lord's Christ' = mashiach YHWH — royal-Davidic Messianic title from Psalm 2:2 and 1 Samuel's Davidic anointing passages.

LUK 2:29.notes: Luke uses ἐν εἰρήνῃ for departing in peace. In Genesis 15:15 Brenton’s Greek also has ἐν εἰρήνῃ, while Rahlfs prints μετ᾽ εἰρήνης. Both have ἀπελεύσῃ for going to one’s ancestors, whereas Simeon says ἀπολύεις, “you release.” Greek Genesis 15:2 separately has δέσποτα and ἀπολύομαι in Abraham’s speech.

LUK 2:30.notes: Simeon says his eyes have seen God’s salvation. The Isaiah 40:5 LXX allusion shares the noun in τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ. Isaiah 52:10 instead pictures all the ends of the earth seeing salvation and uses σωτηρία.

LUK 2:31.notes: 'prepared before all peoples' echoes Psa 98:2-3 LXX where God's salvation is made known to all nations.

LUK 2:32.notes: The allusion to Isaiah 49:6 shares light and nations. Luke places εἰς ἀποκάλυψιν between them, expressing revelation. Compare Isaiah 42:6. Greek Isaiah 46:13 uses τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εἰς δόξασμα, while Luke speaks of the glory of God’s people Israel.

LUK 2:34.notes: Isaiah 8:14 in Greek makes the trusted one a sanctuary and describes an encounter with a stumbling stone in the negative, using λίθου προσκόμματι. Verse 15 speaks of many falling. Luke speaks of the fall and rising of many without directly quoting the Greek noun phrase.

LUK 2:36.notes: The noun προφῆτις occurs here of Anna and in Revelation 2:20 of a woman who calls herself a prophetess. Anna and Simeon both speak about the child. Deuteronomy 19:15 concerns witnesses establishing a charge. Luke describes no corresponding legal proceeding.

LUK 2:37.notes: Anna (Hebrew Hannah) + temple-devotion + widow-piety motifs parallel Hannah in 1 Sam 1. Namesake connection reinforces the infancy-narrative's Samuel typology.

LUK 2:38.notes: Anna speaks to those awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem. The allusion to Isaiah 52:9 is thematic in Greek. Isaiah uses verbs for showing mercy and rescuing (ἐλεέω and ῥύομαι), while Luke uses the noun λύτρωσις. The Hebrew of Isaiah uses the language of redeeming Jerusalem.

LUK 2:4.notes: Joseph's Davidic descent + Bethlehem is not cited explicitly; Luke trusts the informed reader to connect with the Messianic birth prophecy.

LUK 2:40.notes: The account of Jesus growing, becoming strong and being filled with wisdom recalls Samuel’s childhood. First Kingdoms 2:21 (1 Samuel) has ἐμεγαλύνθη and ἐνώπιον κυρίου, and 2:26 describes Samuel going on and being good. Luke’s allusion develops the image with his own verbs and the theme of divine favor.

LUK 2:41.notes: Luke says both parents went to Jerusalem for Passover each year. Deuteronomy 16:16 requires males to appear at three festivals including Unleavened Bread. Exodus 12 describes the Passover sacrifice and seven days of unleavened bread.

LUK 2:47.notes: Boy Jesus's understanding (synesis) + wise answers echo Messianic Isa 11:2 'spirit of wisdom and understanding' resting on the Messiah.

LUK 2:49.notes: Jesus's 'my Father' (tou patros mou) at his first recorded words signals unique Sonship awareness — Ps 2:7 'you are my son, today I have begotten you' thematically underlies, though not directly quoted.

LUK 2:52.notes: Luke describes progress in wisdom, stature and favor with God and people. First Samuel 2:26 offers a thematic parallel in Samuel’s development. In Greek Proverbs 3:3–4, grace (χάριν) and the reference to God and people occur in nearby clauses. Luke’s wording is an allusion.

LUK 2:7.notes: firstborn (prōtotokos) motif anticipates the explicit firstborn-consecration at vv.22-23.

LUK 2:8.notes: Migdal Eder (Tower of the Flock) Messianic-shepherd-locale; shepherds near Bethlehem tending Temple flocks is Jewish tradition consistent with this.

LUK 2:9.notes: doxa kyriou = kavod YHWH — theophanic language: Exod 40 tabernacle, Isa 60 returning light. Luke signals incarnational theophany.

LUK 3:1.notes: Prophetic-call chronological-formula: extended dating by multiple rulers echoes OT prophetic-call conventions (Isaiah 6:1 Uzziah; Jeremiah 1:1-3 Josiah-Jehoiakim-Zedekiah; Ezekiel 1:1-3 Jehoiachin-exile year). Luke 3:1-2 seven-ruler catalog launches narrative in classical prophetic style.

LUK 3:11.notes: Share-with-those-in-need ethic of Torah poverty-law: Deut 15:7-11 (open hand to poor brother) + Lev 19:9-10 (gleaning-leave for poor+sojourner). John's concrete ethic of repentance = obedience to Torah neighbor-love. Anticipates early-church community-of-goods (Acts 2:44-45; 4:34-35).

LUK 3:13.notes: Just-weights/honest-measures ethic: Lev 19:35-36 prohibits dishonest weights; Mic 6:11 condemns deceitful scales; Pro 11:1 false-balance-abomination. John rebukes tax-collector extortion within the same prophetic-moral tradition.

LUK 3:14.notes: Just-war ethics (Deut 20) + contentment theology (Prov 30:7-9) converge in John the Baptist's instruction to soldiers. Unique-to-Luke material.

LUK 3:15.notes: Elijah-forerunner expectation (Mal 4:5-6) fuels the crowd's speculation whether John is the Messiah. Unique-to-Luke.

LUK 3:16.notes: Baptism-with-Spirit-and-fire: ISA 4:4 spirit-of-judgment/burning; MAL 3:2-3 refiner's fire; JOL 2:28-29 Spirit outpoured (explicitly fulfilled ACT 2:16-18). Dual-destination polysemy preserves both refining-purification and eschatological-judgment readings. Synoptic parallel MAT 3:11.
